title: Week 1: C for Embedded, STM32F401 Peripherals, and Measurement Habits

Why C for embedded?

Direct hardware access (memory-mapped registers)
Predictable memory layout and execution
No hidden overhead (unlike C++ virtual functions)
Portable across MCU families

title: Week 1: Baseline Firmware, C Programming Review, and Measurement Habits
text:
Pointers: The Foundation
uint32_t value = 0x1234;
uint32_t *ptr = &value;  // ptr holds address of value

*ptr = 0x5678;           // Write through pointer
uint32_t read = *ptr;    // Read through pointer
Key concept: Pointers store addresses, not values.

title: Week 1: Baseline Firmware, C Programming Review, and Measurement Habits
text:
Pointer Arithmetic
uint32_t array[4] = {10, 20, 30, 40};
uint32_t *p = array;     // Points to array[0]

p++;                     // Now points to array[1]
uint32_t val = *p;       // val = 20

p += 2;                  // Now points to array[3]
val = *p;                // val = 40
Important: p++ moves by sizeof(uint32_t) bytes (4 bytes), not 1 byte!

title: Week 1: C for Embedded, STM32F401 Peripherals, and Measurement Habits
text:
Pointers to Registers (Embedded Reality)
// GPIO Port A Output Data Register at address 0x40020014
#define GPIOA_ODR  ((volatile uint32_t*)0x40020014)

*GPIOA_ODR |= (1 << 5);   // Set bit 5 (LED ON)
*GPIOA_ODR &= ~(1 << 5);  // Clear bit 5 (LED OFF)
This is how all peripheral access works under the hood.

Every HAL call eventually reads/writes a memory-mapped register
Unlike a PC (where the OS randomizes addresses every run), MCU registers live at fixed physical addresses defined by the chip manufacturer
0x40020014 is always GPIOA’s output register — on every board, every reset, forever

text:
Timer configuration example
Goal: 1 kHz interrupt (1 ms period)
STM32F401RE: APB1 timer clock = 84 MHz
Prescaler = 8400 - 1  (divide by 8400)
Period = 10 - 1       (count to 10)

Timer freq = 84 MHz / 8400 / 10 = 1 kHz
Verify in CubeMX: Timer update frequency should show 1000 Hz

title: Week 2: Power Input Regulation
text:
Why regulate voltage?
Problem: Raw power sources have variable voltage

Battery: 4.2V (full) → 3.0V (empty)
USB: 4.75V to 5.25V (±5% spec)
Wall adapter: varies with load
Automotive: 9V to 16V (engine cranking to alternator)

Solution: Voltage regulator maintains constant output

title: Week 2: Power Input Regulation
text:
What MCUs need
STM32F401RE requirements:

VDD: 1.7V to 3.6V (typical 3.3V)
Maximum ripple: < 50 mV
Current: 15-100 mA depending on peripherals

Consequences of bad power:

Brown-out resets (voltage dips)
ADC measurement errors
Communication failures (UART, SPI timing)
Random crashes and data corruption

title: Week 2: Power Input Regulation
text:
Power and efficiency


Input power: \[P_{in} = V_{in} \times I_{in}\]
Output power: \[P_{out} = V_{out} \times I_{load}\]
Efficiency: \[\eta = \frac{P_{out}}{P_{in}} \times 100\%\]
Power dissipated in regulator: \[P_{diss} = P_{in} - P_{out}\]

Example: 12V → 3.3V at 200 mA

Power delivered to load: \[P_{out} = 3.3V \times 0.2A = 0.66W\]


Power drawn from source: \[P_{in} = 12V \times 0.2A = 2.4W\]


Power dissipated as heat: \[P_{diss} = 2.4W - 0.66W = 1.74W\]

title: Week 2: Power Input Regulation
text:
The efficiency problem
Example: 12V → 3.3V at 200 mA
For a perfect regulator (100% efficient): \[P_{out} = 3.3V \times 0.2A = 0.66W\]
But where does the extra power go? \[P_{available} = 12V \times 0.2A = 2.4W\] \[P_{wasted} = 2.4W - 0.66W = 1.74W\]
This 1.74W becomes heat!

title: Week 2: Power Input Regulation
text:
Thermal basics





Power flow and heat dissipation



Junction temperature: \[T_j = T_a + (P_{diss} \times \theta_{ja})\]
Where:

\(T_j\) = junction temperature (°C)
\(T_a\) = ambient temperature (°C)
\(\theta_{ja}\) = thermal resistance (°C/W)

title: Week 2: Power Input Regulation
text:
Thermal limit example
AMS1117 thermal resistance: θja = 88°C/W (SOT-223)

Step 1: Calculate power dissipation \[P_{diss} = (12V - 3.3V) \times 0.2A = 1.74W\]


Step 2: Calculate junction temperature (at 25°C ambient) \[T_j = 25°C + (1.74W \times 88°C/W) = 178°C\]



Step 3: Compare to max rating (125°C) → THERMAL FAILURE!

title: Week 2: Power Input Regulation
text:
LDO thermal design
Design question: Can we use AMS1117 for 12V → 3.3V @ 100mA?
Step 1: Calculate power dissipation \[P_{diss} = (12V - 3.3V) \times 0.1A = 0.87W\]
Step 2: Calculate junction temperature \[T_j = 40°C + (0.87W \times 88°C/W) = 117°C\]
Step 3: Compare to maximum (125°C)
Result: Marginal! Works but runs very hot.
Better solution: Add heatsink or use buck converter

title: Week 2: Power Input Regulation
text: Part 3: Switching Regulators (Buck)

title: Week 2: Power Input Regulation
text:
How a buck converter works



Buck converter topology













Key insight: Energy stored in inductor during ON, released during OFF → LC filter smooths output

title: Week 2: Power Input Regulation
text:
Buck converter switching






Result: High-frequency switching (100kHz-1MHz) + LC filter → smooth DC output

title: Week 2: Power Input Regulation
text:
Duty cycle and output voltage
Ideal buck converter (continuous mode): \[V_{out} = D \times V_{in}\]
Where D = duty cycle (0 to 1)
Solving for duty cycle: \[D = \frac{V_{out}}{V_{in}}\]
Example: 12V → 3.3V \[D = \frac{3.3V}{12V} = 0.275 = 27.5\%\]
Switch is ON only 27.5% of the time!

title: Week 2: Power Input Regulation
text:
Why buck is efficient
LDO: Drops 8.7V across pass element continuously \[P_{diss} = 8.7V \times I_{load}\]
Buck: Switch is either ON (low resistance) or OFF (no current)

ON state: Small voltage drop (< 0.5V)
OFF state: Zero current through switch

Real-world efficiency: 80-95% typical

title: Week 2: Power Input Regulation
text:
Buck converter trade-offs
Advantages:

High efficiency (80-95%)
Can step down large voltage differences
Less heat to manage
Higher current capability

Disadvantages:

Output ripple (switching noise)
EMI (electromagnetic interference)
More complex design
Larger footprint (inductor required)
Higher cost

title: Week 2: Power Input Regulation
text:
Output ripple
Buck converters have inherent ripple:



Output voltage ripple


LM2596 typical ripple: 30-100 mV peak-to-peak
Factors affecting ripple:

Output capacitor value and ESR
Inductor value
Load current
Switching frequency

text:
When to use buck converter
Good applications:

Large Vin-Vout difference
Battery-powered systems
High current loads
Efficiency is critical

Consider adding post-regulation:

Buck (high efficiency) → LDO (low noise)
Example: 12V → 5V (buck) → 3.3V (LDO)

text: Part 3.5: Powering the MCU

title: Week 2: Power Input Regulation
text:
From regulator to MCU
The regulator is only half the story!
Getting 3.3V from your regulator doesn’t guarantee clean power at the MCU.
Problems between regulator and MCU:

Wire/trace inductance causes voltage drops during current spikes
High-frequency noise from digital switching
Transient current demands (GPIO toggling, ADC sampling)
Multiple power pins need individual attention

title: Week 2: Power Input Regulation
text:
Why MCUs need decoupling capacitors





Current spikes cause voltage dips



Current spike → Voltage dip

GPIO/ADC/CPU draw 10-100 mA spikes
Wire inductance resists rapid change
\(\Delta V = L \frac{di}{dt}\) causes voltage dip
MCU may reset or malfunction!

Solution: Decoupling capacitors provide local energy storage

title: Week 2: Power Input Regulation
text:
Decoupling capacitor placement





MCU decoupling



Critical rules:

Place capacitor as close as possible to VDD/VSS pins
Short, wide traces (or direct connection)
Each VDD pin needs its own capacitor
Ground return path must be short

title: Week 2: Power Input Regulation
text:
VDDA: Special analog power
VDDA powers sensitive analog circuits:

ADC reference and conversion circuits
PLL (clock generation)
Internal voltage reference

Requirements (from STM32F401 datasheet):

VDDA ≥ VDD (never lower!)
Additional filtering: 1µF + 100nF
Consider ferrite bead for noise isolation

Poor VDDA filtering = noisy ADC readings

title: Week 2: Power Input Regulation
text:
Capacitor selection for decoupling
Why 100nF ceramic?

Low ESR and ESL (parasitic inductance)
Effective at high frequencies (1-100 MHz)
Small size, cheap

Why add bulk capacitor (4.7-10µF)?

Handles longer current transients
Effective at lower frequencies
Supplements regulator output cap

Capacitor type matters:

X7R or X5R ceramic (stable vs temperature)
Avoid Y5V (loses 80% capacitance at voltage)

Reading the datasheet
STM32F401xE Datasheet (DS10086):

Section 6.1.6: “Power supply scheme”

AN4488 — STM32F4xx Hardware Development App Note:

Detailed decoupling guidelines per pin

VDDA: 100nF + 1µF

Always check datasheet for:

Minimum/recommended capacitor values
Special requirements (VDDA, VBAT)

Maximum power consumption per supply

PCB layout guidelines
Power delivery best practices:

Solid ground plane - Low impedance return path

title: Week 3: Signal Conditioning & GPIO Protection
text:
The problem: Signal mismatch
Your sensor outputs 0-10V
Your ADC accepts 0-3.3V

Signal MismatchSolution: Scale the signal down with a voltage divider

title: Week 3: Signal Conditioning & GPIO Protection
text:
Voltage divider fundamentals

Voltage Divider\[V_{out} = V_{in} \times \frac{R2}{R1 + R2}\]

title: Week 3: Signal Conditioning & GPIO Protection
text:
Voltage divider design
Goal: Scale 0-10V sensor to 0-3.3V for ADC
Step 1: Calculate ratio needed
\[\frac{V_{out}}{V_{in}} = \frac{3.3V}{10V} = 0.33\]
Step 2: Choose resistor values
\[\frac{R2}{R1 + R2} = 0.33\]
If R2 = 10kΩ, then R1 = 20kΩ
Verify: \(V_{out} = 10V \times \frac{10k}{20k + 10k} = 3.33V\) ✓

title: Week 3: Signal Conditioning & GPIO Protection
text:
Why resistor values matter
Too low (100Ω + 200Ω):

High current draw from sensor
Wastes power
May overload sensor output

Too high (1MΩ + 2MΩ):

Susceptible to noise pickup
ADC settling error if source impedance too high
Slow response due to stray capacitance

Sweet spot: 1kΩ to 100kΩ range

title: Week 3: Signal Conditioning & GPIO Protection
text:
Input impedance loading
Problem: ADC has finite input impedance

Voltage Divider with ADC LoadingSTM32F401 ADC input impedance: ~50kΩ (varies with sampling time)
R2 in parallel with Zin changes the divider ratio!

title: Week 3: Signal Conditioning & GPIO Protection
text:
Accounting for ADC impedance
Effective R2:
\[R2_{eff} = R2 \parallel Z_{in} = \frac{R2 \times Z_{in}}{R2 + Z_{in}}\]
Example: R2 = 10kΩ, Zin = 50kΩ
\[R2_{eff} = \frac{10k \times 50k}{10k + 50k} = 8.33k\Omega\]
New output: \(V_{out} = 10V \times \frac{8.33k}{20k + 8.33k} = 2.94V\)
Error: 12% low! Use lower resistor values or longer ADC sampling time.

title: Week 3: Signal Conditioning & GPIO Protection
text:
RC low-pass filter
Problem: High-frequency noise on analog signal
Solution: RC filter attenuates frequencies above cutoff

RC Low-Pass Filter\[f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi RC}\]

Where does fc = 1/(2πRC) come from?
This is a voltage divider — but instead of two resistors, we have R and the capacitor’s impedance Z_C.
The capacitor impedance in the frequency domain is:
Z_C = 1 / (jωC)
where ω = 2πf is the angular frequency.
Apply the voltage divider formula with R on top and C on the bottom:
V_out / V_in = Z_C / (R + Z_C) = [1/(jωC)] / [R + 1/(jωC)]
Multiply numerator and denominator by jωC:
V_out / V_in = 1 / (1 + jωRC)
The magnitude (gain) is:
|H(f)| = 1 / √(1 + (ωRC)²)
At the cutoff frequency, gain = 1/√2 ≈ 0.707 (−3 dB). Set the denominator:
1 + (ω_c RC)² = 2 → ω_c RC = 1 → ω_c = 1/RC → f_c = 1/(2πRC)
Physical intuition: At low frequencies the capacitor is essentially open (high impedance), so all of V_in appears across it → V_out ≈ V_in. At high frequencies the capacitor is essentially a short (low impedance), so V_out → 0. The crossover point where |Z_C| = R is exactly f_c.
Note for students: This is the same voltage divider math from the beginning of the lecture — just with a frequency-dependent component replacing R2.

title: Week 3: Signal Conditioning & GPIO Protection
text:
RC filter design
Goal: Filter noise above 100 Hz, pass signal below 10 Hz
Choose cutoff: fc = 50 Hz (between signal and noise)
Choose C: 100nF (common value)
Calculate R:
\[R = \frac{1}{2\pi f_c C} = \frac{1}{2\pi \times 50 \times 100 \times 10^{-9}} = 31.8k\Omega\]
Use: 33kΩ (standard value)

title: Week 3: Signal Conditioning & GPIO Protection
text:
Combined divider + filter


This circuit:

Scales 0-10V → 0-3.3V (voltage divider)
Filters noise above ~240 Hz (R1∥R2 + C form filter)

Cutoff: \(f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi \times R_{th} \times C}\)
\(R_{th} = R1 \| R2 = \frac{20k \times 10k}{20k + 10k} = 6.67\,k\Omega\)
\[f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi \times 6.67k \times 100nF} = 239\text{ Hz}\]




Voltage Divider with RC Filter

text:
Filter response

RC Low-Pass Filter Bode PlotAt cutoff (fc): Signal is -3dB (71% of original)
Above cutoff: -20dB per decade rolloff

title: Week 3: Signal Conditioning & GPIO Protection
text:
ADC sampling considerations
Nyquist theorem: Sample at ≥ 2× highest frequency
With RC filter at 100 Hz:

Maximum signal frequency: 100 Hz
Minimum sample rate: 200 Hz
Recommended sample rate: 500-1000 Hz

STM32 ADC: Can easily achieve > 1 MHz, so no problem

title: Week 3: Signal Conditioning & GPIO Protection
text:
Why protection matters
Your MCU GPIO pins are vulnerable:

Maximum voltage: 3.3V (some 5V tolerant)
Maximum current: ±20 mA typical
ESD rating: 2-4 kV (human body can generate 15 kV!)

One mistake = dead MCU

title: Week 3: Signal Conditioning & GPIO Protection
text:
STM32 internal protection

Internal GPIO Protection DiodesThese diodes protect against small overvoltage (< 0.5V beyond rails)
They are NOT designed to handle sustained current!

title: Week 3: Signal Conditioning & GPIO Protection
text:
When internal protection fails
Overvoltage scenario:

5V applied to 3.3V GPIO
Internal diode conducts to VDD
Current = (5V - 3.6V) / Rsource
If Rsource is low → excessive current → damage

The diodes can handle ~5mA safely, not 50mA!

title: Week 3: Signal Conditioning & GPIO Protection
text:
External protection: Current limiting resistor

GPIO Protection with Series ResistorPurpose: Limit current through internal protection diodes
Example: 5V signal, 1kΩ series resistor
\[I = \frac{5V - 3.6V}{1k\Omega} = 1.4mA\] ✓ Safe!
Rule of thumb: 1kΩ minimum for unknown signals

title: Week 3: Signal Conditioning & GPIO Protection

External clamping diodes

Schottky Clamping DiodesSchottky diodes: Lower forward voltage (~0.3V vs 0.7V)
Clamps signal to: -0.3V to VDD+0.3V

title: Week 3: Signal Conditioning & GPIO Protection
text:
Why Schottky diodes?
Regular diode (1N4148): Vf = 0.7V

Clamps at VDD + 0.7V = 4.0V
MCU sees overvoltage before clamp activates

Schottky (BAT54): Vf = 0.3V

Clamps at VDD + 0.3V = 3.6V
MCU stays within safe range

title: Week 3: Signal Conditioning & GPIO Protection
text:
Zener clamp

Zener Clamp ProtectionZener diode: Conducts when reverse voltage exceeds rating
3.3V Zener: Clamps signal to 3.3V regardless of VDD
Use when: VDD might be absent (power sequencing)

title: Week 3: Signal Conditioning & GPIO Protection
text:
TVS diodes for ESD

TVS ProtectionTVS (Transient Voltage Suppressor):

Very fast response (< 1 ns)
High current capability (> 10A peak)
Designed specifically for ESD events

Common part: PESD5V0S1BL (5V standoff, SOD-523)
Place at every exposed connector — USB, sensor headers, motor connections.

title: Week 4: Motor Control & H-Bridge
text:
Back-EMF explained
When motor spins, it generates voltage:
\[V_{back} = K_v \cdot \omega\]
At steady state (no load):
\[V_{applied} = I \cdot R_m + V_{back}\]
\[V_{back} = V_{applied} - I_0 \cdot R_m = 6V - 0.07A \cdot 7.5\Omega = 5.48V\]
The motor “fights” the applied voltage!

title: Week 4: Motor Control & H-Bridge
text:
Startup current spike

Motor Startup Current ProfileAt t=0: No rotation \(\rightarrow\) No back-EMF \(\rightarrow\) Full stall current
Problem: Power supply and transistors must handle startup surge

title: Week 4: Motor Control & H-Bridge
text:
The inductive kickback problem
When you turn off current through an inductor:
\[V_L = -L \frac{di}{dt}\]
If current drops quickly, voltage spikes HIGH:

100 mA over 1 \(\mu\)s through 10 mH inductor:

\[V_L = -0.01\,\text{H} \cdot \frac{0.1\,\text{A}}{1\,\mu\text{s}} = -1000\,\text{V}\]

The MOSFET drain sees \(V_{DS} = V_{supply} + |V_L| = 6 + 1000 = \boldsymbol{1006}\) V
MOSFET rated for 55 V → destroyed!

title: Week 4: Motor Control & H-Bridge
text:
Why this happens


Switch ON:





flowchart LR
  subgraph "Switch ON"
    V1[Vcc] --> S1[Switch Closed]
    S1 --> M1[Motor]
    M1 --> G1[GND]
  end






Current flows, inductor stores energy: \(E = \frac{1}{2}LI^2\)

Switch OFF:





flowchart LR
  subgraph "Switch OFF"
    V2[Vcc] --> S2[Switch Open]
    M2[Motor] --> SPIKE[⚡ Energy?]
  end






Energy must go somewhere - it arcs across the switch!

text:
MOSFET selection example
Motor: 6V, 800 mA stall current
Requirements:

Id(max) > 800 mA × 1.5 = 1.2A (safety margin)

title: Week 4: Motor Control & H-Bridge
text:
Power dissipation in MOSFET
When MOSFET is fully on:
\[P_{diss} = I_d^2 \times R_{ds(on)}\]
Example: 800 mA through 22 mΩ:
\[P_{diss} = (0.8A)^2 \times 0.022\Omega = 14 mW\]
This is negligible! MOSFET stays cool.
Compare to linear control: Would dissipate \((V_{supply} - V_{motor}) \times I\) = several watts

The shoot-through problem

Shoot-Through Short CircuitIf S1 and S2 both ON (or S3 and S4): Direct short from power to ground!
Prevention: Dead-time between switch transitions

title: Week 4: Motor Control & H-Bridge
text:
Dead-time insertion





Dead-Time Protection




Complementary switching (one leg):
S1 and S2 alternate, but MOSFETs don’t switch instantly.
Dead-time = small gap (100 ns – 1 µs) where both S1 and S2 are OFF, preventing any overlap.
During dead-time, current freewheels through body diodes briefly.
STM32 timers have built-in dead-time generators — set a register value and hardware inserts the gap automatically.

title: Week 4: Motor Control & H-Bridge
text:
High-side switching challenge
Problem: N-channel MOSFETs need Vgs > Vth
For high-side switch: Source is at Vmotor when ON
Gate needs: Vmotor + Vth = higher than supply!
Solutions:

Use P-channel MOSFET (Vgs negative)
Use charge pump/bootstrap circuit
Use gate driver IC
Use integrated motor driver IC (Recommended)

title: Week 4: Motor Control & H-Bridge
text:
Motor driver ICs
Why use a dedicated IC?

Integrated H-bridge with protection
Built-in dead-time
Shoot-through prevention
Thermal shutdown
Current limiting
Logic-level inputs


Building a discrete H-bridge with four MOSFETs requires careful design: you need gate drivers for the high-side switches, dead-time insertion to prevent shoot-through, and protection against overcurrent and overtemperature. A dedicated motor driver IC handles all of this internally. For example, if you forget dead-time in a discrete design, a few nanoseconds of overlap between high-side and low-side switches creates a direct short from supply to ground — the MOSFETs are destroyed instantly. Driver ICs also include thermal shutdown — if the chip overheats due to excessive current, it turns off automatically instead of burning out. For hobbyist and prototyping work, a $2-5 driver module saves hours of debugging and many destroyed components.

title: Week 4: Motor Control & H-Bridge
text: Part 4: PWM Speed Control

title: Week 4: Motor Control & H-Bridge
text:
Why PWM for motors?
Alternative: Variable voltage

Requires linear regulator or DAC
Wastes power as heat
Motor torque drops at low speed

PWM advantage:

MOSFET is either fully ON or fully OFF
Average voltage controls speed
High efficiency (>90%)
Full torque at low speeds


You might ask: why not just lower the voltage to slow the motor down? You could use a linear regulator or a DAC to produce a variable voltage, but that has serious drawbacks. A linear regulator drops the excess voltage across itself as heat — if you want 3V from a 6V supply at 500mA, that’s 1.5W wasted as heat in the regulator. Worse, at lower voltages the motor produces less torque, so it may stall under load.
PWM solves this elegantly. The MOSFET is always either fully on (milliohms of resistance, negligible loss) or fully off (no current, zero loss). The motor sees full supply voltage during the ON pulses, so it gets full torque even at low average speeds. The motor’s own inductance smooths the pulsed current into a nearly steady DC current. You’re essentially trading voltage regulation for time-domain control — and because the switching losses are small, efficiency stays above 90%.

title: Week 5: Sensors & ADC Applications
text:
SAR ADC operation



Successive Approximation Register (STM32 uses this):




SAR ADC block diagram




Binary search algorithm (12 cycles for 12-bit):

Sample/Hold captures input voltage, holds stable
SAR Logic starts with MSB (bit 11 = 2048)
DAC outputs reference voltage for comparison
Comparator: if V_in > V_DAC → bit=1, else bit=0
Repeat for each bit (11→10→…→0)

Example: V_in = 1.65V, V_REF = 3.3V
\[\frac{1.65V}{3.3V} \times 4095 = 2048\]

title: Week 5: Sensors & ADC Applications
text:
SAR conversion process
12-bit conversion in 12 clock cycles:
Step 1: Try 100000000000 (2048) → Compare → Too high? Clear bit
Step 2: Try 010000000000 (1024) → Compare → Too low? Keep bit
Step 3: Try 011000000000 (1536) → Compare → ...
...
Step 12: Final result
Example: Converting 1.65V (with 3.3V reference)

Expected: 1.65V / 3.3V × 4095 ≈ 2048
Binary: 100000000000

Ready → Running: Scheduler picks highest-priority ready task
Running → Ready: Higher-priority task became ready (preemption) or time slice expired
Running → Blocked: Task calls osDelay() or waits on a resource
Blocked → Ready: Delay expired or event arrived — back to ready queue
Suspend / Resume: Manual control, rarely used
Key: Blocked → Running never happens directly — always goes through Ready first (scheduler must decide).
Most tasks spend 90%+ of time in Blocked.

text:
Task creation API (manual)


Native FreeRTOS API:
xTaskCreate(
    LEDTask,        // function
    "LED",          // name
    128,            // stack (words)
    NULL,           // parameter
    2,              // priority
    &ledTaskHandle  // handle
);
CMSIS-RTOS2 wrapper (CubeMX uses this):
const osThreadAttr_t led_attr = {
    .name = "LED",
    .stack_size = 128 * 4, // bytes
    .priority = osPriorityNormal,
};
osThreadNew(LEDTask, NULL, &led_attr);


Key differences:

Native API — stack in words (×4 for bytes)
CMSIS wrapper — stack in bytes, portable across RTOS implementations

Parameters explained:

function — task entry point (infinite loop)
name — string for debugger display
stack — memory for local vars + call chain
parameter — data to pass (usually NULL)
priority — higher number = runs first
handle — pointer to control task later

Use CMSIS-RTOS2 — it’s what CubeMX generates.

title: Week 6: RTOS Foundations
Week 6: RTOS Foundations
text:
Delay functions
osDelay() — relative delay:
osDelay(500);  // "sleep 500ms starting from NOW"

Task moves to Blocked state, other tasks can run
Total period = work time + 500ms → drifts if work time varies


If the task works for 30ms then calls osDelay(500), the actual period is 530ms. The drift accumulates every cycle.

vTaskDelayUntil() — absolute periodic timing:
TickType_t lastWake = xTaskGetTickCount();
for(;;) {
    // Task work here
    vTaskDelayUntil(&lastWake, 500);  // "sleep until next 500ms mark"
}

Compensates for work time automatically → no drift


If the task works for 30ms, it sleeps only 470ms to hit the next 500ms mark exactly. Use this for motor control, sensor sampling, or anything needing consistent timing.

Race conditions are non-deterministic. They may work 999 times and fail on the 1000th. Testing alone cannot prove their absence — use queues or mutexes.

Communication vs Synchronization

  Semaphore

  
  
  1010

  This week: Queues + Mutexes



Let me explain each of these four mechanisms.
A queue is like a mailbox between tasks. One task puts data in, another takes data out, in first-in-first-out order. The key point is that queues actually transfer data — they copy bytes from the sender to the receiver. If the queue is full, the sender can wait. If it’s empty, the receiver can wait. This is how you safely pass sensor readings, commands, or any data between tasks without shared variables.
A mutex — short for mutual exclusion — is like a bathroom key. Only one task can hold it at a time. If Task A holds the mutex and Task B tries to acquire it, Task B blocks until Task A releases it. You use this when multiple tasks need to access the same resource, like UART or a display. Without it, two tasks printing simultaneously produce garbled output.
A semaphore is like a traffic light. It signals that something happened. The classic use case is an ISR signaling a task: the ISR “gives” the semaphore, the task “takes” it. Unlike a mutex, a semaphore can be given by one context and taken by another — so it works for ISR-to-task signaling where mutexes cannot be used.
Event flags let a task wait for multiple conditions at once — for example, “wait until both the sensor is ready AND the network is connected.” Each bit in a flag group represents one event.
This week we focus on queues and mutexes. Semaphores and event flags come in a future week.

How large? Enough to hold data while the consumer can’t keep up (busy processing, preempted by higher-priority task, etc.).

section: Clock Sources (Where Does 84 MHz Come From?)
text:
Clock Sources (Where Does 84 MHz Come From?)






Clock Sources on STM32


The Nucleo board clock options:

HSI (High-Speed Internal): 16 MHz RC oscillator, ±1% accuracy - default
HSE (High-Speed External): 8 MHz clock signal from ST-LINK’s MCO pin (X3 crystal slot is empty!)
LSE (Low-Speed External): 32.768 kHz crystal (X2) for RTC

The PLL multiplies HSI or HSE to 84 MHz for the CPU and peripherals.
For this course: HSI is sufficient for UART and timers. For custom PCB designs requiring better accuracy, you’d add a crystal with load capacitors at X3 - that’s a hardware design topic beyond our scope.
CubeMX default: Uses HSI with PLL. Check Clock Configuration tab to see the full clock tree.

title: Week 8: I2C Protocol & IMU Application
text:
Week 8
I2C Protocol & IMU Application

Welcome students. Tell them this is the week where embedded work starts to feel “real”: we move from static GPIO and PWM to a protocol that connects the microcontroller to intelligent sensors. By the end they will have read motion data from an MPU6050 over a two-wire bus, which is the same protocol used in phones, game controllers, and automotive sensors.

title: Week 8: I2C Protocol & IMU Application
text:
Why this week matters

I2C is the most common sensor interface in embedded systems
Found in nearly every device: phones, laptops, appliances, vehicles
IMUs (Inertial Measurement Units) enable motion-aware applications
Understanding both gives you tools for real-world sensor integration
Debugging protocols requires understanding the physical layer


Emphasise that I2C is not academic trivia — any datasheet they read for the rest of their career will likely assume they know it. Mention that protocol bugs are the #1 reason student projects fail in the lab, and that the skills we build here (oscilloscope captures, pull-up math, ACK/NACK reasoning) transfer directly to SPI, UART, and CAN in later weeks.

title: Week 8: I2C Protocol & IMU Application
text:
Learning objectives

Explain I2C bus architecture and transaction protocol
Calculate appropriate pull-up resistor values for a given bus
Configure STM32 I2C peripheral using CubeIDE
Interface with MPU6050 IMU and interpret sensor data
Convert raw sensor readings to physical units
Capture and decode I2C waveforms using an oscilloscope (logic analyzer optional)
Diagnose common I2C communication failures


Walk through each bullet and tell students which ones map to exam questions versus which map to lab deliverables. The calculation objective (pull-up sizing) and the diagnostic one (decoding an oscilloscope capture) are the two most likely exam targets. Interfacing and data conversion are assessed in the lab.

title: Week 8: I2C Protocol & IMU Application
text:
Agenda (90 minutes)
Part 1: I2C Protocol Fundamentals (25 min)

Bus architecture and signals

Addressing and acknowledgment

Part 2: I2C Hardware Design (20 min)

Part 3: IMU Fundamentals (20 min)

Part 4: MPU6050 Interface (15 min)

Data conversion

Part 5: Protocol Debugging (10 min)

Interpreting captures
Lab preview


Promise a tight schedule: Parts 1 and 2 are theory-heavy (protocol and hardware), Part 3 is a short detour into sensor physics because otherwise the register names in Part 4 are meaningless, and Part 5 is short but often skipped in textbooks — we cover it because it is what students will actually do in the lab.

title: Week 8: I2C Protocol & IMU Application
text: Part 1: I2C Protocol Fundamentals

title: Week 8: I2C Protocol & IMU Application
text:
What is I2C?
Inter-Integrated Circuit (Philips/NXP, 1982)

I2C bus topology
I2C was invented at Philips in 1982 to let a TV’s microcontroller talk to tuners, volume pots, and EEPROMs with just two wires instead of a huge parallel bus. The name pronunciation varies (“I-squared-C” or “I-two-C”); both are accepted. Point out the bus topology: one master clocking the bus, many slaves hanging off the same two wires — this is the key mental model for the rest of the lecture.

title: Week 8: I2C Protocol & IMU Application
text:
I2C key characteristics



Feature
Description




Wires
2 (SDA + SCL) + ground


Topology
Multi-drop bus


Addressing
7-bit (128 devices) or 10-bit (1024 devices)


Direction
Half-duplex (bidirectional on SDA)


Speed modes
Standard (100 kHz), Fast (400 kHz), Fast+ (1 MHz)


Driver type
Open-drain with external pull-ups




Walk the table row by row. Two wires plus ground is the headline — compare with SPI’s four wires. The 7-bit address space of 128 is rarely exhausted in practice; chip vendors reuse addresses, which is why you will sometimes see two modules on the same bus refuse to coexist. For breadboard work in this course we will stay at 100 kHz Standard mode.

title: Week 8: I2C Protocol & IMU Application
text:
Open-drain signaling





Push-pull vs Open-drain



Why open-drain?

Multiple devices share wire
Any device can pull LOW
No bus contention
Pull-up returns to HIGH



This is the single most important electrical concept of the week. In a push-pull output (left), if two devices drive opposite levels, VCC shorts to ground through the transistors — fire and brimstone. Open-drain (right) only has a pull-down transistor; nobody can drive HIGH, so there is no conflict. The pull-up resistor restores HIGH when everyone releases the line. This is called a “wired-AND”: the bus is HIGH only when all drivers release it. Make sure students understand this before moving on, because every later concept (ACK, clock stretching, bus arbitration) relies on it.

title: Week 8: I2C Protocol & IMU Application
text:
I2C signal definitions
SDA (Serial Data): Bidirectional data line
SCL (Serial Clock): Clock generated by master

I2C data sampling timingRules:

Data must be stable when SCL is HIGH
Data can only change when SCL is LOW
Exception: START and STOP conditions


The two rules on this slide are the entire I2C data protocol in a nutshell. Data is allowed to change only while SCL is LOW — this creates a clean “setup” window. When SCL rises, whatever SDA is at that instant is what the receiver latches. START and STOP are the only times SDA is allowed to move while SCL is HIGH, which is exactly what makes them unambiguous framing markers. Point to the diagram and trace one bit period: LOW phase → transition → HIGH phase → sample.

title: Week 8: I2C Protocol & IMU Application
text:
START and STOP conditions
START: SDA falls while SCL is HIGH
STOP: SDA rises while SCL is HIGH

I2C START and STOP conditionsRepeated START: START without preceding STOP

Used to change direction (write → read)
Keeps bus ownership (no arbitration)


START and STOP are the only events where SDA changes while SCL is HIGH — that violation is exactly the signal the protocol uses as framing. Repeated START is a common source of confusion: it looks like the master is starting again, but logically it is one long transaction split in two halves. MPU6050 reads use repeated START to switch from “write register pointer” to “read data” without releasing the bus, so other masters cannot cut in. We will see this pattern in the write and read transaction diagrams coming up.

title: Week 8: I2C Protocol & IMU Application
text:
I2C byte format
Every byte is 8 bits + 1 ACK/NACK bit:

  7
  6
  5
  4
  3
  2
  1
  0
  ACK
  MSB first
  9th clock

ACK (Acknowledge): Receiver pulls SDA LOW
NACK (Not Acknowledge): Receiver leaves SDA HIGH

I2C byte format with ACK
Every byte on the bus is actually 9 clock cycles: 8 for the data bits (MSB first, unlike SPI which can be either) and 1 for the acknowledgment. The ACK bit is where the receiver gets the chance to say “yes, I got it” by pulling SDA LOW during the 9th clock. If nothing pulls the line down, the pull-up keeps it HIGH, which the master interprets as NACK — “nobody is there, or the receiver refused.” Students often miss the fact that ACK is not a separate byte, it is one clock pulse at the end of every byte.

title: Week 8: I2C Protocol & IMU Application
text:
Address byte format
First byte after START contains address + R/W bit:

  A6
  A5
  A4
  A3
  A2
  A1
  A0
  R/W
  ACK
  
  
  7-bit address
  
  0 = Write
  1 = Read

Example: MPU6050 address 0x68



Operation
Address byte
Binary




Write to 0x68
0xD0
1101 0000


Read from 0x68
0xD1
1101 0001



Note: STM32 HAL expects the 7-bit address already shifted left (addr << 1); HAL then sets the R/W LSB itself based on Read vs Write.
#define MPU6050_ADDR  0x68                       // 7-bit address from datasheet
HAL_I2C_Mem_Write(..., MPU6050_ADDR << 1, ...);  // → 0xD0 on the wire
HAL_I2C_Mem_Read (..., MPU6050_ADDR << 1, ...);  // → 0xD1 on the wire

This is the classic gotcha. Datasheets print 7-bit addresses (0x68 for MPU6050), but the byte that actually goes on the wire is 8 bits because the R/W flag rides in the LSB. Libraries differ on who does the shift: some take the 7-bit value and shift it for you, others expect you to hand them the already-shifted byte. STM32 HAL is in the second camp — you must pass ADDR << 1, and HAL then flips the LSB to 0 for write or 1 for read based on which function you called. If a student’s I2C scanner shows a device at 0x34 instead of 0x68, the forgotten shift is almost always the cause.

I2C write transactionSTART → Address+W → Register → Data → STOP (slave ACKs each byte)

Point out the three ACKs: one after the address to confirm “I am here”, one after the register pointer to confirm “I understood you want to talk about register X”, and one after the data byte to confirm “I stored the value.” If any of these ACKs is missing in a real capture, you know exactly where the conversation broke down — that is the debugging superpower you get from understanding this diagram.

A read is really a “write-then-read”. The write half tells the slave which register pointer to use (WHO_AM_I = 0x75 in this example), and the read half pulls that register’s contents back. For the MPU6050 we read a 14-byte block that contains a complete, atomic snapshot of all three accel axes, temperature, and all three gyro axes — critical, because if you read them one at a time they would be from slightly different moments in time and the sensor fusion math would drift.

text: Part 2: I2C Hardware Design

title: Week 8: I2C Protocol & IMU Application
text:
Why pull-up resistors?





Pull-up resistor effect



Open-drain problem:

Transistor can only pull LOW
When released → line floats!

Solution: Pull-up resistor

Pulls line to VCC when idle
Size affects speed & power



Show students the waveform comparison: without pull-ups the released line just floats and picks up noise — the receiver sees garbage. With a pull-up it snaps back to VCC cleanly. The pull-up is not optional, it is part of the protocol. Many sensor modules ship with onboard 4.7 kΩ pull-ups soldered on the breakout board, which is why students sometimes get away without adding their own — but they should still know how to size them from first principles.

title: Week 8: I2C Protocol & IMU Application
text:
Pull-up resistor calculation
Two constraints:


1. Minimum resistance (current limit):
\[R_{min} = \frac{V_{CC} - V_{OL(max)}}{I_{OL}}\]

\(V_{OL(max)}\) = 0.4V typical
\(I_{OL}\) = 3 mA typical

\[R_{min} = \frac{3.3V - 0.4V}{3mA} = 967\Omega\]

2. Maximum resistance (rise time):
\[R_{max} = \frac{t_r}{0.8473 \times C_b}\]

\(t_r\) = 1000 ns (100 kHz), 300 ns (400 kHz)
\(C_b\) = Bus capacitance
\(0.8473 = \ln(7/3)\) — from 30 %–70 % rise time of an RC exponential (I²C spec)

\[R_{max} = \frac{1000ns}{0.8473 \times 50pF} = 23.6k\Omega\]


The pull-up value is squeezed between two limits. Lower bound: the resistor must be big enough that the output transistor can pull the line below VOL with its rated sink current (usually 3 mA). Upper bound: the resistor must be small enough that, together with bus capacitance, the RC rise time fits inside the spec. Students should see that “bigger is slower, smaller is hotter” and that 4.7 kΩ sits in the comfortable middle for 100 kHz breadboard work. The 0.8473 factor comes from 30%-70% rise time of an exponential, which is the I2C spec.

For 100 kHz with 50 pF: \(R_{max} = \frac{1000ns}{0.8473 \times 50pF} = 23.6k\Omega\)

Capacitance is usually the “unknown unknown” on a breadboard. Every jumper, every breadboard row, every device input pin adds a few picofarads, and they all add up. A typical short breadboard setup is around 50 pF; a sprawl of long jumper wires can easily hit 150 pF. The calculation shows that at 50 pF we have a lot of headroom, but as the wiring gets longer the maximum pull-up value shrinks fast. If a student’s signal has slow, rounded rise times, the first question is “how long are your wires?”

    100);                 // Timeout ms

    100);                 // Timeout ms

Return values:



Value
Meaning




HAL_OK
Success


HAL_ERROR

HAL_BUSY
Bus busy


HAL_TIMEOUT
Timeout elapsed



Key point: You must pass the 7-bit address shifted left by 1 (addr << 1). HAL then fills in the R/W bit automatically based on Read vs Write.
#define MPU6050_ADDR 0x68             // 7-bit address from datasheet
HAL_I2C_Mem_Write(..., MPU6050_ADDR << 1, ...);  // sends 0xD0 on the wire
HAL_I2C_Mem_Read (..., MPU6050_ADDR << 1, ...);  // sends 0xD1 on the wire


HAL_I2C_Mem_Read and Mem_Write are the two functions students will use 95% of the time — they wrap up the “set register pointer, then transfer data” pattern from the read transaction diagram into a single call. The I2C_MEMADD_SIZE_8BIT argument matters: the MPU6050 uses single-byte register addresses, but some EEPROMs use 16-bit addresses. The return value discipline is important: always check HAL_OK, and if you get HAL_BUSY the HAL has checked the bus and found that either SDA or SCL is still LOW when it expects an idle bus — almost always because SDA is being clamped LOW by a slave that crashed mid-transaction (classic bus lockup), or less commonly because SCL is stuck LOW from a hung clock-stretching slave. The recovery is to toggle SCL nine extra times by hand to unstick the slave, then retry.

title: Week 8: I2C Protocol & IMU Application
text: Part 3: IMU Fundamentals

title: Week 8: I2C Protocol & IMU Application
text:
What is an IMU?

IMU structureInertial Measurement Unit — measures motion without external reference

Switch gears — we are done with the protocol, now we need to understand what is on the other end of the wire. “Inertial” means it measures motion using inertia, not external references like GPS or cameras. A typical IMU combines an accelerometer, a gyroscope, and sometimes a magnetometer; the MPU6050 has the first two. The whole reason people use IMUs is that they work anywhere, they work in the dark, and they are cheap.

title: Week 8: I2C Protocol & IMU Application
text:
MEMS accelerometer principle





MEMS accelerometer



Micro-Electro-Mechanical System

Proof mass on springs
Capacitance changes with displacement
At rest: measures gravity (1g down)



A MEMS accelerometer is a tiny silicon spring-mass system etched into the chip. When the chip accelerates, the mass lags behind and deflects the springs; capacitive pickoff plates detect the deflection and convert it to voltage. Point out the counterintuitive result: at rest on a desk, the accelerometer is NOT reading zero — it reads 1 g on the Z axis, because gravity is pulling the mass downward against the spring exactly as if the sensor were accelerating upward at 1 g. This is the equivalence principle that Einstein made famous, and it is baked into every accelerometer reading.

title: Week 8: I2C Protocol & IMU Application
text:
Accelerometer axes and gravity





Accelerometer axes



Pitch — rotation about the \(y\) axis (nose up / down)
Roll — rotation about the \(x\) axis (wing up / down)
Tilt from gravity vector:
\(\theta_{pitch} = \arctan\dfrac{A_x}{\sqrt{A_y^2 + A_z^2}}\)
\(\theta_{roll} = \arctan\dfrac{A_y}{\sqrt{A_x^2 + A_z^2}}\)


Because gravity is always pointing down in the world frame, we can use the accelerometer as a tilt sensor. Rotate the chip and the gravity vector projects differently onto the three body-frame axes; the atan2 formulas recover pitch and roll. This only works when the device is stationary or moving slowly — any real acceleration (shake, throw, drive) contaminates the gravity reading, which is why we later add the gyro. Quick demo idea: lay the board flat, ask students what they expect Az to be; tilt it 90°, ask again.

title: Week 8: I2C Protocol & IMU Application
text:
Accelerometer limitations





Gravity vs acceleration



Problems:

Can’t distinguish gravity from acceleration
High-frequency noise from vibration
Can’t measure yaw rotation

title: Week 8: I2C Protocol & IMU Application
text:
MEMS gyroscope principle





MEMS gyroscope



Coriolis effect:

Vibrating mass deflects when rotated
Measures angular velocity (°/s)
Zero when stationary (ideally)



A MEMS gyro uses the Coriolis effect: a small mass is kept vibrating back and forth, and when the chip rotates, the Coriolis force deflects the mass perpendicular to its vibration direction. That deflection is picked off capacitively, just like the accelerometer. The key output is angular velocity in degrees per second, not an angle — if you want an angle you have to integrate, and integration accumulates error (drift). That drift is exactly why we pair the gyro with the accelerometer.

title: Week 8: I2C Protocol & IMU Application
text:
Gyroscope characteristics





Gyroscope drift



Strengths:

Fast response, direct rotation measurement

Weaknesses:

Bias (non-zero at rest)
Drift accumulates over time

title: Week 8: I2C Protocol & IMU Application
text:
Accelerometer vs gyroscope summary



Property
Accelerometer
Gyroscope




Measures
Linear acceleration + gravity
Angular velocity


At rest
Shows gravity (~1g)
Should be ~0 (has bias)


Units
g or m/s²
°/s or rad/s


Noise
High frequency
Drift over time


Best for
Static tilt, detecting motion
Fast rotation tracking


Limitation
Can’t separate gravity/accel
Drift accumulates




Frame this slide as “two sensors with opposite weaknesses.” This table is the single most important page of the IMU section — if students remember nothing else, they should remember why we need both sensors.
What each sensor actually measures. The accelerometer measures proper acceleration — the sum of linear motion and the reaction force holding the chip up against gravity. That is why at rest on a desk it reads 1 g on Z, not zero: gravity is pulling the proof mass down, and the springs push back exactly as hard. The gyroscope measures angular velocity directly via the Coriolis force on a vibrating mass; it says nothing about linear motion and nothing about absolute orientation — only “how fast am I rotating right now.”
Frequency-domain intuition. The accelerometer is trustworthy at low frequencies (slow tilts, stationary reference) but terrible at high frequencies because every vibration, bump, or hand tremor shows up as noise. The gyroscope is the exact opposite: trustworthy at high frequencies (sub-second rotations tracked cleanly) but its integrated angle drifts over seconds to minutes as tiny bias errors accumulate. This is why the complementary filter passes the accelerometer through a low-pass and the gyro through a high-pass — they are literally designed to cover opposite halves of the spectrum.
Concrete numbers. A typical MPU6050 gyro has a bias of around 0.1–1 °/s after factory calibration. Integrate that for one minute of standing still and your yaw estimate has already drifted 6–60°. Meanwhile, a stationary accelerometer’s tilt estimate is noisy bit by bit but has zero long-term drift — average it long enough and it converges to the true tilt within fractions of a degree.
Degrees of freedom. The accelerometer cannot see yaw (rotation about the gravity vector) at all, because rotating around vertical does not change the gravity projection. The gyroscope can see yaw but cannot tell you which way is up — it only knows changes. Together they give you roll and pitch (absolute, from gravity) plus yaw-rate (from the gyro), which is five of six degrees of freedom. For absolute yaw you need a magnetometer, which is why 9-DOF IMUs exist.
Teaching anchors. Three real-world analogies that land well: - A carpenter’s level (accelerometer) — absolute tilt reference, but useless if you shake it. - A spinning top (gyroscope) — smooth short-term rotation tracking, but it slowly precesses and drifts. - GPS + dead reckoning in a car — GPS is noisy but absolute (like the accel), dead reckoning is smooth but drifts (like the gyro); combining both gives a stable position estimate. The I2C week is where students first meet this fusion pattern, and it comes back repeatedly in robotics, drones, and navigation.
Common student confusions to pre-empt. 1. “Why doesn’t the accelerometer read zero when I hold the board still?” → because of gravity; the chip cannot tell a 1 g upward acceleration apart from sitting still in Earth’s gravity (Einstein’s equivalence principle). 2. “Can I just integrate the accelerometer twice to get position?” → no, the noise and gravity make double-integration diverge in seconds. This is why inertial-only dead reckoning is a hard problem. 3. “Why do I read nonzero gyro values when I am holding the board perfectly still?” → that is bias, and you usually calibrate it out at startup by averaging a few hundred samples while the device is stationary.
Encourage the students to hold the board flat, tilt it, and spin it while they watch the accel and gyro values; the “which sensor responds to which motion” instinct is what this table is trying to build.

title: Week 8: I2C Protocol & IMU Application
text:
Why sensor fusion?





Sensor fusion



Complementary filter:
\(\theta = \alpha(\theta + \omega \cdot dt) + (1-\alpha)\theta_{accel}\)

\(\alpha \approx 0.98\)
Trust gyro short-term
Trust accel long-term



This slide is where the previous “accel vs gyro” table pays off — we now actually combine them into something useful. Take the time to walk through the equation term by term rather than just reading it off the slide.
Why fusion is necessary. Repeat the two failure modes students just saw: the accelerometer gives you absolute tilt but is noisy and confused by motion; the gyroscope is smooth and fast but drifts without bound. Either one on its own produces a useless orientation estimate after a few seconds. Fusion is not a nice-to-have — it is the only way to get a stable angle from a cheap 6-axis IMU.
Reading the complementary filter equation. Write θ on the board and break the right-hand side into its two pieces. - The first term, α · (θ + ω·dt), is the prediction step: take the previous angle estimate and advance it by how far the gyro says we just rotated during this time step. This is essentially dead reckoning with the gyro. - The second term, (1 − α) · θ_accel, is the correction step: the accelerometer’s current best guess at the true tilt from the gravity vector. It pulls the estimate back toward reality whenever the device is approximately stationary. - α blends the two. With α = 0.98 and a 10 ms loop, the filter trusts the gyro almost completely for fast motions but leaks 2 % of the accelerometer truth back in every cycle, which is enough to cancel gyro drift over seconds.
What α actually does — pick a number and show the effect. Walk through extremes so students build intuition: - α = 1.0: pure gyro integration → smooth, but drifts forever. Show the yaw angle wandering away from zero while the board sits still. - α = 0.0: pure accelerometer → no drift, but every hand tremor and footstep shows up as a jitter on the angle. Show the plot bouncing around. - α ≈ 0.98: the compromise. Gyro handles the fast motion cleanly and the accelerometer slowly corrects the drift. Not perfect, but very usable. The choice of α is a low-pass filter cutoff in disguise: τ = (α · dt) / (1 − α). For α = 0.98 and dt = 10 ms, τ ≈ 0.5 s, meaning the filter “forgets” the gyro integration error with a half-second time constant.
Frequency-domain framing (for stronger students). The complementary filter is literally a high-pass on the gyro plus a low-pass on the accelerometer, summed together, and the two filters are designed so their magnitude responses add to exactly 1.0 — hence “complementary.” This is why the gyro’s high-frequency detail comes through unattenuated while its low-frequency drift is blocked, and the accelerometer’s slow truth gets through while its high-frequency noise is suppressed.
Why we are not using a Kalman filter. A Kalman filter does the same job but dynamically adjusts the equivalent of α based on how much it trusts each sensor at this instant (e.g., reduce accelerometer weight during vigorous motion). It is strictly better but much more math to implement, and the tuning is harder. For teaching, the complementary filter gets students 90 % of the benefit with 5 % of the code. Kalman filters come back in EE0919 / the final project Track C.
Practical gotchas when students try this themselves. 1. Compute θ_accel with atan2, not asin — atan2 handles all four quadrants and never divides by zero. 2. Watch your units: the gyro gives °/s, so ω · dt must have dt in seconds. 3. The filter update must run at a consistent rate (e.g., from a timer interrupt) — if dt jitters, the integration drifts faster. 4. Calibrate the gyro bias at startup: average 200–500 samples while the device is stationary and subtract that from every subsequent reading.
What the lab will and will not ask students to do. In this week’s lab they will only read and print the raw accel/gyro values and the converted units — no fusion. The reason we still teach fusion here is so the lab’s raw numbers make sense in context: they can see the drift of the gyro and the noise of the accelerometer with their own eyes, and they understand why neither is the whole answer. Students who pick the final-project Track C will implement this equation for real.

The MPU6050 is the classic 6-axis IMU — it is ancient by chip standards (2012) but it is still the go-to for teaching because it is cheap, well-documented, and has a huge ecosystem. text:
Summary

This is the section divider before the recap. Pause here for questions; the five-part structure is complete and this is a natural breakpoint. If students look lost on any particular topic, loop back now rather than pushing through the takeaways.

title: Week 8: I2C Protocol & IMU Application
text:
Key takeaways

I2C is a 2-wire protocol with addressing and ACK/NACK handshaking
Open-drain signaling requires pull-up resistors (4.7 kΩ typical)
Pull-up sizing depends on bus capacitance and speed
MPU6050 provides 6-axis motion sensing over I2C
Accelerometer measures linear acceleration + gravity
Gyroscope measures angular velocity (rotation rate)
Sensor fusion combines both for robust orientation
Oscilloscope captures are essential; a logic analyzer is optional


Walk the list briefly. The exam will pick two or three of these as concept questions. The single most testable item is pull-up sizing — given a bus capacitance and speed, compute Rmin and Rmax. Second most likely is interpreting a byte format diagram. The IMU side is mostly assessed in the lab, not on exams.

title: Week 8: I2C Protocol & IMU Application
text:
Connection to other weeks
Builds on:

Week 5 (Sensors): IMU is a digital sensor vs analog
Week 6-7 (RTOS): Sensor reading in tasks

Leads to:

Week 10 (DMA + SPI): SPI protocol, DMA for high-speed transfers
Final project Track C: IMU sensor fusion


Remind students that the I2C skills from this week come back in Week 10 when we introduce SPI — SPI is faster but follows the same “master clocks the bus, addresses a slave, transfers bytes” pattern, so understanding I2C first makes SPI easy. Also point out that Track C of the final project uses exactly the MPU6050 code they write in the lab, so this lab is not throwaway work.

title: Week 2: Power Input Regulation
text:
Buck converter waveforms





Inductor current (linear): \[\frac{di_L}{dt} = \begin{cases} \frac{V_{in} - V_{out}}{L} & \text{ON} \\ \frac{-V_{out}}{L} & \text{OFF} \end{cases}\]
Output voltage (smooth): \[V_{out} = V_C + ESR \cdot i_C\]
Capacitor ESR causes sawtooth ripple: \[\Delta V_{out} \approx \Delta I_L \times ESR\]



This plot is a real simulation of the LM2596 buck converter using differential equations, not an idealized sketch.
Top plot — Inductor current (green): The green shaded regions are the ON phase, blue shaded regions are the OFF phase. During ON, current ramps up linearly because (Vin - Vout) / L is constant and positive. During OFF, current ramps down linearly because -Vout / L is constant and negative. The result is a triangular sawtooth waveform. The dashed gray line shows the average current which equals the load current (about 500mA for a 6.6 ohm load). The red annotation shows the peak-to-peak current ripple (delta-I), which depends on L, Vin, Vout, and switching frequency. A larger inductor means smaller current ripple.
Bottom plot — Output voltage (blue): The output voltage looks almost flat compared to the inductor current — that is the whole point of the LC filter. The ripple you see here is much smaller (in millivolts) and comes from two sources: (1) the capacitor charging and discharging as inductor current varies above and below the load current, and (2) the capacitor ESR — when current flows through the ESR, it creates a voltage drop proportional to the current. The ESR component creates the sharp sawtooth shape you see in the ripple, while the capacitance component creates a smoother triangle. For electrolytic capacitors, ESR dominates the ripple, which is why the formula delta-V approximately equals delta-I times ESR is a good estimate. With a 220µF electrolytic cap at 100 milliohm ESR, we get roughly a few millivolts of ripple — well within the STM32’s 50mV tolerance.

text:
CMSIS: Registers as a Struct
CMSIS = Cortex Microcontroller Software Interface Standard (defined by ARM)
typedef struct {
    __IO uint32_t MODER;    // offset 0x00 — Mode register
    __IO uint32_t OTYPER;   // offset 0x04 — Output type
    __IO uint32_t OSPEEDR;  // offset 0x08 — Output speed
    __IO uint32_t PUPDR;    // offset 0x0C — Pull-up/pull-down
    __IO uint32_t IDR;      // offset 0x10 — Input data (read-only)
    __IO uint32_t ODR;      // offset 0x14 — Output data
    // ... BSRR, LCKR, AFR[2]
} GPIO_TypeDef;

#define GPIOA ((GPIO_TypeDef *) 0x40020000)
GPIOA->ODR = read 32-bit value at address 0x40020000 + 0x14 = 0x40020014
This is exactly what the datasheet register map shows!

Accounting for ADC source impedance
Effective R2: (R2 in parallel with max source impedance)
\[R2_{eff} = R2 \parallel R_{source,max} = \frac{R2 \times R_{source,max}}{R2 + R_{source,max}}\]
Example: R2 = 10kΩ, Rsource,max = 50kΩ (at 84 sampling cycles)
\[R2_{eff} = \frac{10k \times 50k}{10k + 50k} = 8.33k\Omega\]
New output: \(V_{out} = 10V \times \frac{8.33k}{20k + 8.33k} = 2.94V\)
Error: 12% low! Use lower resistor values or longer ADC sampling time.

title: Week 3: Signal Conditioning & GPIO Protection
text:
ADC settling error
Problem: The ADC doesn’t see your voltage instantly — it samples through an internal RC circuit.



During sampling, internal CADC charges through RADC + your source resistance (RAIN).
If RAIN is too high, CADC doesn’t fully settle → voltage reads low.

title: Week 3: Signal Conditioning & GPIO Protection
text:
What is RAIN?
RAIN is the impedance your circuit presents to the ADC pin — i.e., the Thévenin output resistance.

Voltage Divider with ADC LoadingFor a voltage divider: \(R_{AIN} = R1 \parallel R2 = \frac{R1 \times R2}{R1 + R2}\)
Example: R1 = 20kΩ, R2 = 10kΩ → RAIN = 6.67 kΩ
DS10086 §6.3.19: RAIN ≤ 50 kΩ for accuracy specs to hold.

title: Week 3: Signal Conditioning & GPIO Protection
text:
Why high RAIN causes error
Settling time constant: \(\tau = (R_{AIN} + R_{ADC}) \times C_{ADC}\)
For ½ LSB accuracy (12-bit), CADC needs ~14τ to settle.
Example with R1 = 200kΩ, R2 = 100kΩ (RAIN = 66.7kΩ):

τ ≈ (66.7kΩ + 6kΩ) × 4pF ≈ 291 ns
Needs ~4 µs to settle → requires 84+ sampling cycles

With only 3 sampling cycles (143 ns), CADC barely charges → voltage reads 10-15% low, as if a resistive load were pulling R2 down.

title: Week 3: Signal Conditioning & GPIO Protection
text:
Why do GPIO pins die?
Your MCU pins connect directly to silicon — there is no built-in margin for abuse.








Danger
Source
What happens




Overvoltage
5V/12V sensor on 3.3V pin
Latchup → thermal destruction


Overcurrent
Short to GND/VDD, LED without R
Bond wire fuse → open pin


ESD
Touch, cable connect, ungrounded tool
Gate oxide punch-through → instant death




One lab accident can kill a pin permanently — and the MCU won’t tell you.
Protection starts with knowing what your pins can tolerate →

Latchup: CMOS chips have parasitic PNPN structures (like an SCR/thyristor) formed by the P-substrate, N-well, and diffusion regions. If you inject enough current into a pin (e.g., overvoltage forcing current through an internal diode), this parasitic SCR can turn on and create a low-impedance path from VDD to GND. Once triggered, it stays latched even after the stimulus is removed — the only way to stop it is to power-cycle the chip. While latched, the chip draws excessive current and can thermally destroy itself in seconds.
Bond wire fuse: Each pin on the silicon die is connected to the package pin by a thin gold or copper wire (25-50 µm). This bond wire can only carry so much current — typically well above the 25 mA GPIO spec, but a hard short to GND or VDD can push hundreds of mA through it. The wire heats up and literally melts open like a fuse, permanently disconnecting the pin. The MCU keeps running but that pin is dead forever.
Gate oxide punch-through (ESD): The MOSFET gate oxide in modern processes is only a few nanometers thick. It takes very little voltage (sometimes as low as 5-10V across the oxide) to break through it. An ESD event can deliver thousands of volts in nanoseconds — far too fast for clamp diodes to fully react. The oxide ruptures, creating a permanent short or leakage path. The pin may seem to work intermittently or just fail silently.

title: Week 3: Signal Conditioning & GPIO Protection
section: When does settling error actually appear?
text:
When does settling error actually appear?
Single channel, DC — error is invisible:
CADC retains its charge between conversions. On repeated reads of the same channel at the same voltage, the capacitor is already at the correct level — even 3 cycles is enough.
After a channel switch — error becomes visible:
When scanning multiple channels, CADC is left at the previous channel’s voltage. The next channel must charge CADC across the full difference through RAIN in one sampling window.



Scenario
3 cycles + 66.7kΩ
480 cycles + 66.7kΩ




Single channel, DC
✓ Accurate
✓ Accurate


Read 0V channel, then divider
✗ Reads low
✓ Settles correctly



This is the real-world case: multi-channel ADC scanning (e.g., reading a temperature sensor and a current sensor in sequence). Each channel switch forces a worst-case settling transient.

A square wave on a single channel can also trigger the error, but only on the few samples that land right after an edge. Since CADC tracks the signal between edges, most samples are already settled. The channel-switch scenario guarantees the error on every single sample, making it much easier to observe.

title: Week 5 Lab: Sensors & ADC Applications
text:
Why These ADC Settings?
Scan Conversion Mode — When disabled, the ADC converts only one channel per trigger. When enabled, it converts multiple channels in sequence. We enable it because we have two sensors (thermocouple on CH0, LDR on CH1).
Number of Conversions = 2 — Tells the scan sequencer how many channels to cycle through. Matches our two ADC inputs.
Rank — The conversion order. Rank 1 is converted first, Rank 2 second. In our code, we override the rank at runtime with read_adc_channel(), so the CubeMX rank order is just a default.
Sampling Time = 84 Cycles — How long the ADC holds the input before converting. Longer = more accurate for high-impedance sources. Our amplifier output has \(R_p = 1\,\text{k}\Omega\) in series, so 84 cycles gives the internal sample capacitor enough time to settle.

title: Week 6: RTOS Foundations
text:
Why interrupts alone aren’t enough







Problem
Why it hurts




No blocking in ISRs
ISRs freeze the system while running, so you can’t do slow work inside them. You’re forced to set flags and handle everything in the main loop — which quickly becomes a hand-built state machine


Global state explosion
ISRs communicate through volatile globals — dozens of flags with subtle ordering dependencies as system grows


Priority inversion
Low-priority ISR holds shared data, high-priority ISR needs it — no resolution mechanism (RTOS has priority inheritance)


No CPU time sharing
Two tasks both needing 40% CPU can’t coexist — one runs to completion before the other starts


Debugging is harder
Timing bugs are non-deterministic and hard to reproduce


Scales badly
3–4 ISRs are manageable; 10+ becomes an interaction nightmare



Where ISRs still win: Response time. An ISR fires in µs. An RTOS context switch takes 5–20µs. For hard real-time below ~10µs, bare-metal ISRs are the only option.

section: osDelay vs vTaskDelayUntil — why it matters
text:
osDelay vs vTaskDelayUntil — why it matters
osDelay(500):        work takes 30ms, total period = 530ms
├──work 30ms──├────── delay 500ms ──────├──work 30ms──├─ ...
|<──────── 530ms ────────>|<──────── 530ms ────────>|
                                        ^ drifts every cycle

vTaskDelayUntil(500): work takes 30ms, total period = 500ms
├──work 30ms──├──── delay 470ms ────├──work 30ms──├─── ...
|<──────── 500ms ──────>|<──────── 500ms ──────>|
                                    ^ no drift
vTaskDelayUntil subtracts the time already spent and sleeps only for the remainder. Use it for motor control, sensor sampling, or anything needing consistent timing.

Timer calculation
\[f_{interrupt} = \frac{f_{clk}}{(PSC + 1) \times (ARR + 1)}\]
Example: 84 MHz clock, want 1 kHz interrupt:
\[(PSC + 1) \times (ARR + 1) = \frac{84{,}000{,}000}{1{,}000} = 84{,}000\]

title: Weeks 1–6 Review

text:
LDO — Linear Regulator
How it works: Variable resistor drops excess voltage as heat.
Key formulas:
\[P_{diss} = (V_{in} - V_{out}) \times I_{load}\]
\[T_j = T_{ambient} + P_{diss} \times \theta_{JA}\]
\[\eta = \frac{V_{out}}{V_{in}} \times 100\%\]
Example: LM1117 — 7V → 3.3V at 200 mA (\(\theta_{JA}\) = 90°C/W, \(T_a\) = 25°C):

\(P_{diss}\) = 3.7 × 0.2 = 0.74 W
\(T_j\) = 25 + 0.74 × 90 = 91.6°C (safe, but warm)
\(\eta\) = 3.3/7 = 47% (still poor)

LDO vs Buck — when to use which









LDO
Buck




Efficiency
\(V_{out}/V_{in}\) (bad at large drop)
80–92% (constant)


Output ripple
Very low (~mV)
Higher (30–100 mV)

3 components

Cheap

Rule of thumb: If \(V_{in} - V_{out}\) > 2V and current > 100 mA → use Buck.

Decoupling capacitors

100 nF ceramic close to every VDD/VSS pin pair — filters high-frequency noise
10–22 µF bulk at board power entry — filters low-frequency ripple
Placement matters — short traces, close to the pin, not on the other side of the board

title: Weeks 1–6 Review
text:
Voltage divider for ADC
\[V_{out} = V_{in} \times \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}\]
Thévenin impedance seen by ADC:
\[R_{AIN} = R_1 \parallel R_2 = \frac{R_1 \times R_2}{R_1 + R_2}\]
STM32 requires \(R_{AIN} \leq 50\,k\Omega\) for accurate sampling.

If source impedance is too high, the ADC’s internal sample capacitor can’t charge fully within the sampling window → settling error.

FT (Five-volt Tolerant)
TT (Three-volt Tolerant)

Use for
5V digital signals
ADC inputs, low-voltage


In analog mode
5V tolerance lost
Same limit



Protection methods:

Series resistor (1–2.2 kΩ) — limits current through ESD diodes
Schottky clamp (BAT54) — \(V_f\) ≈ 0.3V, clamps close to VDD
Zener diode — clamps at specific voltage
TVS diode — fast transient suppression

text:
RC low-pass filter
\[f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi RC}\]
Example: R = 1 kΩ, C = 100 nF → \(f_c\) = 1.6 kHz
Passes slow sensor signals, blocks high-frequency noise. Place between sensor output and ADC input.

Inductive kickback
When current through an inductor is interrupted:
\[V_L = -L \times \frac{di}{dt}\]
Example: L = 30 mH, I = 300 mA, collapse in 1 µs:
\[V_L = -0.03 \times \frac{0.3}{1 \times 10^{-6}} = -9{,}000\,\text{V}\]
Solution: Flyback diode (Schottky preferred — fast, low \(V_f\))

text:
Two-point calibration
When sensor output isn’t factory-calibrated (e.g., thermocouple + amplifier):
\[T = T_1 + \underbrace{\frac{T_2 - T_1}{ADC_2 - ADC_1}}_{\text{slope: °C per count}} \times \underbrace{(ADC_{raw} - ADC_1)}_{\text{how far from point 1}}\]

You measure two known temperatures and record their ADC values. The slope tells you how many degrees each ADC count is worth. Then for any new reading, you calculate how far it is from point 1 (in counts), multiply by the slope, and add the starting temperature.

Example: At 20°C → ADC = 450, at 80°C → ADC = 1650:
\[T = 20 + \frac{60}{1200} \times (ADC_{raw} - 450) = 20 + 0.05 \times (ADC_{raw} - 450)\]
ADC = 1050 → T = 20 + 0.05 × 600 = 50°C

title: Week 7: RTOS Communication
text:
Queue states

  
    
    
  

  
  
  Empty

  
  
  Partial

  
  
  Full

  
  
  Put()

  
  
  Get()

  
  
  Put()

  
  
  Get()

  
  
  Get() → blocks

  
  
  Put() → blocks


Empty: No items in queue. Get() blocks the calling task until a producer adds data
Partial: Normal operating state. Both Put() and Get() succeed immediately
Full: No space left. Put() blocks the calling task until a consumer removes an item
Blocking behavior depends on timeout: 0 = return error, osWaitForever = block indefinitely


When we say Get() “blocks” the calling task, here’s what actually happens at the RTOS level. The task calls osMessageQueueGet and the RTOS checks the queue. If it’s empty, the RTOS moves that task from the Ready state to the Blocked state — it’s essentially put to sleep. The task uses zero CPU time while blocked. It doesn’t spin in a loop checking “is there data yet?” — it’s completely suspended.
The moment another task calls Put() and adds an item to the queue, the RTOS wakes up the blocked task and moves it back to Ready. If it has high enough priority, it runs immediately and receives the data.
The same thing happens in reverse with Put() on a full queue — the producer gets blocked until the consumer frees a slot.
This is fundamentally different from polling with HAL_Delay. With HAL_Delay, the task burns CPU cycles doing nothing. With queue blocking, the CPU is free to run other tasks. That’s the whole point of an RTOS — efficient use of CPU time through event-driven blocking instead of busy-waiting.
The timeout parameter gives you control: osWaitForever means “I’m willing to wait as long as it takes,” 0 means “give me data now or return an error immediately,” and any number in between is a deadline in milliseconds.

title: Week 8: I2C Protocol & IMU Application
text:
HAL Master_Transmit / Master_Receive
When there is no register map — just raw byte transfers:


Send raw bytes to a slave:
uint8_t cmd[3] = {0xAE, 0x01, 0xFF};
HAL_I2C_Master_Transmit(&hi2c1,
    device_addr << 1,   // 7-bit shifted
    cmd,                // byte buffer
    3,                  // num bytes
    100);               // timeout ms
Read raw bytes from a slave:
uint8_t buf[4];
HAL_I2C_Master_Receive(&hi2c1,
    device_addr << 1,
    buf,
    4,
    100);

Mem_* vs Master_* — when to use which:







Pattern
Use




Register-mapped sensor (MPU6050, EEPROM)
Mem_Write / Mem_Read


Display / command-stream device (SSD1306, PCA9685)
Master_Transmit


Write-then-read with your own protocol
Manual: Master_Transmit then Master_Receive


Probe a device address
HAL_I2C_IsDeviceReady



Key difference: Mem_* adds the register pointer and the repeated START for you; Master_* just streams the bytes you give it.

All HAL I²C functions come in 3 flavours: blocking (default), _IT (interrupt), _DMA (DMA for bulk transfers).

Introduce this slide as “the other half of the HAL I2C API.” Mem_Write / Mem_Read are perfect for register-mapped sensors but not every device on I²C is register-mapped. OLED displays like the SSD1306 expect a stream of command and data bytes where the first byte selects command vs data mode; there is no “read from register 0x25” concept. PWM drivers like the PCA9685 can be accessed either way. For these devices you hand Master_Transmit your own byte buffer and it streams every byte you asked for between a START and a STOP — nothing more, nothing less.
Walk through the small example on the left: three raw bytes being pushed to a device. Compare with the Mem_Write version from the previous slide — note that here there is no “register address” argument because the device does not have one. Students should see that Mem_Write is just a convenient wrapper that internally does Master_Transmit with {reg_addr, data_byte} prepended for them.
Also mention HAL_I2C_IsDeviceReady: it sends just the address byte with the write bit, waits for ACK, and returns HAL_OK on ACK or HAL_ERROR on NACK. Loop it from 0x00 to 0x7F and you have a bus scanner — we show this exact pattern in the W08 lab. Students often ask “how do I check if my MPU6050 is even wired up?” and the answer is HAL_I2C_IsDeviceReady in a loop, not reading WHO_AM_I, because if the wiring is wrong the read itself will fail on NACK anyway.
Finally the three-flavour line is important for anyone going beyond this week: _IT variants fire a callback when the transfer finishes and are the right choice in an RTOS or when you want to start an I²C transfer and do other work while it runs; _DMA variants are for high-throughput bulk transfers where even interrupt overhead matters. For this week’s lab the blocking versions are fine because we read the sensor once every 100 ms and can afford to wait the ~1 ms a transfer takes.

Pull-ups: Don’t Trust the Ohmmeter
Most GY-521 boards have onboard 2.2 kΩ or 4.7 kΩ pull-ups — but they sit on the output of the onboard 3.3 V LDO, not on the VCC pin.






Important


Measuring resistance from VCC to SDA with the board unpowered reads through the LDO in series → hundreds of kΩ to MΩ. That is not a pull-up failure.



Correct check (powered, bus idle):

SDA → GND ≈ 3.3 V
SCL → GND ≈ 3.3 V

If either sits near 0 V with no master driving: pull-ups missing, add external 4.7 kΩ to 3.3 V.
