title: Week 10: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
Week 10
SPI Protocol & DMA

Welcome students. This week is the second half of the “talking to peripherals” arc that began in Week 8 with I2C. We added one wire and gained a full order of magnitude in throughput, plus full-duplex transfers. In the second half of the lecture we layer on DMA — the trick that lets the CPU set up a transfer once and walk away while a hardware engine moves the data. Together, SPI + DMA is the combination behind audio codecs, displays, SD cards, and basically every “fast peripheral” in modern embedded systems.

title: Week 10: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
Why this week matters

SPI is the highest-throughput common bus on a microcontroller (10–50 MHz routinely)
It is the protocol used for SD cards, displays, flash memory, fast ADCs, audio codecs
DMA is what lets a small MCU keep up with that throughput without melting the CPU
Almost every “real” embedded product uses SPI + DMA somewhere
Understanding both unlocks the rest of your career — these are not academic


Reinforce the throughput point. I2C at 400 kHz reads ~50 kB/s of MPU data; SPI at 25 MHz can stream a megabyte per second comfortably, which is what makes SD-card logging and graphical displays feasible. DMA is what makes that throughput sustainable — without it the CPU spends 100% of its time servicing the SPI peripheral and has nothing left for control loops, UI, or comms. Many graduate-level embedded jobs assume you understand DMA on day one.

title: Week 10: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
Learning objectives

Explain the SPI 4-wire bus and the master/slave shift-register model
Identify the four SPI modes (CPOL/CPHA) and pick the correct one from a datasheet
Compare SPI and I2C and choose the right bus for a given peripheral
Explain how DMA moves data without CPU involvement and what HT/TC interrupts mean
Configure HAL SPI + DMA on STM32 in CubeIDE
Use a W25Q SPI flash: read JEDEC ID, read/write data with proper CS timing
Use an oscilloscope or logic analyzer to verify SPI bus health


The two highest-leverage objectives are the mode-selection one (CPOL/CPHA) and the DMA flow (HT/TC). These are the two places students get the most stuck and where the lab failure-injection tests will catch them. Mode selection is a pure datasheet-reading skill; DMA is a mental-model skill.

title: Week 10: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
Agenda (90 minutes)
Part 1: SPI Protocol Fundamentals (25 min)

4-wire bus: SCK, MOSI, MISO, CS
Shift-register model and full-duplex
The four SPI modes (CPOL/CPHA)

Part 2: SPI Hardware & Multi-Slave (15 min)

Push-pull driver, no pull-ups
One CS per slave, shared SCK/MOSI/MISO
SPI vs I2C: when to pick which

Part 3: DMA Fundamentals (25 min)

Why polling and interrupts hit a wall
DMA controller, streams, requests
Circular mode and HT/TC interrupts

Part 4: SPI Flash (W25Q) (15 min)

Memory hierarchy: chip, block, sector, page
JEDEC ID handshake
Read/Erase/Program command structure

Part 5: Lab Preview & Debugging (10 min)

Bring-up checklist
Failure injection tests


We deliberately spend more time on DMA than on the W25Q itself. The flash is a good vehicle for the lab, but DMA is the transferable skill — students will reuse it for ADC, UART, I2S, and DAC for the rest of their careers. The W25Q knowledge is useful, but the DMA understanding is fundamental.

title: Week 10: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
What is SPI?
Serial Peripheral Interface (Motorola, mid-1980s)

Standard 4-wire SPI bus
SPI was created at Motorola for the 68000 family in the mid-1980s. Unlike I2C it was never formally licensed — there is no “SPI standard document” you can buy, only a de-facto convention that everyone implements slightly differently. This is why SPI peripherals come in four modes and why MOSI/MISO sometimes have other names (SDI/SDO, COPI/CIPO). Pronounce it “S-P-I” or “spy” — both are common. Walk through the four signals on the slide: SCK is the master’s clock, MOSI carries master-to-slave data, MISO carries slave-to-master data, and CS (chip select, often called SS — slave select, or NSS for “not slave select”) tells one specific slave “this transfer is for you.”

title: Week 10: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
The four signals








Signal
Direction
Purpose




SCK
Master → Slave
Clock; every edge shifts data


MOSI
Master → Slave
Master Out, Slave In


MISO
Slave → Master
Master In, Slave Out


CS (or SS, NSS)
Master → Slave
Chip Select; LOW = “talk to me”



Key properties

Synchronous — clock travels with the data, no shared time reference needed
Full-duplex — every clock cycle, master sends one bit AND receives one bit
Push-pull — drivers actively drive HIGH and LOW, no pull-ups required
No addressing — selecting a slave is a physical-layer act (assert CS LOW)


Push-pull is the most important difference from I2C. I2C was open-drain, slow, and needed pull-ups; SPI is push-pull, fast, and the driver actively switches both rails. That’s why SPI hits 50 MHz routinely while I2C tops out around 1 MHz. The “no addressing” point is also worth dwelling on: I2C had 7-bit addresses baked into every byte, but SPI just uses a wire — assert CS, the slave responds; release CS, it ignores the bus. This is simpler in software but costs one GPIO per slave.

title: Week 10: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
The shift-register model

SPI is two shift registers connected in a ring
This is THE mental model for SPI. Both the master and the slave have an 8-bit shift register; MOSI connects the master’s output to the slave’s input, MISO connects the slave’s output to the master’s input, and SCK clocks both. After 8 clock pulses, every bit that started in the master is now in the slave, and every bit that was in the slave is now in the master. They have exchanged a byte. This is why SPI is full-duplex for free — there is no “send” mode or “receive” mode, just an exchange. If you only want to read, you still have to write something (often 0xFF or 0x00) to clock the data out of the slave. If you only want to write, the data the slave returns is usually meaningless and you discard it.

title: Week 10: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
Full-duplex in practice
Reading a byte from a slave register requires two transfers, each exchanging one byte:

Master sends register address; slave sends garbage → discard
Master sends 0xFF (dummy); slave sends register value → keep

uint8_t tx[2] = { REG_ADDR | 0x80, 0xFF };  // 0x80 = read bit on W25Q
uint8_t rx[2];
HAL_GPIO_WritePin(CS_PORT, CS_PIN, GPIO_PIN_RESET);   // CS low
HAL_SPI_TransmitReceive(&hspi1, tx, rx, 2, HAL_MAX_DELAY);
HAL_GPIO_WritePin(CS_PORT, CS_PIN, GPIO_PIN_SET);     // CS high
uint8_t value = rx[1];                                 // rx[0] is garbage

This is the single most common student bug in the W10 lab: students send 1 byte expecting to “trigger a read” and get nothing back. They have to send a dummy byte to clock the response out of the slave. Walk through the code line by line. The 0x80 OR is a W25Q-specific convention (high bit = read direction); other chips use different read commands. Stress that CS must be asserted before the first SCK edge and held until after the last SCK edge — releasing CS in the middle of a transfer aborts it on most slaves.

title: Week 10: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
CS timing matters
CS    ‾‾|_______________________|‾‾    (LOW = active)
        |                       |
SCK    _|‾|_|‾|_|‾|_|‾| ... |_|‾|_     (8 clocks per byte)
         ↑                     ↑
         |                     |
       first edge          last edge
Rules

Assert CS before clocking begins
Hold CS LOW for the entire multi-byte command (e.g., command + address + data)
Release CS after the last bit completes
Some slaves require minimum CS-LOW and CS-HIGH times (read the datasheet)


Many devices (W25Q included) interpret a CS rising edge as “command ended; commit/cancel.” If you accidentally release CS between the address byte and the data byte of a read, you get garbage. Conversely, if you forget to release CS at the end of a write, the chip waits forever for the next byte. CS timing is invisible until you scope it; this is why the lab requires a CS-on-scope verification check.

title: Week 10: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
The four SPI modes
The SPI spec leaves two clock-related parameters undefined:

CPOL (Clock Polarity) — what is SCK’s idle level? 0 = LOW, 1 = HIGH
CPHA (Clock Phase) — which edge samples the data? 0 = first, 1 = second

Four combinations → four modes:



Mode
CPOL
CPHA
SCK idle
Sample edge




0
0
0
LOW
rising


1
0
1
LOW
falling


2
1
0
HIGH
falling


3
1
1
HIGH
rising



Mode 0 is the most common. The W25Q supports modes 0 and 3.

The four modes are not interoperable: a master in mode 0 cannot talk to a slave in mode 2. The mode is fixed by the slave’s datasheet and the master must match. The naming is unintuitive on purpose (CPHA=0 means “sample on the first edge,” not “sample on the rising edge”) so just memorize the table or pull it up when reading a datasheet. CubeIDE shows mode as two separate dropdowns (CPOL and CPHA), so you don’t usually pick a “mode number” in code, you pick the two parameters.

title: Week 10: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
SPI mode timing

All four modes side-by-side
Read across each box: the SCK waveform tells you CPOL (where it sits when nothing is happening), and the red sample arrows tell you CPHA (which SCK edge the slave latches MOSI on). The rule of thumb: data must be stable across the sample edge and is allowed to change on the opposite edge. Mode mismatches usually show up as data that “looks shifted by one bit” or as ACKs that arrive with the wrong polarity — students will see this in the failure-injection part of the lab.

title: Week 10: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
Push-pull driver advantages



Property
I2C (open-drain)
SPI (push-pull)




Idle state
Pulled up by R
Driven HIGH or LOW by gate


Edge speed
Limited by RC
Limited by gate alone


Pull-ups
Required
Not used


Bus speed
100 kHz – 1 MHz
1 MHz – 50 MHz


Power
μA leakage through R
Per-edge dynamic only




The fundamental advantage of push-pull is the rising edge. In I2C, the line rises by being released and pulled up through R; the speed of that rise is set by R × C_bus, which is why we burned a slide last week on pull-up sizing math. In SPI, both the rise and the fall are actively driven by FET gates, so the edge speed is limited only by the silicon, not by the bus. This is the entire reason SPI is faster than I2C. The cost: SPI cannot share wires between drivers, because if two devices try to drive the bus at once, you get a short circuit. Hence one CS per slave.

title: Week 10: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
Multi-slave: shared bus, separate CS

SPI multi-slave with shared SCK/MOSI/MISO and individual CS lines
Walk through the topology. SCK, MOSI, and MISO are wired in parallel to all slaves. The slaves’ MISO outputs are tri-stated when their CS is HIGH, so they don’t fight each other on the bus. Only the slave whose CS is LOW responds. The cost of this scheme is one extra GPIO per slave — for three slaves you need three CS pins. The benefit is that you don’t have any addressing protocol overhead; selecting a slave is one GPIO write.

title: Week 10: SPI Protocol & DMA
section: SPI vs I2C: when to pick which
text:
SPI vs I2C: when to pick which

Side-by-side comparison
This is the slide students will reference when designing their final projects. Quick rules of thumb: many cheap sensors on a board → I2C (one bus, share addresses, save GPIOs). One fast peripheral (display, SD, flash, ADC) → SPI (full-duplex throughput). Mixed bus → both, on different STM32 peripherals. Note that some chips support both (BME280 is the classic example) and you pick by wiring; the device autodetects which protocol is being used.

title: Week 10: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
The CPU bottleneck
A 25 MHz SPI runs at ~3 MB/s. To service it byte-by-byte the CPU must:

Wait for “TX-empty” interrupt
Push next byte into SPI->DR
Wait for “RX-not-empty” interrupt
Read SPI->DR
Repeat 3 million times per second

At ~30 cycles per byte and an 84 MHz CPU, the SPI alone burns ~100 % of CPU time.
The CPU has nothing left for control loops, UI, or other peripherals.

This is the motivation for DMA. Walk through the math: 84 MHz CPU / 30 cycles per byte = 2.8 MB/s — almost exactly the SPI bus speed. So at full SPI speed, polled or interrupt-driven SPI consumes the entire CPU. That’s a non-starter if you also need to run a 1 kHz control loop or update an LCD or service a UART. DMA is the way out: a hardware engine inside the MCU does the byte-shoveling, and the CPU only gets interrupted at the start and end of the whole transfer.

title: Week 10: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
Polled vs IRQ vs DMA

CPU activity timeline for the three modes
Polled SPI is the simplest API (HAL_SPI_Transmit) but blocks the CPU for the entire transfer. IRQ-driven SPI (HAL_SPI_Transmit_IT) lets the CPU run between bytes, but the per-byte interrupt overhead means there is still significant CPU load — and the latency of entering the interrupt is often longer than the transfer of one byte at high speeds. DMA-driven SPI (HAL_SPI_Transmit_DMA) only interrupts the CPU once at the end. The CPU is free to do other work for the entire duration of the transfer. This is the only viable approach above ~5 MHz SPI.

title: Week 10: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
What DMA actually is
DMA = Direct Memory Access
A small hardware state machine inside the MCU that can:

Move data between memory and peripherals without CPU intervention
Be triggered by peripheral events (SPI ready, ADC done, UART byte received)
Optionally raise an interrupt at half-transfer (HT) and transfer-complete (TC)
Run multiple “streams” or “channels” in parallel


Mention that DMA is not magic: it shares the AHB bus with the CPU, so heavy DMA traffic can stall CPU memory accesses (this is called “bus contention” and matters for hard-real-time work). On STM32F4 there are 2 DMA controllers each with 8 streams; the SPI peripheral has dedicated stream/channel assignments that you’ll see in the reference manual. The reference manual table is the single source of truth — students should bookmark it.

title: Week 10: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
DMA block diagram

How DMA, the SPI peripheral, RAM and the CPU connect
Walk through the path. The SPI peripheral asserts a “request” line every time its TX register has space (or RX register has data). The DMA controller, configured to listen to that request, performs one read from RAM (TX direction) or one write to RAM (RX direction) over the AHB bus matrix, completely bypassing the CPU. The CPU only sees the start (where it kicked off the DMA) and the end (TC interrupt). For a 1024-byte transfer, the CPU does ~5 instructions instead of ~30,000.

title: Week 10: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
Circular mode and double-buffering

Circular DMA with HT and TC interrupts
Circular mode is the killer feature for streaming applications (audio, ADC, continuous SPI). The DMA wraps around at the end of the buffer and starts over — forever, with no CPU intervention. The half-transfer (HT) and transfer-complete (TC) interrupts let you process one half of the buffer while the DMA fills the other half. This is the classic ping-pong pattern. Audio codecs use this; ADC streaming uses this; high-speed ADCs in W12 will use this. The W10 lab uses non-circular (one-shot) DMA to keep the cognitive load down, but the circular pattern is what they’ll need for any “real” streaming work.

title: Week 10: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
Double-buffer pattern

Ping-pong: process one half while DMA fills the other
The flow: DMA writes into buffer A; when half-full it raises HT; CPU starts processing buffer A; meanwhile DMA continues writing into buffer A’s second half; when full it raises TC and wraps to buffer A’s start (or to buffer B in true double-buffer mode). The processing rate just needs to keep up with the average data rate, not the instantaneous one — that’s the entire point of buffering. If processing falls behind, you get an “overrun” and lose data.

title: Week 10: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
DMA configuration in CubeIDE
For SPI1 TX + RX with single-shot transfer:

Open the SPI1 peripheral → “DMA Settings” tab
Click Add twice — once for SPI1_TX, once for SPI1_RX
Set Mode = Normal (one-shot) or Circular (continuous)
Set Data Width = Byte for both peripheral and memory
Increment = Memory only (peripheral is a single register, doesn’t move)
In NVIC tab, enable the SPI1 global interrupt (for the TC callback)
Generate code

HAL_SPI_TransmitReceive_DMA(&hspi1, tx_buf, rx_buf, len);
// Returns immediately; HAL_SPI_TxRxCpltCallback() fires on TC

This is the workflow the lab walks through. The “Memory increment yes, Peripheral increment no” setting is the most common mistake — both default to “yes” in some HAL versions, which makes the DMA walk off the end of the SPI register space. The NVIC enable is also easy to forget and produces a silent failure: the transfer happens, but the callback never fires because the CPU has no idea it completed.

title: Week 10: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
Why flash, and why W25Q
The Winbond W25Q-series is the de-facto SPI flash family on dev boards.

8 Mbit – 256 Mbit, ~$1 in single quantities
4-pin SPI (mode 0 or mode 3), runs to 104 MHz (we use 1–10 MHz in lab)
Standard JEDEC command set — same code works across capacities
Used in: BIOS chips, IoT firmware storage, audio sample storage, data loggers

In the lab, we will use it as a fault log — a place to write event records that survive a power cycle, ready for fault-injection work in W12.

The W25Q is to SPI what the MPU6050 was to I2C: cheap, well-documented, and a legitimate part you’d ship in a real product. We chose it for the lab specifically so the W12 work (fault logging and recovery) can reuse the same chip. The JEDEC ID handshake we’ll do today is the exact equivalent of the WHO_AM_I check we did with the MPU6050 — a sanity check that the bus is wired right before any real work happens.

title: Week 10: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
W25Q breakout pinout

Common 8-pin breakout
Six pins matter for basic SPI use: VCC, GND, CS, CLK, DI (= MOSI from the master’s view), DO (= MISO from the master’s view). The other two (WP, HOLD) enable hardware write protection and clock-pause; for the lab we tie them to VCC to disable both features. Stress that the chip is 3.3 V only — connecting it to a 5 V system will destroy it.

title: Week 10: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
Memory hierarchy

Chip → Block → Sector → PageErase granularities (from finest to coarsest):

4 KB sector — the smallest erasable unit
32 KB block — middle option
64 KB block — fastest erase per byte

Program granularity: 256-byte page (cannot cross page boundaries)

This is the single biggest difference from RAM. Flash can only transition bits from 1 to 0 by programming; to set a bit back to 1 you must erase. And erase only works in chunks: 4 KB minimum, even if you only want to change one byte. This drives the entire architecture of flash file systems and wear-leveling. For the lab we will only erase one sector and write a few bytes inside one page, so we don’t need to worry about wear yet — but flash wears out at ~100,000 erase cycles per sector, which matters in real products.

title: Week 10: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
Standard W25Q commands








Command
Hex
What it does




JEDEC ID
0x9F
Read manufacturer + device ID (3 bytes) — sanity check


Read Status
0x05
Read status register (busy bit, write-enable bit)


Write Enable
0x06
Allow next write/erase command


Read Data
0x03
Read N bytes starting at 24-bit address


Page Program
0x02
Write up to 256 bytes (within one page)


Sector Erase
0x20
Erase a 4 KB sector



Pattern: Write Enable → wait for ready → Erase or Program → poll busy bit until done

The JEDEC ID command is the W10 equivalent of the WHO_AM_I we used in W08. Always run it first — if it returns the right manufacturer + device ID, you know your bus, mode, CS timing, and clock are all correct, and the rest of your code can assume a working channel. If it returns 0xFF or 0x00, you have a hardware problem and writing real code is a waste of time. Walk through the program/erase pattern: every modifying operation requires a Write Enable first, and you must poll the busy bit before issuing the next command (page program takes ~1 ms, sector erase takes ~50 ms — much longer than any single SPI transfer).

title: Week 10: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
JEDEC ID timing

Reading 0x9F returns 3 bytes — manufacturer + 2 device bytes
The expected response for a Winbond W25Q part is 0xEF (Winbond manufacturer) followed by two device-ID bytes that encode capacity. For example, W25Q16 returns 0xEF 0x40 0x15. Students will see this on a logic analyzer in the lab. If they see 0x00 0x00 0x00 the chip isn’t powered or CS is broken; if they see 0xFF 0xFF 0xFF the chip is missing or MISO is floating; if they see “almost right but shifted” it’s a CPHA mistake.

title: Week 10: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
Lab structure
Part 1 (45 min): SPI bring-up, JEDEC ID, polled mode

Wire the W25Q to the Nucleo
Configure SPI1 in CubeIDE
Read JEDEC ID — verify 0xEF as the first byte

Part 2 (40 min): Write/Erase/Read with proper command pattern

Sector erase, page program, read back
Failure injection: skip Write Enable, observe failure

Part 3 (60 min): Convert polled to DMA

Same code path, replace HAL_SPI_TransmitReceive with HAL_SPI_TransmitReceive_DMA
Add TC callback, measure CPU free time

Part 4 (35 min): Scope/LA verification + analysis

Capture SCK, MOSI, MISO, CS together
Decode protocol, verify ID matches


The single most important pedagogical move in this lab is Part 3: students get the polled version working first, then just change the function call to get a DMA version. This makes DMA feel like a refactoring step, not a foreign concept. The first time they see the LED toggle 100x faster while the SPI transfer continues in the background, the lightbulb goes on.

title: Week 10: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
Bring-up checklist (memorize this)
Before you write any “real” code, prove the channel works:

Power & ground — chip has 3.3 V on VCC, ground continuous to STM32 GND
CS is high at idle — scope the CS pin, should sit at 3.3 V when nothing is happening
SCK only toggles inside CS-LOW — never any clocks while CS is high
JEDEC ID returns 0xEF as first byte — known-good response, your “WHO_AM_I” for SPI flash
Same response over 100 reads — if it varies, your bus has a signal-integrity problem


This is the SPI equivalent of the I2C bring-up checklist from W08. Students who skip these checks and dive straight into the read/write code spend an hour debugging mystery bugs that a 30-second scope check would have caught. Encourage them to pin this list to their workbench.

title: Week 10: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
Common SPI failures








Symptom
Most likely cause
Fix




All-0xFF responses
MISO not connected, or slave not responding
Check wiring; check CS asserted


All-0x00 responses
MISO shorted to GND, or chip unpowered
Check VCC; remove short


First byte garbage
Read after CS-low transient
Use a tx-rx pair, discard rx[0]


Data shifted by 1 bit
Wrong CPHA setting
Try the other phase (datasheet)


Works at low speed, fails at high
Signal integrity (long wires, no ground return)
Shorten wires, add ground wire


Write succeeds but readback is original data
Forgot Write Enable, or didn’t wait for busy
Add 0x06 + poll busy




The “first byte garbage” issue is interesting and worth pausing on. Some slaves need a brief stabilization time after CS goes low before they sample. Some HAL versions also have a one-byte latency in the rx FIFO. The robust pattern is to always discard the first received byte after CS-low for command-style transfers. The “shifted by 1 bit” failure is the CPHA classic — students will deliberately trigger this in the failure-injection part of the lab so they recognize it on a scope.

title: Week 10: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
DMA debugging tips

Callback never fires? NVIC interrupt not enabled, or wrong stream/channel mapping
First half of buffer is right, second half is wrong? Memory-increment is OFF (should be ON)
DMA seems to corrupt RAM? Forgot to set buffer size correctly, or buffer is on stack and got reused
Transfer hangs? SPI peripheral not enabled, or DMA stream still busy from a previous transfer
Use STM32CubeIDE Live Expressions to watch the DMA controller registers (NDTR counts down)


The “buffer on stack” gotcha bites everyone exactly once. If you declare uint8_t buf[1024] inside a function, kick off DMA, and return from the function, the stack frame is gone but the DMA controller is still happily writing into what is now random stack space. Always allocate DMA buffers as static, global, or heap. Mention __attribute__((aligned(4))) for systems where DMA requires alignment (Cortex-M7 with cache, less of an issue on M4).

title: Week 10: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
Self-check before lab

Can you draw the 4-wire SPI bus from memory?
Do you know what CPOL and CPHA mean?
Can you explain why SPI has no addressing in the protocol?
Can you list the steps from “polled” to “DMA” in CubeIDE?
Do you know which command reads JEDEC ID and what response you expect?
Can you explain what HT and TC interrupts mean?


Use this slide as a 3-minute end-of-lecture self-check. Have students raise hands if they can’t answer any one of these — don’t shame, just identify who needs office-hours help before the lab.

title: Week 10: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
Summary

SPI: 4-wire, full-duplex, push-pull, 1–50 MHz, no addressing, one CS per slave
Four modes via CPOL/CPHA — read the slave datasheet to pick
DMA moves data without CPU; HT/TC interrupts let you ping-pong process buffers
Polled → IRQ → DMA is a strict efficiency progression — pay the complexity cost only when you need to
W25Q: JEDEC ID first, then Write Enable + Erase + Program + Read pattern
Bring-up = scope the four signals first, write code second

Next week (W11): USB CDC + interactive shell — talk to your board from a terminal.

End-of-lecture: confirm that everyone has a Nucleo and a W25Q breakout for the lab session, and remind them to bring a logic analyzer or to plan to share one. Office hours before lab are the highest-leverage hour they can spend this week.

title: Week 10: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
Questions?

Open the floor. Common questions: - “Why is full-duplex useful if I only want to read?” → Answer: full-duplex is free; you don’t have to use the read direction. But many slaves use the master-write side to send commands while sending status back on the read side — like the W25Q’s read-status command. - “Can I do SPI in software?” → Yes (it’s called bit-banging). It works for slow chips. Don’t. - “Why does the W25Q support both mode 0 and mode 3?” → Some FPGAs and CPLDs prefer one over the other; supporting both makes the chip universal.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Week 9
I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization

We keep DMA — that is the transferable skill — and apply it to streaming IMU samples from the I²C peripheral into a sample buffer at a fixed rate, freeing the CPU to run a complementary filter and stream roll/pitch over UART to a live 3D plot on the laptop. The DMA mental model here transfers directly to ADC, UART, I2S, and SPI with no new ideas.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Why this week matters

Last week you talked to the MPU6050 by polling. That works at 50 Hz; it falls over at 1 kHz.
DMA is the trick that lets the CPU hand a hardware engine a sample buffer and walk away.
Orientation estimation is the canonical “real-time signal processing on an MCU” problem.
Drones, phones, VR headsets, balancing robots — all of them do exactly what you’re about to do.
By the end of the lecture you will know how to stream IMU samples into RAM with zero CPU cost and turn them into a smooth 3D visualization.


The pitch to students is: last week your code did one thing (read the IMU). This week it does three things at once (DMA pulls samples, CPU runs the filter, UART pushes results) — and that is what real embedded systems look like. Reinforce that DMA is everywhere: STM32 ADC, UART, I2S audio, DAC, SPI displays, and yes I²C all use the same DMA controller. Once you understand the pattern here, the others are just register-name changes.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Learning objectives

Explain how DMA moves data without CPU involvement and what HT/TC interrupts mean
Configure HAL I²C in DMA mode for periodic burst reads of an MPU6050
Convert raw accel/gyro readings to physical units (g, °/s) at fixed scale
Implement a complementary filter for roll and pitch and explain the α tradeoff
Stream orientation over UART in a parser-friendly format
Reason about why yaw drifts without a magnetometer


The two highest-leverage objectives are the DMA mental model (HT/TC, double-buffer) and the complementary-filter intuition (gyro fast, accel slow). These are the parts students get stuck on and that the lab failure-injection tests will catch them on. The unit-conversion and UART-format objectives are mechanical but matter for the visualization to actually work.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Agenda (90 minutes)

From polled to streamed — 15 min
DMA fundamentals — 20 min
I²C + DMA on STM32 — 15 min
Orientation estimation — 25 min
Visualization & lab preview — 15 min


We deliberately spend the most time on orientation, because that is where the physical intuition lives and where students will remember the lecture months later. DMA gets 35 minutes total across Parts 1–3, which is enough to install the mental model without belaboring register-level details — the lab teaches those.

title: Week 9: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
What is SPI?
Serial Peripheral Interface (Motorola, mid-1980s)

Standard 4-wire SPI bus
SPI was created at Motorola for the 68000 family in the mid-1980s. Unlike I2C it was never formally licensed — there is no “SPI standard document” you can buy, only a de-facto convention that everyone implements slightly differently. This is why SPI peripherals come in four modes and why MOSI/MISO sometimes have other names (SDI/SDO, COPI/CIPO). Pronounce it “S-P-I” or “spy” — both are common. Walk through the four signals on the slide: SCK is the master’s clock, MOSI carries master-to-slave data, MISO carries slave-to-master data, and CS (chip select, often called SS — slave select, or NSS for “not slave select”) tells one specific slave “this transfer is for you.”

title: Week 9: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
The four signals








Signal
Direction
Purpose




SCK
Master → Slave
Clock; every edge shifts data


MOSI
Master → Slave
Master Out, Slave In


MISO
Slave → Master
Master In, Slave Out


CS (or SS, NSS)
Master → Slave
Chip Select; LOW = “talk to me”



Key properties

Synchronous — clock travels with the data, no shared time reference needed
Full-duplex — every clock cycle, master sends one bit AND receives one bit
Push-pull — drivers actively drive HIGH and LOW, no pull-ups required
No addressing — selecting a slave is a physical-layer act (assert CS LOW)


Push-pull is the most important difference from I2C. I2C was open-drain, slow, and needed pull-ups; SPI is push-pull, fast, and the driver actively switches both rails. That’s why SPI hits 50 MHz routinely while I2C tops out around 1 MHz. The “no addressing” point is also worth dwelling on: I2C had 7-bit addresses baked into every byte, but SPI just uses a wire — assert CS, the slave responds; release CS, it ignores the bus. This is simpler in software but costs one GPIO per slave.

title: Week 9: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
The shift-register model

SPI is two shift registers connected in a ring
This is THE mental model for SPI. Both the master and the slave have an 8-bit shift register; MOSI connects the master’s output to the slave’s input, MISO connects the slave’s output to the master’s input, and SCK clocks both. After 8 clock pulses, every bit that started in the master is now in the slave, and every bit that was in the slave is now in the master. They have exchanged a byte. This is why SPI is full-duplex for free — there is no “send” mode or “receive” mode, just an exchange. If you only want to read, you still have to write something (often 0xFF or 0x00) to clock the data out of the slave. If you only want to write, the data the slave returns is usually meaningless and you discard it.

title: Week 9: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
Full-duplex in practice
Reading a byte from a slave register requires two transfers, each exchanging one byte:

Master sends register address; slave sends garbage → discard
Master sends 0xFF (dummy); slave sends register value → keep

uint8_t tx[2] = { REG_ADDR | 0x80, 0xFF };  // 0x80 = read bit on W25Q
uint8_t rx[2];
HAL_GPIO_WritePin(CS_PORT, CS_PIN, GPIO_PIN_RESET);   // CS low
HAL_SPI_TransmitReceive(&hspi1, tx, rx, 2, HAL_MAX_DELAY);
HAL_GPIO_WritePin(CS_PORT, CS_PIN, GPIO_PIN_SET);     // CS high
uint8_t value = rx[1];                                 // rx[0] is garbage

This is the single most common student bug in the W10 lab: students send 1 byte expecting to “trigger a read” and get nothing back. They have to send a dummy byte to clock the response out of the slave. Walk through the code line by line. The 0x80 OR is a W25Q-specific convention (high bit = read direction); other chips use different read commands. Stress that CS must be asserted before the first SCK edge and held until after the last SCK edge — releasing CS in the middle of a transfer aborts it on most slaves.

title: Week 9: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
CS timing matters
CS    ‾‾|_______________________|‾‾    (LOW = active)
        |                       |
SCK    _|‾|_|‾|_|‾|_|‾| ... |_|‾|_     (8 clocks per byte)
         ↑                     ↑
         |                     |
       first edge          last edge
Rules

Assert CS before clocking begins
Hold CS LOW for the entire multi-byte command (e.g., command + address + data)
Release CS after the last bit completes
Some slaves require minimum CS-LOW and CS-HIGH times (read the datasheet)


Many devices (W25Q included) interpret a CS rising edge as “command ended; commit/cancel.” If you accidentally release CS between the address byte and the data byte of a read, you get garbage. Conversely, if you forget to release CS at the end of a write, the chip waits forever for the next byte. CS timing is invisible until you scope it; this is why the lab requires a CS-on-scope verification check.

title: Week 9: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
The four SPI modes
The SPI spec leaves two clock-related parameters undefined:

CPOL (Clock Polarity) — what is SCK’s idle level? 0 = LOW, 1 = HIGH
CPHA (Clock Phase) — which edge samples the data? 0 = first, 1 = second

Four combinations → four modes:



Mode
CPOL
CPHA
SCK idle
Sample edge




0
0
0
LOW
rising


1
0
1
LOW
falling


2
1
0
HIGH
falling


3
1
1
HIGH
rising



Mode 0 is the most common. The W25Q supports modes 0 and 3.

The four modes are not interoperable: a master in mode 0 cannot talk to a slave in mode 2. The mode is fixed by the slave’s datasheet and the master must match. The naming is unintuitive on purpose (CPHA=0 means “sample on the first edge,” not “sample on the rising edge”) so just memorize the table or pull it up when reading a datasheet. CubeIDE shows mode as two separate dropdowns (CPOL and CPHA), so you don’t usually pick a “mode number” in code, you pick the two parameters.

title: Week 9: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
SPI mode timing

All four modes side-by-side
Read across each box: the SCK waveform tells you CPOL (where it sits when nothing is happening), and the red sample arrows tell you CPHA (which SCK edge the slave latches MOSI on). The rule of thumb: data must be stable across the sample edge and is allowed to change on the opposite edge. Mode mismatches usually show up as data that “looks shifted by one bit” or as ACKs that arrive with the wrong polarity — students will see this in the failure-injection part of the lab.

title: Week 9: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
Push-pull driver advantages



Property
I2C (open-drain)
SPI (push-pull)




Idle state
Pulled up by R
Driven HIGH or LOW by gate


Edge speed
Limited by RC
Limited by gate alone


Pull-ups
Required
Not used


Bus speed
100 kHz – 1 MHz
1 MHz – 50 MHz


Power
μA leakage through R
Per-edge dynamic only




The fundamental advantage of push-pull is the rising edge. In I2C, the line rises by being released and pulled up through R; the speed of that rise is set by R × C_bus, which is why we burned a slide last week on pull-up sizing math. In SPI, both the rise and the fall are actively driven by FET gates, so the edge speed is limited only by the silicon, not by the bus. This is the entire reason SPI is faster than I2C. The cost: SPI cannot share wires between drivers, because if two devices try to drive the bus at once, you get a short circuit. Hence one CS per slave.

title: Week 9: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
Multi-slave: shared bus, separate CS

SPI multi-slave with shared SCK/MOSI/MISO and individual CS lines
Walk through the topology. SCK, MOSI, and MISO are wired in parallel to all slaves. The slaves’ MISO outputs are tri-stated when their CS is HIGH, so they don’t fight each other on the bus. Only the slave whose CS is LOW responds. The cost of this scheme is one extra GPIO per slave — for three slaves you need three CS pins. The benefit is that you don’t have any addressing protocol overhead; selecting a slave is one GPIO write.

title: Week 9: SPI Protocol & DMA
section: SPI vs I2C: when to pick which
text:
SPI vs I2C: when to pick which

Side-by-side comparison
This is the slide students will reference when designing their final projects. Quick rules of thumb: many cheap sensors on a board → I2C (one bus, share addresses, save GPIOs). One fast peripheral (display, SD, flash, ADC) → SPI (full-duplex throughput). Mixed bus → both, on different STM32 peripherals. Note that some chips support both (BME280 is the classic example) and you pick by wiring; the device autodetects which protocol is being used.

title: Week 9: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
The CPU bottleneck
A 25 MHz SPI runs at ~3 MB/s. To service it byte-by-byte the CPU must:

Wait for “TX-empty” interrupt
Push next byte into SPI->DR
Wait for “RX-not-empty” interrupt
Read SPI->DR
Repeat 3 million times per second

At ~30 cycles per byte and an 84 MHz CPU, the SPI alone burns ~100 % of CPU time.
The CPU has nothing left for control loops, UI, or other peripherals.

This is the motivation for DMA. Walk through the math: 84 MHz CPU / 30 cycles per byte = 2.8 MB/s — almost exactly the SPI bus speed. So at full SPI speed, polled or interrupt-driven SPI consumes the entire CPU. That’s a non-starter if you also need to run a 1 kHz control loop or update an LCD or service a UART. DMA is the way out: a hardware engine inside the MCU does the byte-shoveling, and the CPU only gets interrupted at the start and end of the whole transfer.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Polled vs IRQ vs DMA





Polled is fine for setup code (one-shot WHO_AM_I read).
Interrupt is fine when you want to react byte-by-byte.
DMA is what you want for periodic, bulk, predictable transfers — exactly the IMU case.



Make sure students understand that “interrupt mode” still spends CPU on each byte’s interrupt handler — for a 14-byte read at 400 kHz that’s 14 ISR entries per sample, which adds up. DMA is genuinely zero-CPU for the data movement; the only CPU cost is the one callback at end-of-transfer.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
What DMA actually is





A second processor that does exactly one thing: copy bytes from peripheral to memory.
Once configured, the CPU issues no instructions during the transfer.
The DMA fires a Transfer Complete (TC) interrupt at the end so the CPU knows new data is ready.



The “second processor” framing is the key idea. DMA is not a software trick or a clever interrupt pattern; it is dedicated silicon that moves bytes in parallel with the CPU. On the F401 there are two DMA controllers (DMA1 and DMA2), each with 8 streams, and each stream can be tied to one peripheral request at a time. That’s 16 simultaneous streams the chip can manage — far more than students will ever wire up at once.

title: Week 9: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
DMA block diagram

How DMA, the SPI peripheral, RAM and the CPU connect
Walk through the path. The SPI peripheral asserts a “request” line every time its TX register has space (or RX register has data). The DMA controller, configured to listen to that request, performs one read from RAM (TX direction) or one write to RAM (RX direction) over the AHB bus matrix, completely bypassing the CPU. The CPU only sees the start (where it kicked off the DMA) and the end (TC interrupt). For a 1024-byte transfer, the CPU does ~5 instructions instead of ~30,000.

title: Week 9: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
Circular mode and double-buffering

Circular DMA with HT and TC interrupts
Circular mode is the killer feature for streaming applications (audio, ADC, continuous SPI). The DMA wraps around at the end of the buffer and starts over — forever, with no CPU intervention. The half-transfer (HT) and transfer-complete (TC) interrupts let you process one half of the buffer while the DMA fills the other half. This is the classic ping-pong pattern. Audio codecs use this; ADC streaming uses this; high-speed ADCs in W12 will use this. The W10 lab uses non-circular (one-shot) DMA to keep the cognitive load down, but the circular pattern is what they’ll need for any “real” streaming work.

title: Week 9: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
Double-buffer pattern

Ping-pong: process one half while DMA fills the other
The flow: DMA writes into buffer A; when half-full it raises HT; CPU starts processing buffer A; meanwhile DMA continues writing into buffer A’s second half; when full it raises TC and wraps to buffer A’s start (or to buffer B in true double-buffer mode). The processing rate just needs to keep up with the average data rate, not the instantaneous one — that’s the entire point of buffering. If processing falls behind, you get an “overrun” and lose data.

title: Week 9: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
DMA configuration in CubeIDE
For SPI1 TX + RX with single-shot transfer:

Open the SPI1 peripheral → “DMA Settings” tab
Click Add twice — once for SPI1_TX, once for SPI1_RX
Set Mode = Normal (one-shot) or Circular (continuous)
Set Data Width = Byte for both peripheral and memory
Increment = Memory only (peripheral is a single register, doesn’t move)
In NVIC tab, enable the SPI1 global interrupt (for the TC callback)
Generate code

HAL_SPI_TransmitReceive_DMA(&hspi1, tx_buf, rx_buf, len);
// Returns immediately; HAL_SPI_TxRxCpltCallback() fires on TC

This is the workflow the lab walks through. The “Memory increment yes, Peripheral increment no” setting is the most common mistake — both default to “yes” in some HAL versions, which makes the DMA walk off the end of the SPI register space. The NVIC enable is also easy to forget and produces a silent failure: the transfer happens, but the callback never fires because the CPU has no idea it completed.

title: Week 9: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
Why flash, and why W25Q
The Winbond W25Q-series is the de-facto SPI flash family on dev boards.

8 Mbit – 256 Mbit, ~$1 in single quantities
4-pin SPI (mode 0 or mode 3), runs to 104 MHz (we use 1–10 MHz in lab)
Standard JEDEC command set — same code works across capacities
Used in: BIOS chips, IoT firmware storage, audio sample storage, data loggers

In the lab, we will use it as a fault log — a place to write event records that survive a power cycle, ready for fault-injection work in W12.

The W25Q is to SPI what the MPU6050 was to I2C: cheap, well-documented, and a legitimate part you’d ship in a real product. We chose it for the lab specifically so the W12 work (fault logging and recovery) can reuse the same chip. The JEDEC ID handshake we’ll do today is the exact equivalent of the WHO_AM_I check we did with the MPU6050 — a sanity check that the bus is wired right before any real work happens.

title: Week 9: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
W25Q breakout pinout

Common 8-pin breakout
Six pins matter for basic SPI use: VCC, GND, CS, CLK, DI (= MOSI from the master’s view), DO (= MISO from the master’s view). The other two (WP, HOLD) enable hardware write protection and clock-pause; for the lab we tie them to VCC to disable both features. Stress that the chip is 3.3 V only — connecting it to a 5 V system will destroy it.

title: Week 9: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
Memory hierarchy

Chip → Block → Sector → PageErase granularities (from finest to coarsest):

4 KB sector — the smallest erasable unit
32 KB block — middle option
64 KB block — fastest erase per byte

Program granularity: 256-byte page (cannot cross page boundaries)

This is the single biggest difference from RAM. Flash can only transition bits from 1 to 0 by programming; to set a bit back to 1 you must erase. And erase only works in chunks: 4 KB minimum, even if you only want to change one byte. This drives the entire architecture of flash file systems and wear-leveling. For the lab we will only erase one sector and write a few bytes inside one page, so we don’t need to worry about wear yet — but flash wears out at ~100,000 erase cycles per sector, which matters in real products.

title: Week 9: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
Standard W25Q commands








Command
Hex
What it does




JEDEC ID
0x9F
Read manufacturer + device ID (3 bytes) — sanity check


Read Status
0x05
Read status register (busy bit, write-enable bit)


Write Enable
0x06
Allow next write/erase command


Read Data
0x03
Read N bytes starting at 24-bit address


Page Program
0x02
Write up to 256 bytes (within one page)


Sector Erase
0x20
Erase a 4 KB sector



Pattern: Write Enable → wait for ready → Erase or Program → poll busy bit until done

The JEDEC ID command is the W10 equivalent of the WHO_AM_I we used in W08. Always run it first — if it returns the right manufacturer + device ID, you know your bus, mode, CS timing, and clock are all correct, and the rest of your code can assume a working channel. If it returns 0xFF or 0x00, you have a hardware problem and writing real code is a waste of time. Walk through the program/erase pattern: every modifying operation requires a Write Enable first, and you must poll the busy bit before issuing the next command (page program takes ~1 ms, sector erase takes ~50 ms — much longer than any single SPI transfer).

title: Week 9: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
JEDEC ID timing

Reading 0x9F returns 3 bytes — manufacturer + 2 device bytes
The expected response for a Winbond W25Q part is 0xEF (Winbond manufacturer) followed by two device-ID bytes that encode capacity. For example, W25Q16 returns 0xEF 0x40 0x15. Students will see this on a logic analyzer in the lab. If they see 0x00 0x00 0x00 the chip isn’t powered or CS is broken; if they see 0xFF 0xFF 0xFF the chip is missing or MISO is floating; if they see “almost right but shifted” it’s a CPHA mistake.

title: Week 9: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
Lab structure
Part 1 (45 min): SPI bring-up, JEDEC ID, polled mode

Wire the W25Q to the Nucleo
Configure SPI1 in CubeIDE
Read JEDEC ID — verify 0xEF as the first byte

Part 2 (40 min): Write/Erase/Read with proper command pattern

Sector erase, page program, read back
Failure injection: skip Write Enable, observe failure

Part 3 (60 min): Convert polled to DMA

Same code path, replace HAL_SPI_TransmitReceive with HAL_SPI_TransmitReceive_DMA
Add TC callback, measure CPU free time

Part 4 (35 min): Scope/LA verification + analysis

Capture SCK, MOSI, MISO, CS together
Decode protocol, verify ID matches


The single most important pedagogical move in this lab is Part 3: students get the polled version working first, then just change the function call to get a DMA version. This makes DMA feel like a refactoring step, not a foreign concept. The first time they see the LED toggle 100x faster while the SPI transfer continues in the background, the lightbulb goes on.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Bring-up checklist (memorize this)

WHO_AM_I returns 0x68 (polled) — proves I²C wiring.
GPIO toggles around Mem_Read_DMA show ~360 µs busy then ~640 µs free per ms.
Raw burst prints something like ax=16384 az=0 az=0 flat on table — proves byte order.
Scaled accel shows ~9.81 m/s² on Z flat — proves units.
Tilt-only angle moves smoothly when tilted, jumps when tapped.
Gyro-only angle drifts when sitting still.
Fused angle is smooth and doesn’t drift — fusion works.


Each step in the checklist is a checkpoint. If step 4 fails, don’t move to step 5 — go back and find why the units are wrong. This staged approach catches 90% of bugs before they cascade into “the cube is upside down” mysteries.

title: Week 9: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
Common SPI failures








Symptom
Most likely cause
Fix




All-0xFF responses
MISO not connected, or slave not responding
Check wiring; check CS asserted


All-0x00 responses
MISO shorted to GND, or chip unpowered
Check VCC; remove short


First byte garbage
Read after CS-low transient
Use a tx-rx pair, discard rx[0]


Data shifted by 1 bit
Wrong CPHA setting
Try the other phase (datasheet)


Works at low speed, fails at high
Signal integrity (long wires, no ground return)
Shorten wires, add ground wire


Write succeeds but readback is original data
Forgot Write Enable, or didn’t wait for busy
Add 0x06 + poll busy




The “first byte garbage” issue is interesting and worth pausing on. Some slaves need a brief stabilization time after CS goes low before they sample. Some HAL versions also have a one-byte latency in the rx FIFO. The robust pattern is to always discard the first received byte after CS-low for command-style transfers. The “shifted by 1 bit” failure is the CPHA classic — students will deliberately trigger this in the failure-injection part of the lab so they recognize it on a scope.

title: Week 9: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
DMA debugging tips

Callback never fires? NVIC interrupt not enabled, or wrong stream/channel mapping
First half of buffer is right, second half is wrong? Memory-increment is OFF (should be ON)
DMA seems to corrupt RAM? Forgot to set buffer size correctly, or buffer is on stack and got reused
Transfer hangs? SPI peripheral not enabled, or DMA stream still busy from a previous transfer
Use STM32CubeIDE Live Expressions to watch the DMA controller registers (NDTR counts down)


The “buffer on stack” gotcha bites everyone exactly once. If you declare uint8_t buf[1024] inside a function, kick off DMA, and return from the function, the stack frame is gone but the DMA controller is still happily writing into what is now random stack space. Always allocate DMA buffers as static, global, or heap. Mention __attribute__((aligned(4))) for systems where DMA requires alignment (Cortex-M7 with cache, less of an issue on M4).

title: Week 9: SPI Protocol & DMA
text:
Self-check before lab

Can you draw the 4-wire SPI bus from memory?
Do you know what CPOL and CPHA mean?
Can you explain why SPI has no addressing in the protocol?
Can you list the steps from “polled” to “DMA” in CubeIDE?
Do you know which command reads JEDEC ID and what response you expect?
Can you explain what HT and TC interrupts mean?


Use this slide as a 3-minute end-of-lecture self-check. Have students raise hands if they can’t answer any one of these — don’t shame, just identify who needs office-hours help before the lab.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Summary

DMA = a second processor that moves bytes for you, with a TC interrupt at the end.
I²C + DMA = HAL_I2C_Mem_Read_DMA in a timer callback, callback re-arms.
Complementary filter = α gyro + (1-α) accel, tuned by sample rate.
Yaw needs a magnetometer; roll/pitch don’t.
Visualization = ASCII CSV over UART → Python script → 3D cube.
This is the same DMA pattern you will reuse for ADC, UART, I2S, and DAC.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Questions?

Likely questions: (1) “Why not a Kalman filter?” — same idea, harder math, bring it up next year. (2) “Why is yaw drifting?” — no magnetometer, expected. (3) “Can we run the filter at 1 kHz?” — yes, on F401 it’s ~5 µs/sample, easy. (4) “What about MPU9250?” — drop-in upgrade, same I²C+DMA, plus magnetometer for yaw, perfect final-project component.

title: Week 9 (DRAFT): I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Week 9 (DRAFT)
I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization

This is the draft replacement for the SPI + W25Q week. We keep DMA — that is the transferable skill — but swap the vehicle. Instead of moving bytes between flash and RAM, we move IMU samples from the I²C peripheral into a sample buffer at a fixed rate, free the CPU to run a complementary filter, and stream roll/pitch over UART to a live 3D plot on the laptop. Same DMA mental model, much more memorable demo.

title: Week 9 (DRAFT): I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Why this week matters

Last week you talked to the MPU6050 by polling. That works at 50 Hz; it falls over at 1 kHz.
DMA is the trick that lets the CPU hand a hardware engine a sample buffer and walk away.
Orientation estimation is the canonical “real-time signal processing on an MCU” problem.
Drones, phones, VR headsets, balancing robots — all of them do exactly what you’re about to do.
By the end of the lecture you will know how to stream IMU samples into RAM with zero CPU cost and turn them into a smooth 3D visualization.


The pitch to students is: last week your code did one thing (read the IMU). This week it does three things at once (DMA pulls samples, CPU runs the filter, UART pushes results) — and that is what real embedded systems look like. Reinforce that DMA is everywhere: STM32 ADC, UART, I2S audio, DAC, SPI displays, and yes I²C all use the same DMA controller. Once you understand the pattern here, the others are just register-name changes.

title: Week 9 (DRAFT): I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Learning objectives

Explain how DMA moves data without CPU involvement and what HT/TC interrupts mean
Configure HAL I²C in DMA mode for periodic burst reads of an MPU6050
Convert raw accel/gyro readings to physical units (g, °/s) at fixed scale
Implement a complementary filter for roll and pitch and explain the α tradeoff
Stream orientation over UART in a parser-friendly format
Reason about why yaw drifts without a magnetometer


The two highest-leverage objectives are the DMA mental model (HT/TC, double-buffer) and the complementary-filter intuition (gyro fast, accel slow). These are the parts students get stuck on and that the lab failure-injection tests will catch them on. The unit-conversion and UART-format objectives are mechanical but matter for the visualization to actually work.

title: Week 9 (DRAFT): I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Agenda (90 minutes)

From polled to streamed — 15 min
DMA fundamentals — 20 min
I²C + DMA on STM32 — 15 min
Orientation estimation — 25 min
Visualization & lab preview — 15 min


We deliberately spend the most time on orientation, because that is where the physical intuition lives and where students will remember the lecture months later. DMA gets 35 minutes total across Parts 1–3, which is enough to install the mental model without belaboring register-level details — the lab teaches those.

title: Week 9 (DRAFT): I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
section: The polled IMU loop you already wrote

title: Week 9 (DRAFT): I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Why 1 kHz changes everything

A control loop that fights gravity wants at least 200 Hz, ideally 1 kHz.
At 1 kHz, every sample period is 1 ms.
A polled HAL_I2C_Mem_Read for 14 bytes at 400 kHz I²C takes ~360 µs.
That’s 36% of the CPU. Just for moving bytes.
And the CPU does nothing else during that time.


Walk through the math: 14 bytes ≈ 140 bits with overhead, at 400 kHz that’s ~350 µs. Plus HAL function-call overhead. So a naïve polled 1 kHz loop burns more than a third of an 84 MHz F401 just shuffling I²C bytes. That is the wall that motivates DMA.

title: Week 9 (DRAFT): I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Polled vs IRQ vs DMA





Polled is fine for setup code (one-shot WHO_AM_I read).
Interrupt is fine when you want to react byte-by-byte.
DMA is what you want for periodic, bulk, predictable transfers — exactly the IMU case.



Make sure students understand that “interrupt mode” still spends CPU on each byte’s interrupt handler — for a 14-byte read at 400 kHz that’s 14 ISR entries per sample, which adds up. DMA is genuinely zero-CPU for the data movement; the only CPU cost is the one callback at end-of-transfer.

title: Week 9 (DRAFT): I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
What DMA actually is





A second processor that does exactly one thing: copy bytes from peripheral to memory.
Once configured, the CPU issues no instructions during the transfer.
The DMA fires a Transfer Complete (TC) interrupt at the end so the CPU knows new data is ready.



The “second processor” framing is the key idea. DMA is not a software trick or a clever interrupt pattern; it is dedicated silicon that moves bytes in parallel with the CPU. On the F401 there are two DMA controllers (DMA1 and DMA2), each with 8 streams, and each stream can be tied to one peripheral request at a time. That’s 16 simultaneous streams the chip can manage — far more than students will ever wire up at once.

title: Week 9 (DRAFT): I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
DMA streams and requests

A stream is one DMA channel: src, dst, count, direction.
A request is the trigger that says “now move one item.”
For I²C1 RX on the F401: DMA1, Stream 0, Channel 1 (look it up in the reference manual).
The peripheral’s request line wakes the stream; the stream does one read+write; counter decrements.
When the counter hits zero, the stream fires the Transfer Complete (TC) interrupt.


Emphasize the stream/channel matrix from RM0383 — it is the single most-consulted page in the reference manual when bringing up DMA. Students cannot guess the stream and channel; they must look it up. CubeMX hides this behind a dropdown, which is convenient but means students often don’t know what was actually configured. Show the table in the reference manual at least once.

title: Week 9 (DRAFT): I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Single-shot vs circular


Single-shot: counter hits zero → stream stops, TC fires once. (We use this for the IMU.)
Circular: counter wraps → stream restarts forever, HT and TC each fire once per lap.

title: Week 9 (DRAFT): I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
Week 9 (DRAFT): I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
CubeMX configuration

Connectivity → I2C1: enable, Standard mode 100 kHz or Fast mode 400 kHz
DMA Settings tab:

Add I2C1_RX → DMA1 Stream 0, Direction Peripheral-to-Memory
Mode: Normal (single-shot, re-armed in callback)
Memory increment: ✅, Peripheral increment: ❌
Data width: Byte / Byte

NVIC: enable I2C1 event interrupt and DMA1 Stream 0 global interrupt
Timer (TIM2): 1 kHz update event → triggers the DMA read in the timer callback


Students will be tempted to enable circular mode “to be safe” — talk them out of it. With circular DMA on I²C, you have to keep the I²C peripheral armed continuously, which complicates clock-stretching handling on the MPU6050 side. Single-shot, re-armed by a timer, is the simpler and more debuggable pattern for periodic sensor reads.

title: Week 9 (DRAFT): I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
The HAL call
void TIM2_PeriodElapsedCallback(TIM_HandleTypeDef *htim) {
    HAL_I2C_Mem_Read_DMA(&hi2c1,
                         MPU_ADDR << 1,
                         ACCEL_XOUT_H,
                         I2C_MEMADD_SIZE_8BIT,
                         (uint8_t*)imu_raw, 14);
}

Returns immediately — the DMA is now armed.
The HAL handles START, address, repeated-START, the burst read, and STOP.
When the 14 bytes have arrived, the MemRxCplt callback fires.


Note that the HAL function returns immediately even though the I²C transaction will take ~360 µs. That’s the entire point: the CPU is free for the next 360 µs to do whatever else (in our case, finish processing the previous sample). Students should profile this with a GPIO toggle to convince themselves it’s true.

title: Week 9 (DRAFT): I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
section: Where your code lives: the callback

title: Week 9 (DRAFT): I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
section: I²C+DMA pitfalls (every student hits at least one)
text:
I²C+DMA pitfalls (every student hits at least one)







Symptom
Likely cause




Buffer always reads zero
Forgot volatile on imu_raw[]


Reads correct once, then dies
Didn’t re-arm DMA in callback


Bytes swapped (ax looks like ay)
Wrong DMA stream/channel for I2C1_RX


Transfer hangs forever
DMA enabled but I²C event interrupt not enabled


Wrong values, occasionally
Buffer not aligned / shared with other DMA




The “I²C event interrupt not enabled” gotcha is the most confusing one because the symptom is silent failure — no callback ever fires. The HAL I²C+DMA driver still uses the I²C event interrupt to handle START/STOP/address phases, even though byte movement is via DMA. Students who only enable the DMA stream interrupt will sit there forever wondering why nothing happens.

title: Week 9 (DRAFT): I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
What we want


Roll and pitch in degrees, updated at the sample rate, smooth and drift-free over a 60-second demo.

3 axes of accel give us the gravity vector → roll and pitch.
3 axes of gyro give us angular rates → integrate for angle.
Yaw rotates about gravity → invisible to accel, drifts forever without a magnetometer.





The setup here is the same one from Week 8. Don’t re-derive MEMS physics; just remind students that accel measures the gravity vector in the body frame, and gyro measures angular rate in body frame. The art is combining these two noisy, incomplete signals into a usable angle estimate.

title: Week 9 (DRAFT): I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Tilt from the accelerometer


The accelerometer reads \(-\vec{g}\) in body frame:

\(a_y = g\sin\phi\), \(a_z = g\cos\phi\)
\(\boxed{\phi = \operatorname{atan2}(a_y, a_z)}\)

For combined roll and pitch:
\[
\theta = \operatorname{atan2}\!\left(-a_x,\, \sqrt{a_y^2 + a_z^2}\right)
\]

Absolute tilt, no integration, no drift; taps/vibration are the failure mode.





Walk through atan2: it’s the four-quadrant arctangent that picks the correct sign and quadrant. Pretty much every orientation library uses it. Show on the board what φ and θ look like geometrically — a yaw rotation does not change the gravity vector, which is why we cannot get yaw from accel alone.

title: Week 9 (DRAFT): I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Angle from the gyroscope


The gyro reads angular rate, so we integrate:
\[
\phi_k = \phi_{k-1} + \omega_x \Delta t
\]

Smooth, fast, low-noise during fast motion.
But integrating any DC offset grows the error linearly: 1°/s bias → 60° in one minute.
Gyro alone always drifts unless another sensor pulls it back.





The drift point is the most important takeaway. Students who think “I’ll just use the gyro because it’s smooth” will be horrified an hour later when their cube is pointing at the floor with the IMU sitting flat on the desk. Show them the failure mode by integrating raw gyro for 30 seconds in front of them.

title: Week 9 (DRAFT): I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
The complementary filter

\[
\phi_k = \alpha \,(\phi_{k-1} + \omega_x \Delta t) + (1 - \alpha) \, \phi_{acc}
\]

\(\alpha\) near 1 (e.g. 0.98) → mostly gyro, accel just nudges back to truth.
\(\alpha\) near 0 → mostly accel, jumpy under any motion.
Cutoff frequency: \(f_c = \frac{1-\alpha}{2\pi\, \alpha\, \Delta t}\). For \(\alpha=0.98\) at 1 kHz: \(f_c \approx 3.2\) Hz.


The α intuition is what students must walk away with. It is essentially a high-pass on the gyro and a low-pass on the accel, summed. The math at the bottom is for the curious; the lab will have them sweep α from 0.9 to 0.999 and watch the cube response change. Madgwick and Kalman are improvements on this same idea — same tradeoff, different math.

title: Week 9 (DRAFT): I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Why yaw is special

Roll and pitch are observable from gravity → accel anchors them.
Yaw is rotation about gravity → accel cannot see it.
Pure-gyro yaw drifts forever, unbounded.
Need a magnetometer (compass) to anchor yaw to magnetic north.
MPU6050 has no mag. MPU9250/9265 do — that’s the upgrade path.


This is the natural lead-in to “if you want a real attitude estimator, get a 9-axis IMU.” For the lab we will demo only roll and pitch, and we will tell students up front that yaw is not part of this week. Optionally show MPU9250 datasheet on screen for ~20 seconds to plant the seed for the final project.

title: Week 9 (DRAFT): I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
UART streaming format
Pick a format the host can parse trivially:
R,P\n
12.4,-3.1
12.5,-3.0
12.7,-2.8
...

ASCII CSV, one line per sample, line-rate ~50–100 Hz (don’t ship 1 kHz over UART).
Easy to debug — open a serial terminal and read the numbers directly.
Easy to plot — Python pyserial + matplotlib in 30 lines.
Don’t use binary unless you’ve measured a real bandwidth problem.


There’s always a temptation to invent a binary protocol with framing bytes and CRCs. Resist it for teaching. ASCII is debuggable from any serial terminal, has zero parsing bugs, and the overhead doesn’t matter at 50 Hz. Save binary protocols for when students hit a real bandwidth wall in the final project.

title: Week 9 (DRAFT): I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Host-side 3D plot
Lab ships with a Python script students just run:
python3 plot_imu.py /dev/ttyACM0 115200

Reads R,P\n lines from serial.
Renders a wireframe cube that rotates with the board.
Updates at the UART rate (50 Hz looks smooth).
Students can rotate the IMU in their hand and see the filter working.


The visualization is the payoff for the whole lecture. Make sure the script is robust — handles disconnects, bad lines, unsupported terminals — because if it doesn’t work on lab night the demo collapses. We will pre-test it on Mac/Win/Linux before lab. Optional stretch: a small web version using Three.js so students can show their parents.

title: Week 9 (DRAFT): I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Lab structure (90 min)
Part 1 (15 min) — Bring-up: wire MPU6050 (reuse W08 wiring), confirm WHO_AM_I via polled read.
Part 2 (20 min) — DMA conversion: add timer + DMA, replace polled read with HAL_I2C_Mem_Read_DMA, GPIO-toggle to confirm CPU is free.
Part 3 (25 min) — Fusion: scale to physical units, implement complementary filter, tune α.
Part 4 (20 min) — Visualization: UART format, run host script, rotate the board.
Part 5 (10 min) — Failure injection: drop volatile, swap DMA stream, set α = 1.0 — observe each failure mode and recover.

The failure injection part is critical and is what makes this a real engineering lab instead of a tutorial. Each failure mode maps to a real bug students will hit later in their careers. They should leave the lab having seen each symptom at least once with a known cause.

title: Week 9 (DRAFT): I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Common pitfalls

Forgetting volatile on the DMA buffer — values look frozen
I²C event interrupt not enabled — DMA never completes

title: Week 9 Lab: I²C + DMA — MPU6050 Orientation & 3D Visualization
text:
Key Takeaways

DMA = a second processor for bytes. TIM2 arms, DMA moves, callback flags, main loop computes.
volatile is non-negotiable for any DMA destination buffer.
The HAL I²C event IRQ is mandatory in DMA mode — DMA only moves the data phase, not START/STOP.
Always subtract gyro bias measured at boot — yaw will drift visibly within seconds otherwise.
α tunes the cutoff, not “the smoothness.” Compute fc = (1-α)/(2π α Δt) and pick the cutoff you actually want.
Yaw needs a magnetometer. MPU6050 doesn’t have one — that’s the MPU9250 upgrade and the obvious final-project lead.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
section: The polled IMU loop you already wrote

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Why 1 kHz changes everything

A control loop that fights gravity wants at least 200 Hz, ideally 1 kHz.
At 1 kHz, every sample period is 1 ms.
A polled HAL_I2C_Mem_Read for 14 bytes at 400 kHz I²C takes ~360 µs.
That’s 36% of the CPU. Just for moving bytes.
And the CPU does nothing else during that time.


Walk through the math: 14 bytes ≈ 140 bits with overhead, at 400 kHz that’s ~350 µs. Plus HAL function-call overhead. So a naïve polled 1 kHz loop burns more than a third of an 84 MHz F401 just shuffling I²C bytes. That is the wall that motivates DMA.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
DMA streams and requests

A stream is one DMA channel: src, dst, count, direction.
A request is the trigger that says “now move one item.”
For I²C1 RX on the F401: DMA1, Stream 0, Channel 1 (look it up in the reference manual).
The peripheral’s request line wakes the stream; the stream does one read+write; counter decrements.
When the counter hits zero, the stream fires the Transfer Complete (TC) interrupt.


Emphasize the stream/channel matrix from RM0383 — it is the single most-consulted page in the reference manual when bringing up DMA. Students cannot guess the stream and channel; they must look it up. CubeMX hides this behind a dropdown, which is convenient but means students often don’t know what was actually configured. Show the table in the reference manual at least once.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Single-shot vs circular


Single-shot: counter hits zero → stream stops, TC fires once. (We use this for the IMU.)
Circular: counter wraps → stream restarts forever, HT and TC each fire once per lap.
When to choose circular: the data arrives faster than you can re-arm.

48 kHz audio mic, I²S DAC playback, ADC continuous sampling for FFT
UART RX of a free-running stream (GPS NMEA, lidar, debug console)

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
The double-buffer pattern






Circular buffer split in half: DMA fills one half while CPU processes the other.
HT fires at midpoint → process bytes 0…N/2-1. TC fires at end → process bytes N/2…N-1.
Use it when: I²S audio, ADC scan capture, any continuous stream where dropping a sample is unacceptable.
Overkill for a 1 kHz IMU read — but the same chip, same DMA controller. You will reach for this in W14.


The double-buffer pattern is critical for audio, ADC streaming, and any high-rate sensor. For the IMU at 1 kHz it’s overkill (you can process each 14-byte sample in a microsecond), but the pattern is worth showing because students will encounter it again in I2S audio and ADC scan mode. For the lab we will use single-shot DMA triggered from a timer, which is simpler.

CubeMX configuration

DMA Settings tab:

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
The HAL call
void TIM2_PeriodElapsedCallback(TIM_HandleTypeDef *htim) {
    HAL_I2C_Mem_Read_DMA(&hi2c1,
                         MPU_ADDR << 1,
                         ACCEL_XOUT_H,
                         I2C_MEMADD_SIZE_8BIT,
                         (uint8_t*)imu_raw, 14);
}

Returns immediately — the DMA is now armed.
The HAL handles START, address, repeated-START, the burst read, and STOP.
When the 14 bytes have arrived, the MemRxCplt callback fires.


Note that the HAL function returns immediately even though the I²C transaction will take ~360 µs. That’s the entire point: the CPU is free for the next 360 µs to do whatever else (in our case, finish processing the previous sample). Students should profile this with a GPIO toggle to convince themselves it’s true.

I²C+DMA pitfalls (every student hits at least one)







Symptom

Buffer always reads zero

The “I²C event interrupt not enabled” gotcha is the most confusing one because the symptom is silent failure — no callback ever fires. text:
What we want from the IMU

3 axes of accel give us the gravity vector → roll and pitch.
3 axes of gyro give us angular rates → integrate for angle.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Tilt from the accelerometer


The accelerometer reads \(-\vec{g}\) in body frame:

\(a_y = g\sin\phi\), \(a_z = g\cos\phi\)
\(\boxed{\phi = \operatorname{atan2}(a_y, a_z)}\)

For combined roll and pitch:
\[
\theta = \operatorname{atan2}\!\left(-a_x,\, \sqrt{a_y^2 + a_z^2}\right)
\]

Absolute tilt, no integration, no drift; taps/vibration are the failure mode.





Walk through atan2: it’s the four-quadrant arctangent that picks the correct sign and quadrant. Pretty much every orientation library uses it. Show on the board what φ and θ look like geometrically — a yaw rotation does not change the gravity vector, which is why we cannot get yaw from accel alone.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Angle from the gyroscope


The gyro reads angular rate, so we integrate:
\[
\phi_k = \phi_{k-1} + \omega_x \Delta t
\]

Smooth, fast, low-noise during fast motion.
But integrating any DC offset grows the error linearly: 1°/s bias → 60° in one minute.
Gyro alone always drifts unless another sensor pulls it back.





The drift point is the most important takeaway. Students who think “I’ll just use the gyro because it’s smooth” will be horrified an hour later when their cube is pointing at the floor with the IMU sitting flat on the desk. Show them the failure mode by integrating raw gyro for 30 seconds in front of them.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
The complementary filter

\[
\phi_k = \alpha \,(\phi_{k-1} + \omega_x \Delta t) + (1 - \alpha) \, \phi_{acc}
\]

\(\alpha\) near 1 (e.g. 0.98) → mostly gyro, accel just nudges back to truth.
\(\alpha\) near 0 → mostly accel, jumpy under any motion.
Cutoff frequency: \(f_c = \frac{1-\alpha}{2\pi\, \alpha\, \Delta t}\). For \(\alpha=0.98\) at 1 kHz: \(f_c \approx 3.2\) Hz.


The α intuition is what students must walk away with. It is essentially a high-pass on the gyro and a low-pass on the accel, summed. The math at the bottom is for the curious; the lab will have them sweep α from 0.9 to 0.999 and watch the cube response change. Madgwick and Kalman are improvements on this same idea — same tradeoff, different math.
