title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Why yaw is special

Roll and pitch are observable from gravity → accel anchors them.
Yaw is rotation about gravity → accel cannot see it.
Pure-gyro yaw drifts forever, unbounded.
Need a magnetometer (compass) to anchor yaw to magnetic north.
MPU6050 has no mag. MPU9250/9265 do — that’s the upgrade path.


This is the natural lead-in to “if you want a real attitude estimator, get a 9-axis IMU.” For the lab we will demo only roll and pitch, and we will tell students up front that yaw is not part of this week. Optionally show MPU9250 datasheet on screen for ~20 seconds to plant the seed for the final project.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
UART streaming format
Pick a format the host can parse trivially:
R,P\n
12.4,-3.1
12.5,-3.0
12.7,-2.8
...

ASCII CSV, one line per sample, line-rate ~50–100 Hz (don’t ship 1 kHz over UART).
Easy to debug — open a serial terminal and read the numbers directly.
Easy to plot — Python pyserial + matplotlib in 30 lines.
Don’t use binary unless you’ve measured a real bandwidth problem.


There’s always a temptation to invent a binary protocol with framing bytes and CRCs. Resist it for teaching. ASCII is debuggable from any serial terminal, has zero parsing bugs, and the overhead doesn’t matter at 50 Hz. Save binary protocols for when students hit a real bandwidth wall in the final project.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Host-side 3D plot
Lab ships with a Python script students just run:
python3 plot_imu.py /dev/ttyACM0 115200

Reads R,P\n lines from serial.
Renders a wireframe cube that rotates with the board.
Updates at the UART rate (50 Hz looks smooth).
Students can rotate the IMU in their hand and see the filter working.


The visualization is the payoff for the whole lecture. Make sure the script is robust — handles disconnects, bad lines, unsupported terminals — because if it doesn’t work on lab night the demo collapses. We will pre-test it on Mac/Win/Linux before lab. Optional stretch: a small web version using Three.js so students can show their parents.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Lab structure (90 min)
Part 1 (15 min) — Bring-up: wire MPU6050 (reuse W08 wiring), confirm WHO_AM_I via polled read.
Part 2 (20 min) — DMA conversion: add timer + DMA, replace polled read with HAL_I2C_Mem_Read_DMA, GPIO-toggle to confirm CPU is free.
Part 3 (25 min) — Fusion: scale to physical units, implement complementary filter, tune α.
Part 4 (20 min) — Visualization: UART format, run host script, rotate the board.
Part 5 (10 min) — Failure injection: drop volatile, swap DMA stream, set α = 1.0 — observe each failure mode and recover.

The failure injection part is critical and is what makes this a real engineering lab instead of a tutorial. Each failure mode maps to a real bug students will hit later in their careers. They should leave the lab having seen each symptom at least once with a known cause.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Common pitfalls

Forgetting volatile on the DMA buffer — values look frozen
I²C event interrupt not enabled — DMA never completes
Using the wrong DMA stream/channel — silent garbage
Computing angles in the DMA callback — ISR overruns, system stalls
Setting α too aggressive (α = 0.999 at 50 Hz → fc = 0.16 Hz, accel correction too slow)
Sending 1 kHz of data over 115200 baud UART — buffer overruns


Walk through each one with a one-sentence diagnosis. Students who recognize the symptom in lab will save 30 minutes of confusion. The α-tuning point matters: there’s no universal best α; it depends on sample rate. Make sure students compute the cutoff frequency for their chosen α, not just copy 0.98 from the slide.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Connection to other weeks

Week 8 (I²C): built the polled MPU6050 driver this week replaces.
Week 10/11 (UART): the streaming format will be reused for telemetry.
Week 12 (fault logging): DMA pattern is reused for ADC capture.
Final project: any project that needs orientation (balancing robot, drone, gimbal) builds directly on this lab.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
section: Pitch is the same idea, about Y
text:
Pitch is the same idea, about Y


Same geometry, now looking down body +Y:

\(-a_x = g\sin\theta\), \(a_z = g\cos\theta\)
\(\boxed{\theta = \operatorname{atan2}(-a_x,\, a_z)}\)

The minus sign makes \(\theta>0\) = nose down — match it to what your firmware emits.
When roll is nonzero, replace \(a_z\) with \(\sqrt{a_y^2+a_z^2}\) — the gravity component perpendicular to body \(X\).




The point of this slide is symmetry: roll about X and pitch about Y are the same construction, just looking down a different body axis. Drive that home so students remember the formula by reasoning, not memorisation. Sign convention here is the firmware’s: -ax positive => nose down => θ positive. If a student wants nose-up positive, just flip the sign in their code; the physics is unchanged. Why pitch needs the sqrt and roll doesn’t: in ZYX Euler order, the cos(θ) factors cancel in roll’s a_y/a_z ratio but not in pitch’s, so pitch decouples cleanly only via the full body-frame projection.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
section: Why yaw is invisible to gravity
text:
Why yaw is invisible to gravity


Top-down view: rotating the board about \(+Z\) (yaw) leaves \(\vec{g}\) aligned with body \(+Z\) in both poses.
The accelerometer reads exactly the same \((0, 0, +g)\) at \(\psi = 0°\) and at \(\psi = 60°\) — the signal carries zero information about \(\psi\).


This is the geometric punchline: yaw is rotation about the gravity vector itself, so the body-frame projection of gravity is unchanged. Any tilt-from-accel algorithm — atan2, Madgwick, Kalman with accel-only updates — has the same blind spot. The accel doesn’t fail noisily; it gives a perfectly valid answer that just doesn’t constrain yaw at all.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
section: So how do we get absolute yaw?
text:
So how do we get absolute yaw?


Gyro alone: integrate \(\omega_z\) → drift is unbounded (1°/s bias = 60° error per minute).
Magnetometer: measures Earth’s field. Its body-frame components rotate with yaw:
\[\psi = \operatorname{atan2}(-b_y,\, b_x)\]
→ absolute anchor for yaw, the same role accel plays for roll/pitch.

In practice:

MPU6050 has no mag → this lab’s yaw is gyro-only and drifts by design.
MPU9250 / 9265 add a mag on the same I²C bus → 9-DoF drop-in upgrade.
Mags fail near motors, speakers, steel — and need hard/soft-iron calibration.



The takeaway is that absolute orientation needs at least one observation that is sensitive to the unknown angle. Gravity sees roll and pitch; the magnetic field sees yaw. With both, you have a 6-DoF reference that fully observes the body’s attitude. The full mag-to-yaw derivation: Earth’s horizontal field \(h\) rotates as \(b_x = h\cos\psi\), \(b_y = -h\sin\psi\) in the body frame, hence the atan2. Hard-iron = constant offset (nearby ferrous metal magnetized by the field), soft-iron = direction-dependent gain (nearby permeable metal distorting the field) — both are calibrated on the bench by spinning the device and fitting an ellipsoid. Visual / optical-flow yaw anchors exist for environments where mags are unreliable (indoor drones, robots near steel) — final-project territory.


This is the natural lead-in to “if you want a real attitude estimator, get a 9-axis IMU.” For the lab we will demo only roll and pitch, and we will tell students up front that yaw is not part of this week. Optionally show MPU9250 datasheet on screen for ~20 seconds to plant the seed for the final project.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Week 9
I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization

We keep DMA — that is the transferable skill — and apply it to streaming IMU samples from the I²C peripheral into a sample buffer at a fixed rate, freeing the CPU to run a complementary filter and stream roll/pitch over UART to a live 3D plot on the laptop. The DMA mental model here transfers directly to ADC, UART, I2S, and SPI with no new ideas.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Why this week matters

Last week you talked to the MPU6050 by polling. That works at 50 Hz; it falls over at 1 kHz.
DMA is the trick that lets the CPU hand a hardware engine a sample buffer and walk away.
Orientation estimation is the canonical “real-time signal processing on an MCU” problem.
Drones, phones, VR headsets, balancing robots — all of them do exactly what you’re about to do.
By the end of the lecture you will know how to stream IMU samples into RAM with zero CPU cost and turn them into a smooth 3D visualization.


The pitch to students is: last week your code did one thing (read the IMU). This week it does three things at once (DMA pulls samples, CPU runs the filter, UART pushes results) — and that is what real embedded systems look like. Reinforce that DMA is everywhere: STM32 ADC, UART, I2S audio, DAC, SPI displays, and yes I²C all use the same DMA controller. Once you understand the pattern here, the others are just register-name changes.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Learning objectives

Explain how DMA moves data without CPU involvement and what HT/TC interrupts mean
Configure HAL I²C in DMA mode for periodic burst reads of an MPU6050
Convert raw accel/gyro readings to physical units (g, °/s) at fixed scale
Implement a complementary filter for roll and pitch and explain the α tradeoff
Stream orientation over UART in a parser-friendly format
Reason about why yaw drifts without a magnetometer


The two highest-leverage objectives are the DMA mental model (HT/TC, double-buffer) and the complementary-filter intuition (gyro fast, accel slow). These are the parts students get stuck on and that the lab failure-injection tests will catch them on. The unit-conversion and UART-format objectives are mechanical but matter for the visualization to actually work.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Agenda (90 minutes)

From polled to streamed — 15 min
DMA fundamentals — 20 min
I²C + DMA on STM32 — 15 min
Orientation estimation — 25 min
Visualization & lab preview — 15 min


We deliberately spend the most time on orientation, because that is where the physical intuition lives and where students will remember the lecture months later. DMA gets 35 minutes total across Parts 1–3, which is enough to install the mental model without belaboring register-level details — the lab teaches those.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
section: The polled IMU loop you already wrote

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Why 1 kHz changes everything

A control loop that fights gravity wants at least 200 Hz, ideally 1 kHz.
At 1 kHz, every sample period is 1 ms.
A polled HAL_I2C_Mem_Read for 14 bytes at 400 kHz I²C takes ~360 µs.
That’s 36% of the CPU. Just for moving bytes.
And the CPU does nothing else during that time.


Walk through the math: 14 bytes ≈ 140 bits with overhead, at 400 kHz that’s ~350 µs. Plus HAL function-call overhead. So a naïve polled 1 kHz loop burns more than a third of an 84 MHz F401 just shuffling I²C bytes. That is the wall that motivates DMA.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Polled vs IRQ vs DMA





Polled is fine for setup code (one-shot WHO_AM_I read).
Interrupt is fine when you want to react byte-by-byte.
DMA is what you want for periodic, bulk, predictable transfers — exactly the IMU case.



Make sure students understand that “interrupt mode” still spends CPU on each byte’s interrupt handler — for a 14-byte read at 400 kHz that’s 14 ISR entries per sample, which adds up. DMA is genuinely zero-CPU for the data movement; the only CPU cost is the one callback at end-of-transfer.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
What DMA actually is





A second processor that does exactly one thing: copy bytes from peripheral to memory.
Once configured, the CPU issues no instructions during the transfer.
The DMA fires a Transfer Complete (TC) interrupt at the end so the CPU knows new data is ready.



The “second processor” framing is the key idea. DMA is not a software trick or a clever interrupt pattern; it is dedicated silicon that moves bytes in parallel with the CPU. On the F401 there are two DMA controllers (DMA1 and DMA2), each with 8 streams, and each stream can be tied to one peripheral request at a time. That’s 16 simultaneous streams the chip can manage — far more than students will ever wire up at once.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
DMA streams and requests

A stream is one DMA channel: src, dst, count, direction.
A request is the trigger that says “now move one item.”
For I²C1 RX on the F401: DMA1, Stream 0, Channel 1 (look it up in the reference manual).
The peripheral’s request line wakes the stream; the stream does one read+write; counter decrements.
When the counter hits zero, the stream fires the Transfer Complete (TC) interrupt.


Emphasize the stream/channel matrix from RM0383 — it is the single most-consulted page in the reference manual when bringing up DMA. Students cannot guess the stream and channel; they must look it up. CubeMX hides this behind a dropdown, which is convenient but means students often don’t know what was actually configured. Show the table in the reference manual at least once.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Single-shot vs circular


Single-shot: counter hits zero → stream stops, TC fires once. (We use this for the IMU.)
Circular: counter wraps → stream restarts forever, HT and TC each fire once per lap.
When to choose circular: the data arrives faster than you can re-arm.

48 kHz audio mic, I²S DAC playback, ADC continuous sampling for FFT
UART RX of a free-running stream (GPS NMEA, lidar, debug console)

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
The double-buffer pattern






Circular buffer split in half: DMA fills one half while CPU processes the other.
HT fires at midpoint → process bytes 0…N/2-1. TC fires at end → process bytes N/2…N-1.
Use it when: I²S audio, ADC scan capture, any continuous stream where dropping a sample is unacceptable.
Overkill for a 1 kHz IMU read — but the same chip, same DMA controller. You will reach for this in W14.


The double-buffer pattern is critical for audio, ADC streaming, and any high-rate sensor. For the IMU at 1 kHz it’s overkill (you can process each 14-byte sample in a microsecond), but the pattern is worth showing because students will encounter it again in I2S audio and ADC scan mode. For the lab we will use single-shot DMA triggered from a timer, which is simpler.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Wiring recap (from W08)


VCC→3.3 V, GND→GND, SCL→PB8, SDA→PB9, AD0→GND (address 0x68).
Optional: tie INT to PA0 if you want the IMU itself to trigger reads instead of the timer.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
CubeMX configuration

Connectivity → I2C1: enable, Standard mode 100 kHz or Fast mode 400 kHz
DMA Settings tab:

Add I2C1_RX → DMA1 Stream 0, Direction Peripheral-to-Memory
Mode: Normal (single-shot, re-armed in callback)
Memory increment: ✅, Peripheral increment: ❌
Data width: Byte / Byte

NVIC: enable I2C1 event interrupt and DMA1 Stream 0 global interrupt
Timer (TIM2): 1 kHz update event → triggers the DMA read in the timer callback


Students will be tempted to enable circular mode “to be safe” — talk them out of it. With circular DMA on I²C, you have to keep the I²C peripheral armed continuously, which complicates clock-stretching handling on the MPU6050 side. Single-shot, re-armed by a timer, is the simpler and more debuggable pattern for periodic sensor reads.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
The HAL call
void TIM2_PeriodElapsedCallback(TIM_HandleTypeDef *htim) {
    HAL_I2C_Mem_Read_DMA(&hi2c1,
                         MPU_ADDR << 1,
                         ACCEL_XOUT_H,
                         I2C_MEMADD_SIZE_8BIT,
                         (uint8_t*)imu_raw, 14);
}

Returns immediately — the DMA is now armed.
The HAL handles START, address, repeated-START, the burst read, and STOP.
When the 14 bytes have arrived, the MemRxCplt callback fires.


Note that the HAL function returns immediately even though the I²C transaction will take ~360 µs. That’s the entire point: the CPU is free for the next 360 µs to do whatever else (in our case, finish processing the previous sample). Students should profile this with a GPIO toggle to convince themselves it’s true.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
section: Where your code lives: the callback

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
section: I²C+DMA pitfalls (every student hits at least one)
text:
I²C+DMA pitfalls (every student hits at least one)







Symptom
Likely cause




Buffer always reads zero
Forgot volatile on imu_raw[]


Reads correct once, then dies
Didn’t re-arm DMA in callback


Bytes swapped (ax looks like ay)
Wrong DMA stream/channel for I2C1_RX


Transfer hangs forever
DMA enabled but I²C event interrupt not enabled


Wrong values, occasionally
Buffer not aligned / shared with other DMA




The “I²C event interrupt not enabled” gotcha is the most confusing one because the symptom is silent failure — no callback ever fires. The HAL I²C+DMA driver still uses the I²C event interrupt to handle START/STOP/address phases, even though byte movement is via DMA. Students who only enable the DMA stream interrupt will sit there forever wondering why nothing happens.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
What is orientation?
Orientation is the rotational state of a rigid body — which way it points in 3D space.

A rigid body in 3D has 6 degrees of freedom:

3 for position (where it is — \(x, y, z\))
3 for orientation (which way it points)

This week the IMU sits still; we track only the orientation.
It changes every time you tilt, twist, or rotate the board.


The split between position and orientation is fundamental — students will see this distinction again in robotics, computer graphics, AR/VR, drones. Make the point that an IMU can only measure orientation directly; tracking position requires a much harder integration of acceleration twice over (and that’s why GPS exists). For this lab, we are firmly in the orientation-only regime: the IMU sits in your hand, and we estimate its rotation.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Representing orientation: roll, pitch, yaw


Three rotations about the body-frame axes:

\(\phi\) (roll) — rotation about body \(+X\)
\(\theta\) (pitch) — rotation about body \(+Y\)
\(\psi\) (yaw) — rotation about body \(+Z\)

These three numbers are Euler angles.




Mention briefly that Euler angles have a known weakness — gimbal lock when pitch reaches ±90° — but that for tilt sensing in the ±60° range we will live in this lab, it is a non-issue. Quaternions and rotation matrices come up in any serious flight controller or game engine; pose them as natural extensions for students who go deeper. The body-frame point is critical: roll/pitch/yaw are rotations about axes that move with the IMU, not fixed to the world.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
section: What we want from the IMU
text:
What we want from the IMU
Roll and pitch in degrees, updated at the sample rate, smooth and drift-free over a 60-second demo.

3 axes of accel give us the gravity vector → roll and pitch.
3 axes of gyro give us angular rates → integrate for angle.
Yaw rotates about gravity → invisible to accel, drifts forever without a magnetometer.
This week: roll and pitch only. Yaw needs a magnetometer (the 9-DOF upgrade).


The setup here is the same one from Week 8. Don’t re-derive MEMS physics; just remind students that accel measures the gravity vector in the body frame, and gyro measures angular rate in body frame. The art is combining these two noisy, incomplete signals into a usable angle estimate.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Tilt from the accelerometer


The accelerometer reads \(-\vec{g}\) in body frame:

\(a_y = g\sin\phi\), \(a_z = g\cos\phi\)
\(\boxed{\phi = \operatorname{atan2}(a_y, a_z)}\)

For combined roll and pitch:
\[
\theta = \operatorname{atan2}\!\left(-a_x,\, \sqrt{a_y^2 + a_z^2}\right)
\]

Absolute tilt, no integration, no drift; taps/vibration are the failure mode.





Walk through atan2: it’s the four-quadrant arctangent that picks the correct sign and quadrant. Pretty much every orientation library uses it. Show on the board what φ and θ look like geometrically — a yaw rotation does not change the gravity vector, which is why we cannot get yaw from accel alone.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
section: Pitch is the same idea, about Y
text:
Pitch is the same idea, about Y


Same geometry, now looking down body +Y:

\(-a_x = g\sin\theta\), \(a_z = g\cos\theta\)
\(\boxed{\theta = \operatorname{atan2}(-a_x,\, a_z)}\)

The minus sign makes \(\theta>0\) = nose down — match it to what your firmware emits.
When roll is nonzero, replace \(a_z\) with \(\sqrt{a_y^2+a_z^2}\) — the gravity component perpendicular to body \(X\).

If a student wants nose-up positive, just flip the sign in their code; the physics is unchanged. title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Angle from the gyroscope


The gyro reads angular rate, so we integrate:
\[
\phi_k = \phi_{k-1} + \omega_x \Delta t
\]

Smooth, fast, low-noise during fast motion.
But integrating any DC offset grows the error linearly: 1°/s bias → 60° in one minute.
Gyro alone always drifts unless another sensor pulls it back.





The drift point is the most important takeaway. Students who think “I’ll just use the gyro because it’s smooth” will be horrified an hour later when their cube is pointing at the floor with the IMU sitting flat on the desk. Show them the failure mode by integrating raw gyro for 30 seconds in front of them.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
The complementary filter

\[
\phi_k = \alpha \,(\phi_{k-1} + \omega_x \Delta t) + (1 - \alpha) \, \phi_{acc}
\]

\(\alpha\) near 1 (e.g. 0.98) → mostly gyro, accel just nudges back to truth.
\(\alpha\) near 0 → mostly accel, jumpy under any motion.
Cutoff frequency: \(f_c = \frac{1-\alpha}{2\pi\, \alpha\, \Delta t}\). For \(\alpha=0.98\) at 1 kHz: \(f_c \approx 3.2\) Hz.


The α intuition is what students must walk away with. It is essentially a high-pass on the gyro and a low-pass on the accel, summed. The math at the bottom is for the curious; the lab will have them sweep α from 0.9 to 0.999 and watch the cube response change. Madgwick and Kalman are improvements on this same idea — same tradeoff, different math.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Choosing α: tilt + tap test


Sweep α from 0.9 to 1.0; watch the response to a tilt-then-tap input.

α = 0.9 → accel-dominated, every tap throws the angle.
α = 1.0 → gyro-only, drifts away even with no motion.
α = 0.98 at 1 kHz → 3.2 Hz cutoff: tap rejected, drift corrected.





The simulated tilt-then-tap test is the canonical α-tuning experiment students will run in lab. Walk through the three regimes: too-low α (accel takes over and rings on every tap), too-high α (drift wins, error grows without bound), sweet-spot α (smooth response with bounded error). The lab will have students sweep α from 0.9 to 0.999 and watch the cube response change in real time.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Lab structure (90 min)
Part 1 (15 min) — Bring-up: wire MPU6050 (reuse W08 wiring), confirm WHO_AM_I via polled read.
Part 2 (20 min) — DMA conversion: add timer + DMA, replace polled read with HAL_I2C_Mem_Read_DMA, GPIO-toggle to confirm CPU is free.
Part 3 (25 min) — Fusion: scale to physical units, implement complementary filter, tune α.
Part 4 (20 min) — Visualization: UART format, run host script, rotate the board.
Part 5 (10 min) — Failure injection: drop volatile, swap DMA stream, set α = 1.0 — observe each failure mode and recover.

The failure injection part is critical and is what makes this a real engineering lab instead of a tutorial. Each failure mode maps to a real bug students will hit later in their careers. They should leave the lab having seen each symptom at least once with a known cause.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Bring-up checklist (memorize this)

WHO_AM_I returns 0x68 (polled) — proves I²C wiring.
GPIO toggles around Mem_Read_DMA show ~360 µs busy then ~640 µs free per ms.
Raw burst prints something like ax=16384 az=0 az=0 flat on table — proves byte order.
Scaled accel shows ~9.81 m/s² on Z flat — proves units.
Tilt-only angle moves smoothly when tilted, jumps when tapped.
Gyro-only angle drifts when sitting still.
Fused angle is smooth and doesn’t drift — fusion works.


Each step in the checklist is a checkpoint. If step 4 fails, don’t move to step 5 — go back and find why the units are wrong. This staged approach catches 90% of bugs before they cascade into “the cube is upside down” mysteries.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Common pitfalls

Forgetting volatile on the DMA buffer — values look frozen
I²C event interrupt not enabled — DMA never completes
Using the wrong DMA stream/channel — silent garbage
Computing angles in the DMA callback — ISR overruns, system stalls
Setting α too aggressive (α = 0.999 at 50 Hz → fc = 0.16 Hz, accel correction too slow)
Sending 1 kHz of data over 115200 baud UART — buffer overruns


Walk through each one with a one-sentence diagnosis. Students who recognize the symptom in lab will save 30 minutes of confusion. The α-tuning point matters: there’s no universal best α; it depends on sample rate. Make sure students compute the cutoff frequency for their chosen α, not just copy 0.98 from the slide.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Summary

DMA = a second processor that moves bytes for you, with a TC interrupt at the end.
I²C + DMA = HAL_I2C_Mem_Read_DMA in a timer callback, callback re-arms.
Complementary filter = α gyro + (1-α) accel, tuned by sample rate.
Yaw needs a magnetometer; roll/pitch don’t.
Visualization = ASCII CSV over UART → Python script → 3D cube.
This is the same DMA pattern you will reuse for ADC, UART, I2S, and DAC.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Connection to other weeks

Week 8 (I²C): built the polled MPU6050 driver this week replaces.
Week 10/11 (UART): the streaming format will be reused for telemetry.
Week 12 (fault logging): DMA pattern is reused for ADC capture.
Final project: any project that needs orientation (balancing robot, drone, gimbal) builds directly on this lab.

title: Week 9: I²C + DMA — IMU Orientation & Visualization
text:
Questions?

Likely questions: (1) “Why not a Kalman filter?” — same idea, harder math, bring it up next year. (2) “Why is yaw drifting?” — no magnetometer, expected. (3) “Can we run the filter at 1 kHz?” — yes, on F401 it’s ~5 µs/sample, easy. (4) “What about MPU9250?” — drop-in upgrade, same I²C+DMA, plus magnetometer for yaw, perfect final-project component.

Demo

title: Week 9 Lab: I²C + DMA — MPU6050 Orientation & 3D Visualization
text:
Step 5.3: Failure Injection
For each: predict, inject, observe, restore.
Test 1 — Drop volatile from imu_raw[]. Rebuild.

Compiler caches the buffer; angles freeze at whatever value the registers happened to hold. Cube becomes a statue.

title: Week 9 Lab: I²C + DMA — MPU6050 Orientation & 3D Visualization
text:
Failure Injection (cont.)
Test 2 — Set α = 1.0. Rebuild.

Filter is now gyro-only. Cube starts correct, drifts away within ~30 s even sitting still.
Test 3 — Set α = 0.5. Rebuild.


Cube is jittery and every tap on the table throws it. That’s the “too much accel” failure mode.

title: Week 9 Lab: I²C + DMA — MPU6050 Orientation & 3D Visualization
text:
Failure Injection (cont.)
Test 4 — Disable the I²C event IRQ in NVIC, regenerate, rebuild.

MemRxCpltCallback never fires; imu_ready stays 0; UART goes silent. Most confusing failure of the day — re-enable the IRQ and it springs back.

title: Week 9 Lab: I²C + DMA — MPU6050 Orientation & 3D Visualization
text:
Key Takeaways

DMA = a second processor for bytes. TIM2 arms, DMA moves, callback flags, main loop computes.
volatile is non-negotiable for any DMA destination buffer.
The HAL I²C event IRQ is mandatory in DMA mode — DMA only moves the data phase, not START/STOP.
Always subtract gyro bias measured at boot — yaw will drift visibly within seconds otherwise.
α tunes the cutoff, not “the smoothness.” Compute fc = (1-α)/(2π α Δt) and pick the cutoff you actually want.
Yaw needs a magnetometer. MPU6050 doesn’t have one — that’s the MPU9250 upgrade and the obvious final-project lead.

title: Week 11: Display Interfacing
text:
Week 11
Display Interfacing: Character LCD and TFT Displays

This revised deck focuses on two practical display classes students are likely to wire in lab projects: HD44780 character LCDs for simple status output and ST7789 TFT modules for color graphical interfaces. Keep the comparison practical: the character LCD is low-resource and slow but robust; the TFT is flexible and visual but demands bandwidth, careful protocol sequencing, and usually DMA.

title: Week 11: Display Interfacing
text:
Why this week matters

Visual feedback turns a sensor into an instrument
Character LCDs are still useful for simple status and debug panels
TFT displays make embedded systems feel like products, not demos
Display selection directly impacts RAM, pins, SPI bandwidth, and CPU load
Display bugs are usually visible, but the cause is often timing or protocol order


Use concrete examples: a bench instrument can use a 16x2 LCD for voltage/current readout, while a motor controller or sensor dashboard may need color graphs on a TFT. The main engineering theme is observability under resource constraints.

title: Week 11: Display Interfacing
text:
Learning objectives

Wire and drive an HD44780 character LCD through an I2C backpack
Explain how the I2C backpack creates HD44780 4-bit nibble transfers
Diagnose common character LCD address, wiring, contrast, and initialization failures
Explain TFT pixels, RGB565 color format, and framebuffer size
Describe the ST7789 command/data protocol over SPI
Explain how bitmap fonts become pixel streams on a TFT
Explain why TFT refresh usually needs high-speed SPI and DMA


The assessment emphasis should be practical: students should be able to explain why the LCD receives two nibbles per byte, calculate TFT frame size, and identify why TFT updates become a bandwidth problem.

Common failure modes and what to measure




Keep the session centered on character LCDs versus color TFTs.

Color TFT is listed for context; it is not covered this week.

Ask students to guess the framebuffer size for 128×64 monochrome: 128 × 64 bits = 8192 bits = 1024 bytes = 1 kB. Point out that for the STM32F401 with 96 kB SRAM, even a full-color 320×240 frame at 16-bit color (150 kB) would exceed the available RAM. That single fact explains why color TFT drivers almost always use DMA and partial-update strategies.

title: Week 11: Display Interfacing
section: Selecting a display for your project
text:
Selecting a display for your project




UI complexity
Text only → Character LCD
Icons/status → Graphical LCD or OLED
Animation → OLED or TFT (RAM check)


MCU resources — STM32F401: 96 kB SRAM, 512 kB Flash
128×64 mono framebuffer = 1 kB ✓
320×240 color framebuffer ≈ 150 kB ✗


Pin availability
4-bit parallel: 6 GPIO
SPI: 3–4 shared pins
I²C: 2 shared pins





Power budget
LCD backlight: 15–30 mA
OLED current scales with pixels ON
No backlight needed for OLED


Environmental factors
Sunlight: transflective LCD > OLED
Viewing angle: OLED > LCD
Temperature: check datasheet


Cost & availability
HD44780 LCD: cheapest, ubiquitous
SSD1306 OLED: cheap, widely available




Walk through the STM32F401 RAM constraint explicitly: 96 kB is not as much as it sounds when you add an RTOS stack, sensor buffers, and a framebuffer. Emphasize that this is a real-world constraint calculation, not an academic exercise. Students regularly blow past RAM on color display projects. The environmental factors row often surprises students: OLED looks beautiful indoors but washes out in direct sunlight, while a transflective LCD is still legible.

title: Week 11: Display Interfacing
text:
HD44780 character LCD overview



The workhorse: still common, cheap, and robust
Text only — displays from internal CGROM (5x8 dot matrix per character)
Up to 8 user-defined 5x8 glyphs in CGRAM (bar graphs, simple icons)
Supply voltage: 2.7-5.5 V; logic often 5 V — check clones for 3.3 V tolerance
Backlight: LED, typically 15-30 mA; check if series resistor is included
Contrast: analog voltage on VO pin via 10 kΩ pot

Common pitfall: incorrect VO makes display appear blank or show solid blocks.




16x2 Character LCD




Hold up a physical HD44780 module if available. Point out the 16-pin header at the top. The contrast potentiometer issue bites almost every student on first use: they power it on and see nothing, or see solid black rectangles. The fix is simply to turn the pot before rewiring everything.

title: Week 11: Display Interfacing
text:
HD44780: 4-bit wiring


MCU Pin  | LCD Pin | Function
---------|---------|----------------------
PB0      | D4      | Data Bit 4
PB1      | D5      | Data Bit 5
PB2      | D6      | Data Bit 6
PB3      | D7      | Data Bit 7
PB4      | RS      | Register Select (0=Cmd, 1=Data)
PB5      | E       | Enable (clock for transfer)
GND      | RW      | Read/Write -> tie LOW
3V3/5V   | VDD     | Power supply
GND      | VSS     | Ground
Wiper    | VO      | Contrast (from 10 kΩ pot)
(Opt)    | A / K   | Backlight anode / cathode

Leave LCD pins DB0-DB3 floating or tied to GND
Each byte is sent as two 4-bit nibbles





HD44780 pin functions




4-bit mode is almost always preferred over 8-bit in practice because it saves four GPIO pins. Explain nibble transmission: upper 4 bits first, then lower 4 bits, with an E pulse for each. The RW pin is tied to GND for this course implementation.

title: Week 11: Display Interfacing
text:
HD44780: critical timing
The E (Enable) pulse still clocks data into the controller

Data is latched on the falling edge of E
With the backpack, E is toggled by I2C writes to the PCF8574
I2C is slower than the E minimum pulse width, but the LCD execution delay still matters
Most commands: ~37 us execution time
ClearDisplay and ReturnHome: ~1.53 ms — use HAL_Delay(2) after these


HD44780 Enable pulse timingDelay rule for this lab:
Use fixed delays after writes; add HAL_Delay(2) after ClearDisplay and ReturnHome.

Students often ask why I2C timing is not enough by itself. I2C makes the external E pulse slow enough, but it does not make the HD44780 finish internal commands faster. Fixed delays are still the required approach.

title: Week 11: Display Interfacing
text:
HD44780: power-on initialization (4-bit mode)





HD44780 initialization flow



Exact command sequence
wait >15 ms after VDD valid

0x30, wait >4.1 ms
0x30, wait >100 us
0x30, wait >100 us

0x20  -> 4-bit mode
0x28  -> 4-bit, 2 lines, 5x8
0x08  -> display off
0x01  -> clear, wait >2 ms
0x06  -> increment cursor
0x0C  -> display on

Key takeaway: initialization is rigid. Miss one step and nothing works.

The triple 0x30 sequence guarantees the interface mode regardless of the controller’s previous state. This is a classic embedded pattern: when you cannot guarantee initial state, send a known sync sequence before starting the real protocol.

For backpacks, wrong I2C address is as common as contrast problems. Train students to run an I2C scanner before changing driver logic.

title: Week 11: Display Interfacing
text:
What makes a graphical LCD?



Pixel control: address individual pixels directly
Internal framebuffer: display RAM mirrors pixel state (e.g., 128×64 = 1 kB)
MCU role: write pixel data into the controller’s RAM over SPI or parallel bus
Examples: Nokia 5110 (PCD8544), ST7920 128×64, ST7735 color TFT

Framebuffer layout (page-addressed, 8 rows/page):
Page 0: [ cols 0-127 ] ← 8 pixel rows
Page 1: [ cols 0-127 ]
...
Page 7: [ cols 0-127 ]
Each byte = 8 pixels stacked vertically in one column of one page.




Graphical LCD module




The key concept shift from character LCD: you no longer tell the controller “print character A at position (2,1)”. Instead you manage a raw pixel buffer yourself and push it to the display. This gives full graphical freedom at the cost of more RAM and a more complex driver. The page addressing layout (bytes are vertical slices of 8 pixels) confuses everyone at first — draw it on the whiteboard: column 0 of page 0 is a byte whose bit 0 is the top-left pixel and bit 7 is the pixel 7 rows below it.

title: Week 11: Display Interfacing
text:
Nokia 5110 (PCD8544) highlights



Resolution: 84×48 pixels monochrome
Framebuffer: 84 × 48 / 8 = 504 bytes (easily fits in STM32F401 SRAM)
Interface: SPI — fewer pins than parallel
Voltage: Strictly 2.7–3.3 V logic — connecting 5 V logic directly will damage it

Pinout:



Pin
Name
Function




RST
Reset
Active low reset


CE / CS
Chip Enable
Active low, selects module


DC / A0
Data/Command
LOW = command, HIGH = data


DIN / MOSI
Data In
Serial data from MCU


CLK / SCLK
Clock
SPI clock from MCU


BL
Backlight
Optional LED control







Nokia 5110 LCD module




The 3.3 V logic constraint is the most important warning for this module. Many students have 5 V Arduinos or 5 V breadboard power rails and will fry the Nokia display immediately. On the STM32F401 Nucleo the 3.3 V MCU I/O is safe. Point out the 504-byte framebuffer: students can verify this by doing the arithmetic in their head, and it is a useful sanity check they should be able to perform for any display.

title: Week 11: Display Interfacing
Week 11: Display Interfacing
text:
Framebuffer strategies









Strategy
RAM cost
Code complexity
Best for




Static array
Full buffer always allocated
Low
Simple projects, enough RAM


Dynamic (malloc)
Freed when idle
Medium
Multi-mode apps


Dirty-page tracking
Full buffer + flags
High
Mostly-static UI, SPI bandwidth limited


Page-buffer (u8g2 style)
One page at a time
Medium
Very RAM-limited MCUs



For STM32F401 (96 kB SRAM):
A 1 kB OLED or 504 B Nokia framebuffer is trivial — use a static array. Optimization matters for color displays (40–150 kB) or RTOS stacks eating into available RAM.

The dirty-page strategy is the standard in production display drivers: keep a flag array of which 8-row pages have changed since the last display update, then only send the modified pages over SPI. For a mostly-static display showing sensor readings that change in one small area, this can cut SPI bandwidth by 90%. u8g2’s page-buffer approach is the opposite extreme: it renders into a 1-page buffer, sends it, renders the next page, etc. Minimal RAM but multiple render passes. For a lab with 96 kB of SRAM, just use a static array and move on.

title: Week 11: Display Interfacing

ST7920 128×64 dual-interface LCD



Resolution: 128×64 monochrome
Interface options:

Parallel (8080): 8 data pins + control signals — fast, many pins
Serial (SPI-like): CS, SID, SCLK — fewer pins, special start byte format

Internal GDRAM: 1 kB graphics RAM (128×64/8), split into two halves
Character mode: built-in ASCII + GB2312 fonts (like HD44780)

ST7920 128×64 module




The ST7920 is the display you often see in 3D printer control panels (Ender, Creality). Its “serial” mode is not quite standard SPI — it uses a specific start byte sequence (0xF8/0xFA/0xFC) before each data byte. Check the datasheet before wiring it up to a standard SPI peripheral. For new designs, serial mode is almost always the right choice — fewer traces, standard HAL_SPI calls once you handle the start byte.

title: Week 11: Display Interfacing
text:
OLED fundamentals


How it works: each pixel is an organic LED that emits its own light
Advantages:

True black: off pixels draw no current, unlimited contrast ratio
Wide viewing angle: consistent image from almost any angle
Fast pixel response: well-suited for animations
No backlight: lower power for predominantly dark content

Disadvantages:

Burn-in: static images degrade organic material over months/years — mitigate with screen savers, pixel shifting
Sunlight readability: washes out in direct bright light vs. transflective LCD
Blue pixel aging: blue channels degrade fastest





SSD1306 OLED module




The burn-in point is worth dwelling on: in a commercial product that shows a static logo or fixed UI element for years, OLED burn-in is a real warranty issue. Smart TV OLEDs implement pixel-shifting algorithms that move the image by 1–2 pixels periodically, invisible to the user but enough to prevent static burn. In a lab instrument that shows the same bar graph for 8 hours a day, rotating or briefly blanking the display matters.

title: Week 11: Display Interfacing
text:
SSD1306: key parameters



Parameter
Value




Resolution
128×64 or 128×32 pixels


Interface
I²C (2 wires) or SPI (3–4 wires)


I²C address
0x3C or 0x3D (selectable by jumper/resistor)


Logic voltage
3.3 V


MCU framebuffer
1 kB (128×64/8)


Current (full white)
~15–25 mA @ 3.3 V


Reset pin
Active low; connect to MCU GPIO for reliable startup



I²C vs SPI trade-off:

I²C: 2 data pins, shareable bus, max ~400 kHz (Fast mode) → ~3 FPS for full refresh
SPI: 3–4 dedicated pins, max 10 MHz → ~80 FPS for full refresh


The frame rate calculation is worth working out with students: a full 1024-byte framebuffer over I²C at 400 kHz (Fast mode) takes roughly 1024 × 9 bits ÷ 400 000 = ~23 ms per frame → ~43 FPS theoretical. In practice, HAL I2C overhead and the control byte overhead bring it closer to 30 FPS. Over SPI at 8 MHz you can do 1024 × 8 bits ÷ 8 000 000 = ~1 ms per frame → ~1000 FPS theoretical. For a lab sensor display at 10 FPS, I²C is perfectly fine.

title: Week 11: Display Interfacing
text:
SSD1306: I²C control byte
Every I²C write to SSD1306 starts with a control byte:



Bit 7 (Co)
Bit 6 (D/C#)
Meaning




0
0
Command — following bytes are commands


0
1
Data — following bytes go into GDDRAM (framebuffer)



// Send one command
uint8_t cmd_buf[2] = { 0x00, cmd };  // control byte 0x00 = command stream
HAL_I2C_Master_Transmit(&hi2c1, 0x3C << 1, cmd_buf, 2, HAL_MAX_DELAY);

// Send entire framebuffer (1024 bytes)
uint8_t data_buf[1025];
data_buf[0] = 0x40;                  // control byte 0x40 = data stream
memcpy(&data_buf[1], fb, 1024);
HAL_I2C_Master_Transmit(&hi2c1, 0x3C << 1, data_buf, 1025, HAL_MAX_DELAY);
Note: SPI uses a dedicated D/C GPIO pin instead of this control byte.

Students are sometimes confused that the “address” they pass to HAL_I2C_Master_Transmit is 0x3C << 1 = 0x78, even though the datasheet says 0x3C. Review the I2C address byte shift from Week 8: the datasheet gives the 7-bit address; HAL expects it pre-shifted left by one, and sets the R/W LSB itself. The 0x40 / 0x00 control byte pattern is unique to SSD1306; other I2C devices have different command framing.

title: Week 11: Display Interfacing
text:
SSD1306: initialization sequence (excerpt)
0xAE          Set Display OFF
0xD5, 0x80    Set display clock divide ratio / oscillator frequency
0xA8, 0x3F    Set multiplex ratio (0x3F = 64 lines)
0xD3, 0x00    Set display offset (0)
0x40          Set display start line to 0
0x8D, 0x14    Charge pump setting — enable internal charge pump
0x20, 0x00    Set memory addressing mode = Horizontal
0xA1          Set segment re-map (column 127 → segment 0)
0xC8          Set COM output scan direction (remapped)
0xDA, 0x12    Set COM pins hardware configuration
0x81, 0xCF    Set contrast control
0xD9, 0xF1    Set pre-charge period
0xDB, 0x40    Set V_COMH deselect level
0xA4          Entire display ON (resume from RAM)
0xA6          Set normal display (not inverted)
0xAF          Set Display ON
Initialization is mandatory — the display will not respond to data until fully configured.

Warn students not to memorize this sequence, but to copy it faithfully from a reference implementation (datasheet application note, or a trusted library init function). The most common error is forgetting to enable the charge pump (0x8D, 0x14): the OLED requires an internal voltage higher than VCC to drive the organic emitters, and without the charge pump the display simply stays blank. If students see nothing after init, charge pump is the first thing to check.

title: Week 11: Display Interfacing
text:
SSD1306: memory addressing modes
Set with command 0x20:









Mode
Code
Cursor behavior
Best use




Horizontal
0x00
Column++, wraps to next page automatically
Full framebuffer update


Vertical
0x01
Page++ within column, then next column
Rarely used


Page
0x02
Column++ within current page only, no auto-wrap
Partial/text update



Horizontal mode (recommended for full refresh):

Set column address range: 0x21, 0x00, 0x7F
Set page address range: 0x22, 0x00, 0x07
Send all 1024 bytes — controller auto-increments across the entire display


Horizontal addressing is the easiest to use for a full framebuffer push: set the window to the full display, then just dump all 1024 bytes. The controller handles all the address arithmetic. Page addressing is useful if you are only updating one line of text and want to avoid the overhead of sending 1024 bytes when only 128 bytes changed. For the lab, use horizontal mode — it is simpler and the throughput difference does not matter at 10 FPS.

GUI libraries: u8g2 and LVGL


u8g2 (Universal 8-bit Graphics Library)

Supports ~200 display controllers (LCD, OLED)
Optimized for low RAM: uses page-buffer approach
Rich font library (hundreds of fonts in multiple sizes)
Primarily monochrome
Porting: implement one byte transfer callback
Excellent for this course’s displays

u8g2_t u8g2;
u8g2_Setup_SSD1306_I2C_128X64_Noname_F_HW_I2C(
    &u8g2, U8G2_R0, U8X8_PIN_NONE, U8X8_PIN_NONE);
u8g2_InitDisplay(&u8g2);
u8g2_SetPowerSave(&u8g2, 0);
u8g2_ClearBuffer(&u8g2);
u8g2_SetFont(&u8g2, u8g2_font_ncenB08_tr);
u8g2_DrawStr(&u8g2, 0, 20, "Hello World");
u8g2_SendBuffer(&u8g2);

LVGL (Light and Versatile Graphics Library)

Feature-rich: animations, widgets, anti-aliasing, themes
Supports color displays
Minimum: ~32 kB RAM, higher Flash
Active community, good docs
Porting: implement disp_flush_cb() + input drivers

When to choose which:




u8g2
LVGL




RAM
<1 kB
≥32 kB


Display type
Mono
Mono + Color


Widget set
Basic
Full


Learning curve
Low
Medium



For this course: use u8g2 unless you need color.


u8g2 is the practical choice for everything in this course. Its page-buffer design means it can drive a 128×64 OLED with only ~128 bytes of working buffer — the library makes multiple passes over the display, rendering one page at a time and sending it. LVGL is the industry standard for color UI on STM32 + TFT displays (ST7789, ILI9341 family); it is worth knowing exists even if you don’t use it today.

Summary
Two display families, two mental models:









HD44780 character LCD
ST7789 TFT




Data unit
Character code / command
RGB565 pixel data / command


Interface
I2C backpack -> 4-bit HD44780
SPI + DC/RES


MCU RAM pressure
Very low
High for full frames


Timing risk
Enable pulse + command delays
SPI bandwidth + DMA state


Best for
Status text
Color UI, graphs



What to remember:

HD44780 bytes become two I2C-backed nibble transfers.
TFT frames are large: 240 x 240 x 2 = 115,200 bytes.
ST7789 drawing is command window first, pixel stream second.
DMA is what keeps TFT refresh from blocking the firmware.


End by contrasting abstractions: character LCDs render text for you; TFTs require you to think in pixels, windows, and bandwidth. Both are useful, but they impose very different firmware architecture constraints.

title: Week 11: Display Interfacing
text:
HD44780: driver flow





HD44780 4-bit driver flow



send_byte(byte, mode):
    RS = mode          # data or command
    send upper nibble to backpack
    I2C write: E high then E low
    send lower nibble to backpack
    I2C write: E high then E low
    wait for LCD to finish

print string:
    for each character:
        send_byte(character, DATA)

Key idea: the LCD never receives an 8-bit byte at once in 4-bit mode.
Every byte becomes two backpack writes, and each nibble is latched by an E pulse generated through I2C.

Keep this slide conceptual. Walk through the call chain before showing HAL implementation later.

text:
PCD8544: update flow


draw UI into framebuffer[504]
    |
    v
send command: X address = 0
    |
    v
send command: Y page = 0
    |
    v
DC = DATA, CS = LOW
    |
    v
SPI transmit framebuffer bytes 0..503
    |
    v
CS = HIGH

update_display():
    cmd(SET_X | 0)
    cmd(SET_Y | 0)

    DC = 1        # data mode
    CS = 0        # select display
    spi_write(framebuffer, 504)
    CS = 1        # release bus
Control signals

DC = 0: byte is a command
DC = 1: byte is pixel data
CS = 0: display listens
CS = 1: SPI bus released


Key idea: draw locally first, then push one contiguous framebuffer burst.

Use this slide to separate the algorithm from HAL syntax. The important sequence is: set the controller address back to the top-left, switch D/C into data mode, select the module, send the full 504-byte framebuffer, and release CS. The next slide shows the same algorithm in STM32 HAL calls.

title: Week 11: Display Interfacing
text:
TFT LCD technology



TFT (Thin-Film Transistor): active matrix LCD

Each pixel is controlled by its own transistor
Faster response and better contrast than passive LCDs

IPS (In-Plane Switching):

Wide viewing angles
Vibrant color reproduction

Controller (ST7789): built-in display RAM stores pixel data





TFT module / structure




Contrast this with the HD44780: the character LCD stores character codes and renders glyphs internally, while the TFT expects pixel color data. The controller has internal RAM, but the MCU still has to stream enough pixel data to create the image.

title: Week 11: Display Interfacing
text:
Pixels & color format: RGB565



Resolution: 240 x 240 grid

Total pixels: 57,600

Color depth: 16-bit (65,536 colors)
RGB565 format:

Red: 5 bits (32 shades)
Green: 6 bits (64 shades)
Blue: 5 bits (32 shades)

Green gets 6 bits because human vision is most sensitive to green detail





RGB565 memory layout




Have students calculate one full frame: 240 x 240 x 2 bytes = 115,200 bytes. That number motivates the DMA discussion.

title: Week 11: Display Interfacing
text:
Why SPI + DMA?


We use the ST7789 TFT driver.

Bandwidth challenge:

Resolution: 240 x 240 pixels
Color: 16-bit = 2 bytes per pixel
Frame size: \(240 \times 240 \times 2 = 115,200\) bytes

For 30 FPS:

Required traffic: \(115,200 \times 30 \approx 3.5\) MB/s
Conclusion: use MHz-range SPI and DMA






240x240 TFT module




Tie this back to firmware architecture: blocking SPI transfers make the CPU unavailable for sensing, control, logging, or RTOS tasks. DMA turns display refresh into a background transfer with a completion callback.

title: Week 11: Display Interfacing
text:
ST7789 pin interface


Standard 4-wire SPI interface:

MOSI (SDA): serial data, commands, and pixels
SCK (SCL): serial clock
RES (RST): hardware reset, active low
DC (WR): data/command selection

Low: command byte
High: data byte or pixel stream


No MISO: most small TFT modules are write-only in this lab setup.




Interfacing STM32F401 with ST7789




The DC signal is the key extra line compared with generic SPI peripherals. If DC is wrong, valid SPI bytes are interpreted in the wrong context.

ST7789 drawing protocol flow






Window and pixels concept




Stress the window concept. You do not always need to redraw the whole screen. You can set a small rectangle and stream only the pixels for that rectangle.

section: HD44780: initialization code matches the flow
text:
HD44780: initialization code matches the flow


extern I2C_HandleTypeDef hi2c1;
#define LCD_ADDR (0x27 << 1)   // try 0x3F if scanner finds it

static void lcd_write4(uint8_t nibble, bool is_data);
static void lcd_write4_raw(uint8_t nibble) {
    lcd_write4(nibble, false);  // command mode, one nibble only
}

void lcd_init(void) {
    HAL_Delay(20);                  // [1] VDD valid -> wait >15 ms

    lcd_write4_raw(0x03);           // [2] force known 8-bit startup state
    HAL_Delay(5);                   //     wait >4.1 ms
    lcd_write4_raw(0x03);
    HAL_Delay(1);                   //     wait >100 us
    lcd_write4_raw(0x03);
    HAL_Delay(1);                   //     wait >100 us

    lcd_write4_raw(0x02);           // [3] switch to 4-bit mode
    HAL_Delay(1);

    lcd_cmd(0x28);                  // [4] 4-bit, 2 lines, 5x8 font
    lcd_cmd(0x08);                  // [5] display off during setup
    lcd_cmd(0x01); HAL_Delay(2);    // [6] clear display: slow command
    lcd_cmd(0x06);                  // [7] cursor increments after write
    lcd_cmd(0x0C);                  // [8] display on, cursor off
}

Connect code to the flow

[1] Power reaches valid VDD
[2] Three startup sync nibbles over I2C
[3] Enter 4-bit interface
[4] Configure function
[5] Disable display while configuring
[6] Clear and wait long enough
[7] Set cursor behavior
[8] Turn display on

Important: lcd_cmd() works only after [3], because full bytes now mean two I2C-backed nibble writes.
lcd_cmd(x) is the command wrapper: lcd_send(x, false).


This is intentionally the same HD44780 sequence as before. The difference is physical transport: each nibble is encoded into a PCF8574 output byte and sent over I2C.

section: Bitmap fonts: a letter is just a pixel mask
text:
Bitmap fonts: a letter is just a pixel mask





7x10 font bitmap example




A font stores each character as a small bitmap
Example: Font_7x10 means 7 columns x 10 rows
Each row is stored as bits inside a uint16_t
A 1 bit means draw foreground color
A 0 bit means draw background color
Text drawing is repeated pixel drawing

Memory point: fonts live in Flash; only the active pixel stream uses RAM.


Connect this to HD44780. The HD44780 hides glyph rendering inside the LCD controller. The TFT does not. If we want text on a TFT, our firmware or library must convert font bitmap bits into RGB565 pixels.

Nucleo Pin       | Backpack Pin | Function

PB8 / D15        | SCL          | I2C1 clock
PB9 / D14        | SDA          | I2C1 data

PCF8574 I2C backpack module




The backpack is still a 4-bit HD44780 interface, but students do not wire D4-D7, RS, or E directly to the MCU. The PCF8574 writes those LCD pins on behalf of the MCU. Address scanning is a practical first debug step because modules commonly ship as 0x27 or 0x3F.

title: Week 11: Display Interfacing
text:
Week 11
Display Interfacing: Character LCD and TFT Displays

This revised deck focuses on two practical display classes students are likely to wire in lab projects: HD44780 character LCDs for simple status output and ST7789 TFT modules for color graphical interfaces. Keep the comparison practical: the character LCD is low-resource and slow but robust; the TFT is flexible and visual but demands bandwidth, careful protocol sequencing, and usually DMA.

title: Week 11: Display Interfacing
text:
Why this week matters

Visual feedback turns a sensor into an instrument
Character LCDs are still useful for simple status and debug panels
TFT displays make embedded systems feel like products, not demos
Display selection directly impacts RAM, pins, SPI bandwidth, and CPU load
Display bugs are usually visible, but the cause is often timing or protocol order


Use concrete examples: a bench instrument can use a 16x2 LCD for voltage/current readout, while a motor controller or sensor dashboard may need color graphs on a TFT. The main engineering theme is observability under resource constraints.

title: Week 11: Display Interfacing
text:
Learning objectives

Wire and drive an HD44780 character LCD through an I2C backpack
Explain how the I2C backpack creates HD44780 4-bit nibble transfers
Diagnose common character LCD address, wiring, contrast, and initialization failures
Explain TFT pixels, RGB565 color format, and framebuffer size
Describe the ST7789 command/data protocol over SPI
Explain how bitmap fonts become pixel streams on a TFT
Explain why TFT refresh usually needs high-speed SPI and DMA


The assessment emphasis should be practical: students should be able to explain why the LCD receives two nibbles per byte, calculate TFT frame size, and identify why TFT updates become a bandwidth problem.

title: Week 11: Display Interfacing
text:
HD44780 character LCD overview



The workhorse: still common, cheap, and robust
Text only — displays from internal CGROM (5x8 dot matrix per character)
Up to 8 user-defined 5x8 glyphs in CGRAM (bar graphs, simple icons)
Supply voltage: 2.7-5.5 V; logic often 5 V — check clones for 3.3 V tolerance
Backlight: LED, typically 15-30 mA; check if series resistor is included
Contrast: analog voltage on VO pin via 10 kΩ pot

Common pitfall: incorrect VO makes display appear blank or show solid blocks.




16x2 Character LCD




Hold up a physical HD44780 module if available. Point out the 16-pin header at the top. The contrast potentiometer issue bites almost every student on first use: they power it on and see nothing, or see solid black rectangles. The fix is simply to turn the pot before rewiring everything.

title: Week 11: Display Interfacing
text:
HD44780: I2C backpack wiring


Nucleo Pin       | Backpack Pin | Function
-----------------|--------------|-----------------------
PB8 / D15        | SCL          | I2C1 clock
PB9 / D14        | SDA          | I2C1 data
GND              | GND          | Common ground
3V3 or 5V*       | VCC          | Backpack + LCD power
Pot on backpack  | VO           | Contrast adjustment

Backpack usually uses PCF8574 I/O expander
Common address: 0x27; some modules use 0x3F
Backpack drives RS, E, and D4-D7 internally
If powered at 5 V, verify SDA/SCL voltage safety or use a level shifter





PCF8574 I2C backpack module




The backpack is still a 4-bit HD44780 interface, but students do not wire D4-D7, RS, or E directly to the MCU. The PCF8574 writes those LCD pins on behalf of the MCU. Address scanning is a practical first debug step because modules commonly ship as 0x27 or 0x3F.

title: Week 11: Display Interfacing
section: HD44780 pins: what the backpack hides
text:
HD44780 pins: what the backpack hides





HD44780 pin functions



LCD pins still matter
The I2C backpack is soldered to the 16-pin LCD header and drives these LCD signals internally:



LCD signal
Backpack role




RS
command/data select


E
latch each nibble


D4-D7
4-bit data bus


RW
usually tied low


VO
contrast pot


A/K
backlight power



Student wiring: connect only SDA, SCL, VCC, and GND to the backpack.


Use this slide to preserve the pin-label visual while preventing direct-wiring confusion. The students should understand that the HD44780 still has RS, E, and D4-D7, but the backpack owns those connections.

title: Week 11: Display Interfacing
text:
HD44780: critical timing
The E (Enable) pulse still clocks data into the controller

Data is latched on the falling edge of E
With the backpack, E is toggled by I2C writes to the PCF8574
I2C is slower than the E minimum pulse width, but the LCD execution delay still matters
Most commands: ~37 us execution time
ClearDisplay and ReturnHome: ~1.53 ms — use HAL_Delay(2) after these


HD44780 Enable pulse timingDelay rule for this lab:
Use fixed delays after writes; add HAL_Delay(2) after ClearDisplay and ReturnHome.

Students often ask why I2C timing is not enough by itself. I2C makes the external E pulse slow enough, but it does not make the HD44780 finish internal commands faster. Fixed delays are still the required approach.

title: Week 11: Display Interfacing
text:
HD44780: power-on initialization (4-bit mode)





HD44780 initialization flow



Exact command sequence
wait >15 ms after VDD valid

0x30, wait >4.1 ms
0x30, wait >100 us
0x30, wait >100 us

0x20  -> 4-bit mode
0x28  -> 4-bit, 2 lines, 5x8
0x08  -> display off
0x01  -> clear, wait >2 ms
0x06  -> increment cursor
0x0C  -> display on

Key takeaway: initialization is rigid. Miss one step and nothing works.

The triple 0x30 sequence guarantees the interface mode regardless of the controller’s previous state. This is a classic embedded pattern: when you cannot guarantee initial state, send a known sync sequence before starting the real protocol.

title: Week 11: Display Interfacing
section: HD44780: initialization code matches the flow
text:
HD44780: initialization code matches the flow


extern I2C_HandleTypeDef hi2c1;
#define LCD_ADDR (0x27 << 1)   // try 0x3F if scanner finds it

static void lcd_write4(uint8_t nibble, bool is_data);
static void lcd_write4_raw(uint8_t nibble) {
    lcd_write4(nibble, false);  // command mode, one nibble only
}

void lcd_init(void) {
    HAL_Delay(20);                  // [1] VDD valid -> wait >15 ms

    lcd_write4_raw(0x03);           // [2] force known 8-bit startup state
    HAL_Delay(5);                   //     wait >4.1 ms
    lcd_write4_raw(0x03);
    HAL_Delay(1);                   //     wait >100 us
    lcd_write4_raw(0x03);
    HAL_Delay(1);                   //     wait >100 us

    lcd_write4_raw(0x02);           // [3] switch to 4-bit mode
    HAL_Delay(1);

    lcd_cmd(0x28);                  // [4] 4-bit, 2 lines, 5x8 font
    lcd_cmd(0x08);                  // [5] display off during setup
    lcd_cmd(0x01); HAL_Delay(2);    // [6] clear display: slow command
    lcd_cmd(0x06);                  // [7] cursor increments after write
    lcd_cmd(0x0C);                  // [8] display on, cursor off
}

Connect code to the flow

[1] Power reaches valid VDD
[2] Three startup sync nibbles over I2C
[3] Enter 4-bit interface
[4] Configure function
[5] Disable display while configuring
[6] Clear and wait long enough
[7] Set cursor behavior
[8] Turn display on

Important: lcd_cmd() works only after [3], because full bytes now mean two I2C-backed nibble writes.
lcd_cmd(x) is the command wrapper: lcd_send(x, false).


This is intentionally the same HD44780 sequence as before. The difference is physical transport: each nibble is encoded into a PCF8574 output byte and sent over I2C.

title: Week 11: Display Interfacing
text:
HD44780: driver flow





HD44780 4-bit driver flow



send_byte(byte, mode):
    RS = mode          # data or command
    send upper nibble to backpack
    I2C write: E high then E low
    send lower nibble to backpack
    I2C write: E high then E low
    wait for LCD to finish

print string:
    for each character:
        send_byte(character, DATA)

Key idea: the LCD never receives an 8-bit byte at once in 4-bit mode.
Every byte becomes two backpack writes, and each nibble is latched by an E pulse generated through I2C.

Keep this slide conceptual. Walk through the call chain before showing HAL implementation later.

title: Week 11: Display Interfacing
text:
HD44780: troubleshooting








Symptom
Most likely cause
Fix




Blank display
Contrast VO wrong
Adjust pot; check power


No response at all
Wrong I2C address
Run scanner; try 0x27 or 0x3F


Scanner finds nothing
SDA/SCL swapped, no power, no pullups
Check wiring and voltage


Solid black blocks on top row
Contrast too low, init failed
Turn pot; verify init sequence


Garbled / ghost characters
Timing violation or backpack bit mapping mismatch
Check PCF8574 mapping


Display works once then freezes
Missing delay after ClearDisplay
Add HAL_Delay(2) after 0x01



Tool of choice: scope SCL/SDA first; if accessible, probe E on the backpack output.

For backpacks, wrong I2C address is as common as contrast problems. Train students to run an I2C scanner before changing driver logic.

title: Week 11: Display Interfacing
text:
TFT LCD technology



TFT (Thin-Film Transistor): active matrix LCD

Each pixel is controlled by its own transistor
Faster response and better contrast than passive LCDs

IPS (In-Plane Switching):

Wide viewing angles
Vibrant color reproduction

Controller (ST7789): built-in display RAM stores pixel data





TFT module / structure




Contrast this with the HD44780: the character LCD stores character codes and renders glyphs internally, while the TFT expects pixel color data. The controller has internal RAM, but the MCU still has to stream enough pixel data to create the image.

title: Week 11: Display Interfacing
text:
Pixels & color format: RGB565



Resolution: 240 x 240 grid

Total pixels: 57,600

Color depth: 16-bit (65,536 colors)
RGB565 format:

Red: 5 bits (32 shades)
Green: 6 bits (64 shades)
Blue: 5 bits (32 shades)

Green gets 6 bits because human vision is most sensitive to green detail





RGB565 memory layout




Have students calculate one full frame: 240 x 240 x 2 bytes = 115,200 bytes. That number motivates the DMA discussion.

title: Week 11: Display Interfacing
text:
Why SPI + DMA?


We use the ST7789 TFT driver.

Bandwidth challenge:

Resolution: 240 x 240 pixels
Color: 16-bit = 2 bytes per pixel
Frame size: \(240 \times 240 \times 2 = 115,200\) bytes

For 30 FPS:

Required traffic: \(115,200 \times 30 \approx 3.5\) MB/s
Conclusion: use MHz-range SPI and DMA






240x240 TFT module




Tie this back to firmware architecture: blocking SPI transfers make the CPU unavailable for sensing, control, logging, or RTOS tasks. DMA turns display refresh into a background transfer with a completion callback.

title: Week 11: Display Interfacing
text:
ST7789 pin interface


Standard 4-wire SPI interface:

MOSI (SDA): serial data, commands, and pixels
SCK (SCL): serial clock
RES (RST): hardware reset, active low
DC (WR): data/command selection

Low: command byte
High: data byte or pixel stream


No MISO: most small TFT modules are write-only in this lab setup.




Interfacing STM32F401 with ST7789




The DC signal is the key extra line compared with generic SPI peripherals. If DC is wrong, valid SPI bytes are interpreted in the wrong context.

title: Week 11: Display Interfacing
text:
ST7789 drawing protocol





ST7789 drawing protocol flow






Window and pixels concept




Stress the window concept. You do not always need to redraw the whole screen. You can set a small rectangle and stream only the pixels for that rectangle.

title: Week 11: Display Interfacing
section: ST7789 driver layers: what the library hides
text:
ST7789 driver layers: what the library hides









Public call
Driver work underneath




ST7789_Init()
reset, sleep out, set RGB565, display on


ST7789_FillScreen(color)
call FillRect() for 240 x 240


ST7789_FillRect(x,y,w,h,color)
set window, stream repeated RGB565 pixels


ST7789_WriteString(...)
draw characters one bitmap at a time



Mental model: application code requests shapes/text; the driver converts that request into command bytes, address windows, and pixel bytes.

application
  ST7789_WriteString()
  ST7789_FillRect()

driver API
  SetWindow()
  WriteCommand()
  WriteData()

hardware transfer
  DC pin selects command/data
  SPI sends bytes
  DMA moves pixel buffers

display controller
  GRAM stores pixels


This slide bridges the lab library and the previous protocol slide. Emphasize that students do not need to memorize every ST7789 command; they need to understand what the driver is doing on their behalf.

title: Week 11: Display Interfacing
section: Bitmap fonts: a letter is just a pixel mask
text:
Bitmap fonts: a letter is just a pixel mask





7x10 font bitmap example




A font stores each character as a small bitmap
Example: Font_7x10 means 7 columns x 10 rows
Each row is stored as bits inside a uint16_t
A 1 bit means draw foreground color
A 0 bit means draw background color
Text drawing is repeated pixel drawing

Memory point: fonts live in Flash; only the active pixel stream uses RAM.


Connect this to HD44780. The HD44780 hides glyph rendering inside the LCD controller. The TFT does not. If we want text on a TFT, our firmware or library must convert font bitmap bits into RGB565 pixels.

TFT failure modes and checks








Symptom
Likely cause
What to check




White/blank screen

RES timing, Sleep Out, Display On

Pixel buffer endianness

Measurement evidence: capture SCK/MOSI/DC during one window update and measure transfer time.

Use this slide as the practical checklist. The TFT is less forgiving than the character LCD because there are more state transitions: reset, init commands, address window, RAM write, pixel stream.

title: Week 11: Display Interfacing
text:
Summary
Two display families, two mental models:









HD44780 character LCD
ST7789 TFT




Data unit
Character code / command
RGB565 pixel data / command


Interface
I2C backpack -> 4-bit HD44780
SPI + DC/RES


MCU RAM pressure
Very low
High for full frames


Timing risk
Enable pulse + command delays
SPI bandwidth + DMA state


Best for
Status text
Color UI, graphs



What to remember:

HD44780 bytes become two I2C-backed nibble transfers.
TFT frames are large: 240 x 240 x 2 = 115,200 bytes.
ST7789 drawing is command window first, pixel stream second.
DMA is what keeps TFT refresh from blocking the firmware.


End by contrasting abstractions: character LCDs render text for you; TFTs require you to think in pixels, windows, and bandwidth. Both are useful, but they impose very different firmware architecture constraints.
